# @ratmath/structures 0.5.0: full documentation

> Abstract algebra for RatMath: finite groups, exact polynomials in several variables, Gröbner bases, ideals, quotient rings, polynomial systems solved exactly, the integers mod n and quadratic integer rings, presentations, abelian groups and modules over Q[x]. From https://ratmath.com/structures/, commit de6732b. Each page ends with a runnable example; in it, PRINT(...) prints.


---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/index.html

@ratmath/structures

## Groups, rings and polynomials, held exactly

A JavaScript library for abstract algebra. Finite groups with their subgroups, quotients, Sylow subgroups, homomorphisms and actions. Polynomials in several variables with exact coefficients, their greatest common divisors, factors and resultants. Ideals and Gröbner bases, quotient rings, and systems of polynomial equations solved exactly. The integers mod n and quadratic integer rings with their ideals and class groups. Character tables with exact entries. Field extensions with their Galois groups, formulas in radicals, and what ruler and compass can reach. Nothing is rounded, so two answers are equal exactly when they print the same.

### Groups

A group is a set with an associative product, an identity, and inverses: the symmetries of a shape, the shuffles of a deck, the invertible matrices over a finite field. This library holds a finite group by listing its elements, so everything a course asks of a group of up to a few thousand elements can be computed outright and checked: its conjugacy classes and centre, every subgroup and which are normal, quotients, Sylow subgroups, whether two groups are isomorphic, and the orbits of an action, with the orbit-counting lemma for colourings up to symmetry.

```js
import { symmetric, dihedral, quaternion, isIsomorphic, identify, PSL, alternating } from "@ratmath/structures";

const S = symmetric(4);
String(S.classEquation());                 // "24 = 1 + 3 + 6 + 6 + 8"
S.normalSubgroups().map((N) => N.order);  // [1, 4, 12, 24]
[2, 3].map((p) => S.sylowCount(p));       // [3, 4]
identify(S.sylowSubgroup(2)).name;         // "D4"
isIsomorphic(dihedral(4), quaternion());   // false
isIsomorphic(PSL(2, 5), alternating(5));   // true
dihedral(6).natural.onColourings(2).countOrbits().count;   // 13 bracelets with 6 beads in 2 colours
```

### Polynomials

A polynomial in several variables is a finite sum of terms, each a coefficient times a product of powers of the variables: x2y−23​xz+1. The polynomials in fixed variables with coefficients in a field K form a ring, written K[x,y,z]: they can be added, subtracted and multiplied, and sometimes divided.

This library holds such a polynomial as the list of its nonzero terms, with every coefficient exact (a fraction of whole numbers by default). The coefficients can instead come from any exact field in RatMath: the integers modulo a prime, a finite field GF(pᵏ), or a number field such as Q(√2).

`@ratmath/structures` is the abstract algebra package of the [RatMath Shelf](https://ratmath.com/shelf/). Representations beyond characters are planned for the same package.

### Ideals and equations

A system of polynomial equations generates an [ideal](https://ratmath.com/structures/ideals.html): everything that follows from the equations by adding and multiplying. A [Gröbner basis](https://ratmath.com/structures/groebner.html) of the ideal makes questions about the system mechanical. Does this equation follow from those? Are there solutions, and how many? What is left after eliminating a variable? When there are finitely many solutions, [solve](https://ratmath.com/structures/systems.html) finds all of them as exact algebraic numbers.

```js
import { ring, ideal, solve } from "@ratmath/structures";

const R = ring("x, y");
const I = ideal(R, ["x^2 + y^2 - 5", "x y - 2"]);
I.basis.map(String);                       // the reduced Gröbner basis
I.contains("x^4 - 5 x^2 + 4");             // true: it follows from the two equations
I.solve().real.map(String);                // ["(x = -2, y = -1)", "(x = -1, y = -2)", "(x = 1, y = 2)", "(x = 2, y = 1)"]
const A = I.quotientRing();                // Q[x, y]/I: arithmetic modulo the equations
```

### Rings of numbers

The [integers mod n](https://ratmath.com/structures/modular.html) show units, zero divisors, idempotents and the Chinese remainder theorem in a ring small enough to list. [Quadratic integer rings](https://ratmath.com/structures/quadratic.html) such as Z[i] and Z[−5​] show what happens to prime factorisation when a square root is adjoined: sometimes it survives, sometimes 6=2⋅3=(1+−5​)(1−−5​), and then ideals and the class group take over.

### Fields

A [tower of field extensions](https://ratmath.com/structures/towers.html) is built one root at a time, and its [automorphisms](https://ratmath.com/structures/galois.html) match subgroups with the fields in between. The Galois group of a polynomial decides whether it can be [solved by radicals](https://ratmath.com/structures/radicals.html), and when it can the formula is produced and checked; the same theory says which regular polygons [ruler and compass](https://ratmath.com/structures/constructions.html) can draw. [Conway polynomials](https://ratmath.com/structures/conway.html) give the finite fields a standard form, and [Schreier–Sims](https://ratmath.com/structures/large-groups.html) handles permutation groups far too large to list.

### A first program

```js
import { ring, gcd, factor, resultant, fractions } from "@ratmath/structures";

const R = ring("x, y, z");                    // the ring Q[x, y, z]
const f = R.poly("x^3 + y^3 + z^3 - 3xyz");
String(f);                                    // "x³ + y³ − 3xyz + z³"
factor(f).factors.map((t) => String(t.factor));
                                              // ["x + y + z", "x² − xy + y² − xz − yz + z²"]
String(gcd(R.poly("x^3 - y^3"), R.poly("x^2 - y^2")));   // "x − y"
String(resultant(R.poly("x^2 + y^2 - 1"), R.poly("y - x^2"), "y"));
                                              // "x⁴ + x² − 1": where the circle meets the parabola
const F = fractions(R);                       // the field Q(x, y, z)
String(F.parse("1/(x + y) + 1/(x - y)"));     // "2x/(x² − y²)"
```

Text is read the way it is written on paper: `3xy^2`, `(x + 1)(x - 1)`, `1.25 x`, `2/3 y`. Numbers are exact, so 0.1 is one tenth.

### What is in it

- Named groups: cyclic, dihedral, dicyclic and quaternion, symmetric and alternating, GL, SL and PSL over Fp​, Heisenberg groups, direct and semidirect products, groups from a table or any multiplication.

- Inside a group: Cayley tables, element orders, conjugacy classes and the class equation, centre, centralisers, normalisers, commutators, derived and central series, solvable, nilpotent and simple tests.

- Subgroups: every subgroup and its conjugacy class, normal subgroups, cosets, quotients, composition series, Sylow subgroups.

- Maps: homomorphisms with kernels and images, the isomorphism theorems, isomorphism tests, automorphism groups, and the groups of order up to 20 by name.

- Actions: orbits, stabilisers, fixed points, and the orbit-counting lemma for necklaces and coloured solids.

- Presentations: groups from generators and relations, built by Todd–Coxeter coset enumeration.

- Abelian groups and modules: the Smith normal form over the integers and over Q[x], the structure theorem, invariant factors and elementary divisors, and the rational canonical form of a matrix.

- Polynomial rings over Q or any exact field, with the monomial orders lex, grlex and grevlex or one of your own.

- Arithmetic and calculus: sums, products, powers, partial derivatives, gradients, substitution, evaluation, change of variables.

- Division by one polynomial or by a list of them, with quotients and remainder.

- Greatest common divisors, least common multiples, contents, square-free parts.

- Factoring into irreducible polynomials over the rationals.

- Determinants, resultants and discriminants of polynomials, plus Jacobians and Hessians.

- Rational functions: the field of fractions, usable as the entries of a matrix with parameters.

- Gröbner bases by Buchberger's algorithm over any exact field, with certificates: any member of an ideal written out in terms of the generators.

- Ideals: membership, sums, products, intersections, quotients, saturation, elimination, radicals, dimension, prime and maximal tests.

- Polynomial systems solved exactly: every solution with its multiplicity, coordinates as algebraic numbers.

- Quotient rings with inverses, zero divisors, nilpotents, minimal polynomials, and the Chinese remainder theorem.

- The integers mod n: units, zero divisors, idempotents, ideals, the unit group, primitive roots.

- Quadratic integer rings: units and Pell's equation, Euclidean division, every factorisation of an element, prime ideals, class groups.

- Symmetric polynomials: the elementary ones, power sums, and rewriting any symmetric polynomial in terms of them.

### Topics

Each topic page explains the mathematics and lets you run it. [Explore](https://ratmath.com/structures/explore.html) is a free-form calculator for all of it; [Reference](https://ratmath.com/structures/reference.html) lists every function.

### Install

```js
bun add github:ratmath/structures    # depends on @ratmath/core and @ratmath/algebraic
```

The library is pure JavaScript with BigInt arithmetic and no floating point anywhere.

### Try it

```js
const S = symmetric(4);
PRINT(S.describe());
PRINT("class equation:", S.classEquation(), "  Sylow counts:", [2, 3].map((p) => S.sylowCount(p)));

const R = ring("x, y, z");
const f = R.poly("x^3 + y^3 + z^3 - 3xyz");
PRINT("f =", f);
for (const { factor: g, multiplicity } of factor(f).factors) PRINT("  factor:", g, "to the power", multiplicity);
PRINT("gcd:", gcd(R.poly("x^3 - y^3"), R.poly("x^2 - y^2")));
PRINT("circle and parabola meet where", resultant(R.poly("x^2 + y^2 - 1"), R.poly("y - x^2"), "y"), "= 0");
fractions(R).parse("1/(x + y) + 1/(x - y)")
```

Reference

## Everything in the library

Every export of `@ratmath/structures`: groups first, then polynomials, ideals and rings of numbers. Group elements are given by value or by their printed label. Coefficients handed back to you are Core Rationals over Q, and the field's own elements otherwise. Wherever a polynomial is expected, text or a number is accepted too.

| Function | What it does |

| Named groups and products |

| cyclic(n), dihedral(n), dicyclic(n), quaternion(), kleinFour() | Cₙ (elements are exponents k, printed aᵏ); Dₙ of order 2n, the symmetries of an n-gon (pairs [k, f] = rᵏsᶠ); the dicyclic group of order 4n; Q₈ printed ±1, ±i, ±j, ±k; C₂ × C₂. |

| symmetric(n), alternating(n), permutationGroup(gens, n), fromPermGroup(P) | Permutation groups. Generators are arrays (p[i] the image of i, from 0) or cycle notation from 1 such as "(1 2 3)(4 5)". mul(a, b) is a∘b: first b, then a. G.toPermGroup() gives algebraic&#x27;s PermGroup. |

| GL(n, p), SL(n, p), PSL(n, p), heisenberg(p), matrixGroup(gens, p) | Matrix groups over F_p for a prime p: matrices of whole numbers 0 … p−1. PSL is SL modulo its centre; its elements are cosets. |

| directProduct(G, H, …), semidirectProduct(N, H, act), metacyclic(m, k, r) | G × H on tuples; N ⋊ H with act(h) the automorphism of N that h gives (checked); Cₘ ⋊ Cₖ with the generator acting by x ↦ xʳ. |

| Group.generate({ generators, mul, identity, key, format, name }), Group.fromElements(list, mul), Group.fromTable(table, { labels }) | Any group: from generators and a multiplication (key tells elements apart, default JSON), from a list of all elements, or from a multiplication table (axioms checked). |

| G.natural | The named groups&#x27; own action: polygon vertices, the points 1 … n, or the vectors of F_pⁿ. |

| PermGroup, cycleString, fromCycles, cycleType | Re-exported from @ratmath/algebraic, where Galois groups are computed. |

| sign(p, n?), isEven, isOdd, inversions | The sign of one permutation (an array of 0-based images, or cycle text such as "(1 2 3 4)" with n points): 1 even, −1 odd; inversions counts out-of-order pairs. |

| Elements |

| G.elements, G.order, G.identity, G.generators, G.name | All elements (identity first), their number, the identity, a generating list, the name. |

| G.mul(a, b, …), G.inv(x), G.pow(x, k), G.conjugate(x, g), G.commutator(a, b) | Products left to right; inverse; powers (negative too); gxg⁻¹; [a, b] = a⁻¹b⁻¹ab. Elements may be given by value or by printed label ("r²s", "r^2 s", "(1 2)", "-i"). |

| G.element(x), G.has(x), G.indexOf(x), G.format(x), G.key(x) | The element for a value or label; membership; its element number; how it prints; its key. |

| G.elementOrder(x), G.orderStatistics(), G.exponent | The order of x; a Map order → how many elements; the lcm of the orders. |

| G.cayleyTable({ order }) | { labels, elements, table } with table[i][j] the position of the product; String(…) prints the grid. |

| G.isAbelian, G.isCyclic, G.isPGroup, G.isTrivial | Tests. |

| G.describe(), String(G) | A one-line summary; the name, or ⟨generators⟩. |

| Classes, centre, commutators |

| G.conjugacyClasses() | [{ representative, elements, indices, size, order }], identity first; size·\|C(x)\| = \|G\|. |

| G.classEquation() | { order, centre, terms } printing as "24 = 1 + 3 + 6 + 6 + 8". |

| G.centre(), G.centraliser(x or list or H), G.normaliser(H) | Z(G); the elements commuting with x (or with all of a list or subgroup); the g with gHg⁻¹ = H. US spellings center, centralizer, normalizer work too. |

| G.derivedSubgroup(), G.commutatorOf(H, K), G.normalClosure(list) | G′ = [G, G]; [H, K]; the smallest normal subgroup containing some elements. |

| G.derivedSeries(), G.lowerCentralSeries(), G.upperCentralSeries() | Lists of subgroups, until they stop. |

| G.isSolvable, G.isNilpotent, G.nilpotencyClass, G.isSimple, G.isPerfect | Tests; the class is null for a group that is not nilpotent. |

| Subgroups and quotients |

| G.subgroup(gens), G.trivialSubgroup() | The subgroup generated by some elements; {e}. A subgroup is a Group with G as its parent. |

| G.subgroups({ maxOrder }), G.subgroupClasses() | Every subgroup, smallest first (groups up to order 1000 by default); the subgroups up to conjugacy: [{ group, order, index, conjugates, normal, members }]. |

| G.normalSubgroups(), G.isNormal(H), G.conjugateSubgroup(H, g) | All normal subgroups (built from classes, no need to list every subgroup); normality; gHg⁻¹. |

| G.isSubgroup(H), H.equals(K), G.contains(H), G.index(H) | Subgroup test; same elements; containment; [G : H]. |

| G.intersection(H, K), G.join(H, K, …), G.product(H, K) | H ∩ K; the subgroup generated by both; the set HK as a list. |

| G.cosets(H, { side }) | Left (or right) cosets: [{ representative, elements, indices }]. |

| G.quotient(N) | G/N for normal N; elements are Cosets printed gN. Q.cosetOf(x), Q.over, Q.normal. |

| G.compositionSeries() | { series, factors } with factors the orders of the simple quotients. |

| Sylow subgroups |

| G.sylowSubgroup(p), G.sylowSubgroups(p), G.sylowCount(p) | One Sylow p-subgroup (order the largest power of p dividing \|G\|); all of them, as conjugates; their number n_p = [G : N(P)]. |

| Homomorphisms and isomorphism |

| homomorphism(G, H, f), tryHomomorphism(G, H, f) | A homomorphism from a function on elements, a list of images of G.generators, or a Map from generating elements to images. Throws (or returns null) when the images do not respect G&#x27;s relations. |

| f.apply(x), f.kernel(), f.image(), f.preimage(K), f.then(g), f.inverse() | Images; ker f (normal in the source); im f; f⁻¹(K); first f then g; the inverse of an isomorphism. |

| f.isInjective, f.isSurjective, f.isIsomorphism, f.table | Tests; the images of all element numbers. |

| identityMap(G), trivialMap(G, H), inclusion(H, G), projection(Q) | Standard maps; projection(G.quotient(N)) is x ↦ xN. |

| firstIsomorphism(f), secondIsomorphism(G, H, N), thirdIsomorphism(G, N, K) | The three isomorphism theorems on an example: the quotients involved and a checked isomorphism between them. |

| isomorphism(G, H), isIsomorphic(G, H) | An isomorphism or null (invariants first, then a pruned search over images of generators); its existence. |

| automorphisms(G), automorphismGroup(G), innerAutomorphism(G, g) | Every automorphism; Aut(G) as a group with .inner = Inn(G); x ↦ gxg⁻¹. |

| smallGroups(n), numberOfGroups(n), identify(G), SMALL_ORDER_LIMIT | One group of each isomorphism type for n ≤ 20, named; how many; { name, group, iso } for a group of order ≤ 20 (null above). |

| Actions |

| action(G, points, act, { key, format, check }) | G acting on a list of points by act(g, x). Checked to be an action. |

| regularAction(G), conjugationAction(G), cosetAction(G, H) | G on itself by left multiplication; by conjugation; on the left cosets of H. |

| A.orbit(x), A.orbits(), A.stabiliser(x), A.fixedPoints(g), A.apply(g, x), A.permutation(g) | Orbits, stabilisers (subgroups of G), fixed points, images, and g as a permutation of point numbers. |

| A.kernel(), A.isTransitive, A.isFaithful, A.isFree | The elements fixing every point; tests. |

| A.countOrbits(), burnside(A) | The orbit-counting lemma: { count, total, order, byClass }, printing the sum class by class; checked against the orbits. |

| A.onColourings(k or colours), A.onSubsets(k) | The induced actions on colourings of the points and on k-element subsets. |

| A.toPermGroup() | The image of G as algebraic&#x27;s PermGroup on point numbers, for @ratmath/discrete&#x27;s cycleIndex, countColourings and patternInventory. |

| Presentations |

| presentation("a, b \| a^4, b^2, (ab)^2"), presentation(names, relators) | A presentation. Relators are words or relations u = v; words read a^2 b^-1, a²b⁻¹, (ab)^3, [a, b] = a⁻¹b⁻¹ab, and A for a⁻¹. Angle brackets are optional. |

| P.order(), P.index(H), P.enumerate(H, { maxCosets }) | Todd–Coxeter coset enumeration of the right cosets of the subgroup generated by the words H: { index, table, inverseTable, representatives, cosetOfWord }. Throws past maxCosets (500,000), as an infinite index does. |

| P.toGroup() | The finite group as a Group, elements printed as shortest words; G.fromWord(w) gives the element of a word. |

| P.abelianInvariants(), abelianInvariants(G or P) | G/G′ as an AbelianGroup; works for infinite presentations. |

| presentationOf(G) | A presentation of a finite Group (Schreier&#x27;s method: one relator per Cayley graph edge outside a spanning tree). |

| parseWord(text, names), formatWord(w, names), reduceWord(w), invertWord(w) | Words as arrays: k for generator k (from 1), −k for its inverse. |

| Abelian groups |

| fromRelations(rows, n), integerModule(rows, n) | Zⁿ modulo the rows: an AbelianGroup, with .generators saying how each cyclic factor is made from the original generators. |

| abelianGroup(invariants, rank), cyclicProduct(orders, rank) | From invariant factors d₁ \| d₂ \| …; from any cyclic orders (0 for Z), put into standard form. |

| A.invariants, A.rank, A.order, A.elementaryDivisors, A.torsion, A.exponent | The structure: invariant factors (BigInts), number of copies of Z, order (null if infinite), prime-power factors. |

| A.isFinite, A.isCyclic, A.isTrivial, A.equals(B), A.times(B), A.toGroup(), String(A) | Tests, comparison, products, the finite group as a Group, and "Z/2 × Z/12 × Z^2" (toString({ primary: true }) by elementary divisors). |

| abelianGroups(n) | One of each abelian group of order n. |

| smithForm(A, domain), ZZ, polynomialDomain("x") | Smith normal form { D, U, V, Vinv, diagonal, rank } with U·A·V = D over the integers or Q[x] (or any Euclidean domain object). |

| Chain complexes and homology |

| chainComplex([∂1, ∂2, …], { sizes }) | A ChainComplex from boundary matrices (∂k: a row per (k−1)-cell, a column per k-cell); checks ∂∂ = 0. sizes gives the cell counts where a map is empty. |

| C.homology(k, { coefficients }), C.homologyGroups(), C.reducedHomology(k) | H_k as an AbelianGroup over Z (with torsion), or a vector space { dimension } over "Q" or "Z/p". |

| C.betti({ coefficients }), C.torsion, C.eulerCharacteristic, C.sizes | Betti numbers, torsion of each H_k, χ = Σ(−1)^k n_k, cells per dimension. |

| C.invariantFactors(k), C.rank(k, p), C.boundary(k), String(C) | Smith invariants and rank of ∂k (mod p when given), the matrix, and "H0 = Z, H1 = Z/2, H2 = 0". |

| Modules over Q[x] |

| matrixModule(A) | Qⁿ as a Q[x]-module with x acting as A: { invariantFactors, elementaryDivisors, minimalPolynomial, characteristicPolynomial, rationalCanonical, blocks, isCyclic, smith }. |

| companionMatrix(f) | The companion matrix of a monic polynomial. |

| Rings |

| ring(vars, { field, order }) | A polynomial ring. vars is text ("x, y, z") or a list of names; field is any RatMath field object (default: the rationals); order is "lex", "grlex", "grevlex" (default) or a comparison of exponent lists. |

| R.vars, R.n, R.gens, R.zero, R.one | The variable names, their number, the variables as polynomials, and the constants 0 and 1. |

| R.poly(text) | Read a polynomial: "x^2 y - 3/2 x z + 1". Juxtaposition multiplies, ^ or ** is a power, numbers are exact, exact division is allowed. |

| R.from(x) | A polynomial of R from a polynomial of R, text, or a coefficient (number, BigInt, Core Rational, field element). |

| R.gen(v), R.constant(c), R.monomial(exps, c) | One variable; a constant from a field element; c·x^exps with exps a list or { x: 2, y: 1 }. |

| R.fromTerms(list), R.fromUnivariate(coeffs, v) | From [[coefficient, exponents], …]; from a constant-first coefficient list in one variable. |

| R.withOrder(order), R.equals(S), String(R) | The same ring with another order; same variables, field and order; a name such as "Q[x, y]". |

| QQ, ORDERS | The field of rationals used by default; the three built-in orders by name. |

| primeField(p), galoisField(p, k), NumberField | Coefficient fields from @ratmath/algebraic, re-exported. |

| A polynomial f |

| f.add(g), f.sub(g), f.mul(g), f.neg(), f.pow(n), f.scale(c) | Ring arithmetic. g may be a polynomial, text or a number. |

| f.equals(g), f.isZero(), f.isConstant(), f.isMonomial(), f.isHomogeneous() | Exact tests. |

| f.degree(), f.degree(v), f.degrees(), f.variables(), f.length | Total degree (−1 for 0); degree in one variable; all of them; the variables that occur; the number of terms. |

| f.terms() | The terms, largest first: [{ coefficient, exponents, monomial }]. |

| f.coefficient(exps), f.coefficients(v), f.constantTerm(), f.toConstant() | One coefficient; f as a polynomial in v (constant first, entries polynomials); the constant term; the value of a constant polynomial. |

| f.leadingTerm(), f.leadingCoefficient(), f.leadingMonomial(), f.leadingExponents() | The largest term in the ring&#x27;s order and its parts. |

| f.monic() | f divided by its leading coefficient. |

| f.diff(v, times), f.gradient() | Partial derivatives. |

| f.subs({ x: … }), f.at(point), f.compose(values, target) | Substitute for some variables (same ring); the exact value at a point; replace every variable by a polynomial of another ring. |

| f.homogenize(name), f.into(S), f.toUnivariate() | Make homogeneous with a new variable; the same polynomial in another ring; a constant-first coefficient list when only one variable occurs. |

| String(f), f.toText(), f.toTeX(), f.toJSON() | "x²y − (3/2)xz + 1"; "x^2*y - 3/2*x*z + 1" (reads back); LaTeX; { vars, terms }. |

| Division |

| f.divmod(g) | { quotient, remainder } on division by one polynomial, in the ring&#x27;s order. |

| f.divmod([g1, g2, …]) | { quotients, remainder } with f = Σ qᵢgᵢ + r and no term of r divisible by a leading term of a divisor. |

| f.rem(g or list), f.div(g), f.isDivisibleBy(g) | The remainder; the exact quotient (throws if there is a remainder); whether g divides f. |

| Greatest common divisors |

| gcd(f, g, …), lcm(f, g, …) | Greatest common divisor and least common multiple, leading coefficient 1. A single list is accepted too. |

| content(f, v), primitivePart(f, v) | The gcd of the coefficients of f as a polynomial in v, and f divided by it. |

| squareFree(f) | { unit, factors: [{ factor, multiplicity }] } with square-free, pairwise coprime factors (characteristic 0). |

| squareFreePart(f) | The product of the distinct irreducible factors. |

| Factoring |

| factor(f) | { unit, factors: [{ factor, multiplicity }] }: the irreducible factors over Q, each with coprime integer coefficients; unit is a Rational. |

| isIrreducible(f) | Whether a non-constant polynomial over Q is irreducible. |

| integerPrimitive(f) | { content, primitive }: f as a rational number times a polynomial with coprime integer coefficients. |

| Determinants and elimination |

| det(matrix, R) | The determinant of a square matrix of polynomials, by fraction-free (Bareiss) elimination. R is needed only when no entry is a polynomial. |

| sylvester(f, g, v) | The Sylvester matrix of f and g as polynomials in v. |

| resultant(f, g, v) | Its determinant: zero exactly where f and g have a common root in v. |

| discriminant(f, v) | (−1)^(n(n−1)/2) Res(f, ∂f/∂v) / lc(f): zero exactly where f has a repeated root in v. |

| jacobian([f1, f2, …]), hessian(f) | The matrix of gradients; the matrix of second partial derivatives. |

| Rational functions |

| fractions(R) | The field of fractions K(x₁, …, xₙ) as a field object: zero, one, add, sub, mul, div, neg, inv, pow, sign, equals, format, gens, name. |

| F.parse(text), F.from(x), F.of(num, den) | Read "(x^2 - 1)/(x y + 1)" (negative powers allowed); convert a polynomial, number or text; a fraction of two polynomials, reduced. |

| q.num, q.den | Numerator and denominator in lowest terms (over Q: coprime integer coefficients, positive leading denominator). |

| q.add(r), q.sub(r), q.mul(r), q.div(r), q.neg(), q.inv(), q.pow(n) | Field arithmetic; n may be negative. |

| q.equals(r), q.isZero(), q.isPolynomial(), q.toPolynomial() | Exact tests; the polynomial when the denominator is constant. |

| q.diff(v), q.subs(values), q.at(point) | Derivative; substitution; exact value (throws at a pole). |

| String(q), q.toText(), q.toTeX() | "2x/(x² − y²)"; text that F.parse reads back; LaTeX. |

| Gröbner bases |

| groebner(polys, { order, certificates, maxPairs, timeLimit }) | The reduced Gröbner basis of the ideal the polynomials generate, by Buchberger&#x27;s algorithm. order replaces the ring&#x27;s monomial order; certificates: true tracks cofactors during the run (express works either way); maxPairs and timeLimit (ms) stop a run that is too large. |

| G.basis, G.length, G.leadingMonomials, G.leadingExponents, G.generators, G.stats | The basis (monic, each term reduced); its size; leading monomials; the original generators; { pairs, zero, skipped, added }. |

| G.reduce(f), G.divide(f), G.contains(f) | The normal form of f; { quotients, remainder }; whether f is in the ideal. |

| G.express(f), G.cofactors | { cofactors, check } with f = Σ cofactors[i]·generators[i], multiplied out to confirm (throws when f is not in the ideal); each basis element in terms of the generators. |

| G.verify() | Buchberger&#x27;s criterion re-checked: { generatorsReduce, sPairsReduce, basisInIdeal, sPairsChecked, ok }. |

| G.isTrivial, G.isZero, G.dimension, G.isZeroDimensional | Basis {1} (no solutions); the zero ideal; the dimension of the solution set (−1 when empty); finitely many solutions. |

| G.standardMonomials({ limit }), G.quotientDimension | The monomials no leading monomial divides; how many (Infinity unless zero-dimensional): the number of solutions with multiplicity. |

| sPolynomial(f, g), eliminationOrder(n, [i, …]) | The S-polynomial; an order for n variables ranking those with the listed indices above the rest. |

| Ideals |

| ideal(R, [f, …]), ideal([f, …]), new Ideal(R, list) | The ideal generated by polynomials (text is read by R). |

| I.generators, I.groebner, I.basis, String(I) | As given; the GroebnerBasis (computed once); its reduced basis; "(f, g)". |

| I.contains(f), I.reduce(f), I.express(f) | Membership; normal form; f as a combination of the generators. |

| I.equals(J), I.isSubsetOf(J), I.isZero, I.isWhole, I.isProper | Comparisons and the two extreme ideals. |

| I.add(J), I.mul(J), I.pow(n), I.intersect(J) | I + J, I·J, Iⁿ, I ∩ J. A polynomial may stand for the ideal it generates. |

| I.quotient(J), I.saturate(f) | I : J = { f : fJ ⊆ I }; I : f^∞ (an ideal J is allowed too). |

| I.eliminate(vars) | I ∩ K[the other variables], as an ideal of the same ring. |

| I.radicalContains(f, { certificate }), I.exponentOf(f) | Whether some power of f is in I. With certificate: true, { holds, power, cofactors, check } with f^power = Σ cofactors[i]·generators[i]. The least such power, or null. |

| I.radical(), I.isRadical() | The radical: for finitely many solutions, one generator, or monomial generators (throws otherwise); isRadical gives null where it cannot decide. |

| I.dimension, I.isZeroDimensional, I.degree, I.standardMonomials() | Dimension of the solution set; finitely many solutions; their number with multiplicity; a basis of the quotient. |

| I.minimalPolynomial(f) | The minimal polynomial of f modulo I, coefficients constant first (finitely many solutions). |

| I.isMaximal(), I.isPrime() | Over Q. isPrime gives null where it cannot decide (positive dimension with several nonlinear generators). |

| chineseRemainder(I, J) | { comaximal, a, b, intersection, productIsIntersection, lift(f, g) } with a ∈ I, b ∈ J, a + b = 1, and lift(f, g) ≡ f mod I, ≡ g mod J. { comaximal: false, sum } otherwise. |

| Solving systems |

| solve(R, [f, …], { complex }), solve([f, …]), I.solve() | Over Q. { finite, dimension, count, multiplicity, radical, real, complex, components, parametrization }; { finite: false, dimension } for infinitely many solutions; count 0 for none. |

| solution.values, .approx, .coordinates, .field, .theta, String(solution) | Exact algebraic numbers by variable; floats (real solutions); elements of Q(θ); the number field and its root θ; "(x = …, y = …)". |

| components | [{ field, minimalPolynomial, degree, realCount, coordinates }]: one per irreducible factor, a set of conjugate solutions. |

| parametrization | { form, minimalPolynomial, coordinates }: the separating form u = Σ form[v]·v, its minimal polynomial, and each variable as a polynomial in u (Rationals, constant first). |

| Quotient rings |

| I.quotientRing(), new QuotientRing(I) | The ring R/I. |

| A.of(x), A.gens, A.zero, A.one, A.ring, A.ideal | The class of a polynomial or text; the classes of the variables. |

| A.dimension, A.isFinite, A.basis | Dimension over the field (Infinity when not finite); the standard monomials. |

| A.isField(), A.isIntegralDomain(), A.isReduced(), A.isZeroRing | Tests (null where undecided). |

| A.asField({ name }) | The quotient by a maximal ideal as a field object for ring(vars, { field }). |

| a.add(b), a.sub(b), a.neg(), a.mul(b), a.pow(n), a.equals(b), a.isZero(), a.rep | Arithmetic of classes; the normal-form representative. |

| a.isUnit(), a.inverse(), a.div(b) | Units and inverses (found through a Gröbner basis of I + (a) with cofactors). |

| a.isZeroDivisor(), a.isNilpotent(), a.minimalPolynomial(), a.matrix() | Tests; minimal polynomial and the matrix of multiplication (finite quotients). |

| The integers mod n |

| Zn(n), new ZnRing(n) | The ring Z/n; elements are BigInts 0 … n − 1. |

| Z.of(a), Z.add, Z.sub, Z.mul, Z.neg, Z.pow(a, e), Z.inverse(a), Z.div(a, b) | Arithmetic; negative powers of units are allowed; inverse throws for a non-unit. |

| Z.isUnit(a), Z.isZeroDivisor(a), Z.isField, Z.isIntegralDomain, Z.isReduced, Z.characteristic, Z.size | Tests and sizes. |

| Z.elements(), Z.units(), Z.zeroDivisors(), Z.nilpotents(), Z.idempotents(), Z.unitCount | Lists (moduli up to a million) and φ(n). |

| Z.additiveOrder(a), Z.orderOf(a), Z.primitiveRoot(), Z.unitGroup() | Orders; the smallest generator of the units or null; { order, invariants, cyclic, text }. |

| Z.ideals(), Z.decompose(), Z.table(op), Z.asField() | [{ generator, size, quotient, isMaximal, isPrime }]; { moduli, to, from, idempotents }; addition or multiplication table; the field Z/p. |

| crt(residues, moduli) | { value, modulus } solving all the congruences, or null when they conflict. Moduli need not be coprime. |

| Quadratic integer rings |

| quadraticRing(d), gaussianIntegers(), eisensteinIntegers() | The integers of Q(√d) for square-free d; d = −1; d = −3. |

| K.of(a, b), K.sqrt(x, y), K.zero, K.one, K.omega, K.d, K.discriminant, K.isReal | a + bω; x + y√d; constants. |

| x.add, x.sub, x.neg, x.mul, x.pow(k), x.conj(), x.norm(), x.trace(), x.equals, x.isZero() | Arithmetic; norm and trace are BigInts. |

| x.isUnit(), x.inverse(), x.divExact(y), x.isDivisibleBy(y), x.isAssociateOf(y), x.toNumber() | Units and exact division (null when not exact). |

| K.units, K.fundamentalUnit | { finite, list, count } for d 0. |

| K.divmod(a, b), K.gcd(a, b), K.isNormEuclidean | { quotient, remainder, euclidean } by rounding; { gcd, s, t, steps } by Euclid (throws when a step fails to shrink the norm). |

| K.elementsOfNorm(m, { bothSigns }), K.canonical(x) | One element of each class of associates with that norm; the preferred associate. |

| K.isIrreducible(x), K.isPrimeElement(x), K.irreducibleDivisors(x) | The two notions that differ when the class number is above 1. |

| K.factorizations(x), K.factor(x) | Every factorisation into irreducibles [{ unit, factors }]; the factorisation { unit, factors: [{ prime, exponent }] } when the ring has unique factorisation (throws otherwise). |

| K.ideal(g1, g2, …), K.primesAbove(p), K.splitting(p) | An ideal from generators; the prime ideals over p; { kind: split \| inert \| ramified, primes, principal }. |

| J.norm, J.generators, J.contains(x), J.equals, J.isSubsetOf, J.add, J.mul, J.pow, J.conj() | Ideals, held in a normal form so equality is exact. |

| J.isPrincipal(), J.generator(), J.isPrime(), J.isEquivalentTo(L), J.factor() | A generator or null; same ideal class; [{ prime, exponent }]. |

| K.classGroup(), K.classNumber(), K.minkowskiBound, K.isPID, K.isUFD | { classNumber, representatives, orders, invariants, cyclic, text, minkowskiBound, primesChecked }. |

| Character tables |

| characterTable(G), new CharacterTable(G, { classLimit }) | The table of a finite group, by the Burnside–Dixon–Schneider method, verified and cached on the group. |

| T.classes, T.exponent, T.inverseClass, T.classOf(x), T.powerMap(k) | Classes [{ name, representative, size, order, centralizerOrder }]; the class of an element; where k-th powers go. |

| T.irreducibles, T.degrees, T.trivial, T.linearCharacters, T.regular | The irreducible characters by degree, and some standard ones. |

| T.verify() | { rows, columns, degrees, ok }: the orthogonality relations and Σχ(1)² = \|G\| on the exact values. |

| T.normalSubgroups(), T.isSimple, T.isAbelian, T.abelianizationOrder, T.derivedSubgroupOrder, T.centreOrder, T.realClasses | What the table says about the group; normal subgroups as [{ order, classes, kernelOf }]. |

| T.classFunction(values \| fn), T.permutationCharacter(action \| subgroup), T.subgroupOfClasses(list) | A class function from values or a function of a representative; fixed-point counts; the subgroup made of whole classes. |

| String(T), T.rows({ tex }), T.toTeX(), T.describe(), T.prime | The table as text, cells or TeX; a summary; the prime the computation used. |

| Cyclotomic.root(n, k), Cyclotomic.int(k), Cyclotomic.fromPowers(n, multiplicities) | ζₙᵏ, a whole number, Σ mₖζₙᵏ. |

| z.add, z.sub, z.mul, z.neg(), z.over(p, q), z.conj(), z.galois(k), z.conjugates(), z.lift(m), z.equals | Exact arithmetic in cyclotomic fields (operands in different fields meet in the smallest common one). |

| z.isZero, z.isRational, z.isInteger, z.isReal, z.toInteger(), z.toFraction(), z.approx(), z.conductor, String(z), z.toTeX() | Tests; a number, [numerator, denominator] or { re, im }; the smallest m with z in Q(ζₘ). |

| Working with characters |

| chi.values, chi.degree, chi.value(x), chi.name, String(chi) | A ClassFunction: one Cyclotomic per class. |

| chi.add, chi.sub, chi.mul / chi.tensor, chi.scale(k), chi.pow(k), chi.conj() / chi.dual(), chi.equals | Sums, products (tensor products) and duals. |

| chi.inner(psi), chi.norm, chi.multiplicities(), chi.decompose(), chi.decomposition() | ⟨χ, ψ⟩ (a number when whole); multiplicities of the irreducibles; [{ character, multiplicity }]; "χ₁ + 2χ₃". |

| chi.adams(k), chi.symmetricSquare(), chi.alternatingSquare(), chi.indicator(), chi.type | g ↦ χ(gᵏ); S² and Λ²; the Frobenius–Schur indicator and "real", "complex" or "quaternionic". |

| Large permutation groups |

| schreierSims(generators, { names, name, base }), new PermChain(…) | The group generated by permutations (arrays of images from 0), held by a base and strong generating set. Points are reported from 1. |

| G.order, G.degree, G.base, G.orbitLengths, G.basicOrbits, G.strongGenerators, G.generators, G.generatorNames | The order (a BigInt, the product of the orbit lengths) and the stabiliser chain. |

| G.contains(g), G.sift(g), G.word(g), G.evaluate(word), G.random({ seed }), G.elements() | Membership; the sifting record; { word, text, length, check } in the generators; a word multiplied out; a uniformly random element; an iterator over all elements. |

| Field extensions and towers |

| extension({ a: "a^2 - 2", b: "b^3 - a" }), new Extension(…) | The tower Q ⊂ Q(a) ⊂ Q(a, b); each polynomial must be irreducible over the field before it. |

| K.names, K.degrees, K.degree, K.generators, K.a, K.of(text), K.basis, K.zero, K.one | The steps and their degrees, generators by name, an element from text, a polynomial or a number; the basis over Q. |

| e.text, e.definitions, e.inline({ maxLength, tex }), e.toTeX(), e.rational | A RadicalExpression: in named steps, written out in one line (null when too long), for typesetting. |

| isSymmetric(f) | Whether every permutation of the ring&#x27;s variables fixes f. |

| toElementary(f, { prefix }) | { polynomial, ring }: f written in e1, …, en (a polynomial of a new ring with those variables). |

### Errors

Bad input throws a `RangeError` or `TypeError` with a message that names the problem: a variable the ring does not have, an inexact division, a field that cannot decide whether a coefficient is zero, a factoring job too large for the method.

### Try it

```js
// A tour of the main entry points.
const G = GL(2, 3);
PRINT(G.describe(), " n2 =", G.sylowCount(2), " Sylow 2-subgroup ≅", identify(G.sylowSubgroup(2)).name);
PRINT("necklaces of 5 beads in 3 colours:", cyclic(5).natural.onColourings(3).countOrbits().count);
const R = ring("x, y");
const f = R.poly("x^3 y - x y^3");
PRINT("factor:", factor(f).factors.map((t) => String(t.factor)));
PRINT("gcd with x² − y²:", gcd(f, "x^2 - y^2"));
PRINT("divmod by x − y:", f.divmod(R.poly("x - y")).quotient);
PRINT("resultant with x + y − 1 in y:", resultant(f, R.poly("x + y - 1"), "y"));
PRINT("as a fraction over x² + xy:", fractions(R).of(f, R.poly("x^2 + x y")));
toElementary(R.poly("x^3 + y^3")).polynomial
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/explore.html

Explore

## Explore

An exact calculator for everything in the library. Type an expression and press Enter (Shift+Enter for a new line). Letters are variables, numbers are exact, and `name = …` keeps a value for later lines.

Click an entry to edit it again.

How to write things
Variables are single letters, and the ring is made from the letters you use. Products can be written side by side: `3xy^2`, `(x + 1)(x - 1)`. Fractions and decimals are exact. Rows of a matrix are separated by `;` as in `det(a, b; c, d)`. `order lex` (or `grlex`, `grevlex`) changes how terms are ordered and how division runs. `groebner`, `member`, `eliminate`, `radical` and `solve` take a list of polynomials (each set to zero); `zmod(n)`, `crt(a, m, b, n)`, `quadratic(d)` and `qfactor(d, x, y)` (which factors x + y√d) work with whole numbers. A kept name such as `f` can be used in later lines: `factor(f)`, `gcd(f, diff(f, x))`.

### Groups

Type a group's name to see its order, classes, subgroups, Sylow counts and more, with the Cayley table for groups of order up to 24. Names: `C6`, `D4` (the square, order 8), `Dic3`, `Q8`, `Q16`, `V4`, `S4`, `A5`, `GL(2,3)`, `SL(2,5)`, `PSL(2,7)`, `Heis(3)`, `SmallGroup(16,4)` (the 4th group of order 16 in [this library's list](https://ratmath.com/structures/homomorphisms.html)), and products such as `S3 × C2` (or `S3 x C2`). A presentation works too: `a, b | a^2, b^3, (ab)^5`.

### Try it

```js
// Groups: the same facts from code
const G = dihedral(6);
PRINT(G.describe(), "  ≅", identify(G).name);
PRINT("normal subgroups:", G.normalSubgroups().map((N) => N.order));

// The explorer's language calls these functions; here they are in JavaScript.
const R = ring("x, y");
const f = R.poly("(x + y)^3 - 8");
PRINT("f =", f);
PRINT("factors:", factor(f).factors.map((t) => String(t.factor)));
PRINT("gcd(f, ∂f/∂x) =", gcd(f, f.diff("x")));
PRINT("where f meets the line y = x:", resultant(f, R.poly("y - x"), "y"));
fractions(R).of(f, R.poly("x + y - 2"))
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/groups.html

Groups

## Groups and how to build them

A group is a set with a way of combining two elements that can always be undone. The symmetries of a square, the shuffles of a deck, the invertible matrices mod 3: each is a group, and this page shows how to make them and look inside.

### What a group is

A group is a set G with a product ab such that

- the product is associative: (ab)c=a(bc);

- there is an identity e with ea=ae=a for every a;

- every element has an inverse a−1 with aa−1=a−1a=e.

The product need not be commutative. When it is (ab=ba always) the group is abelian. The number of elements is the order ∣G∣, and the order of an element a is the least k≥1 with ak=e.

The library holds a finite group by listing all of its elements, so it suits groups of up to a few thousand elements: every group a course meets, and many more. Elements can be anything (numbers, permutations, matrices, pairs) as long as the group knows how to multiply them and how to tell two of them apart.

### The named families

| Call | Group | Order | Elements are |

| cyclic(n) | Cn​, the turns of a regular n-gon | n | exponents k, printed ak |

| dihedral(n) | Dn​, all symmetries of a regular n-gon | 2n | pairs [k, f] printed rksf |

| symmetric(n), alternating(n) | Sn​ and the even permutations An​ | n!, n!/2 | permutations, printed in cycle notation |

| quaternion() | Q8​={±1,±i,±j,±k} | 8 | printed 1, i, −1, … |

| dicyclic(n) | Dicn​: a2n=1, x2=an, xax−1=a−1 | 4n | pairs [k, f] printed akxf |

| kleinFour() | V4​=C2​×C2​ | 4 | pairs |

| GL(n, p), SL(n, p) | invertible matrices over Fp​, and those of determinant 1 | ∏i​(pn−pi) | matrices of whole numbers mod p |

| PSL(n, p) | SL(n,p) modulo its centre | e.g. 60, 168 | cosets |

| heisenberg(p) | upper unitriangular 3×3 matrices over Fp​ | p3 | matrices |

The dihedral group is written Dn​ with n the number of sides, so D4​, the symmetries of a square, has 8 elements. (Some books call it D8​.) Here r turns the polygon by 1/n of a revolution and s reflects it, so sr=r−1s.

```js
import { dihedral, symmetric, quaternion, GL } from "@ratmath/structures";

const D = dihedral(4);
D.elements.map((x) => D.format(x));   // ["e", "r", "s", "r²", "rs", "r³s", "r³", "r²s"]
D.format(D.mul("r", "s"));            // "rs"
D.format(D.mul("s", "r"));            // "r³s": the product depends on the order
D.elementOrder("rs");                 // 2: every reflection has order 2

const S = symmetric(3);
S.format(S.mul("(1 2)", "(2 3)"));    // "(1 2 3)": first (2 3), then (1 2)

const Q = quaternion();
Q.format(Q.mul("i", "j"));            // "k"
Q.format(Q.mul("j", "i"));            // "−k"

const G = GL(2, 3);
G.order;                              // 48
G.centre().elements.map((x) => G.format(x));   // ["[1 0; 0 1]", "[2 0; 0 2]"]
```

Elements can be named by the way they print: `"r²s"` or `"r^2 s"`, `"(1 2 3)"`, `"-i"`. Products of permutations follow the rule for composing functions: `mul(a, b)` means first b, then a, the same convention as algebraic's `PermGroup`.

### Even and odd permutations

Every permutation is a product of transpositions, and the number of them is always even or always odd. A k-cycle is k−1 transpositions, (1234)=(14)(13)(12), so the sign of a permutation of n points with c cycles (fixed points counted) is (−1)n−c. The same parity is the parity of the number of inversions, pairs i put out of order. The sign is a homomorphism onto {±1} and its kernel is the alternating group.

```js
import { sign, isEven, inversions } from "@ratmath/structures";

sign("(1 2 3 4)", 4);       // −1: odd
isEven("(1 2)(3 4)", 4);    // true
inversions([2, 0, 1]);      // 2, so (1 3 2) is even
```

### New groups from old

The direct product G×H is the set of pairs (g,h) multiplied entry by entry. The semidirect product N⋊H twists this: each h acts on N by an automorphism φh​, and

(n1​,h1​)(n2​,h2​)=(n1​φh1​​(n2​),h1​h2​).
With N=Cm​ and H=Ck​, where the generator of H acts by x↦xr, this is `metacyclic(m, k, r)`; it needs rk≡1(modm). The dihedral group is Cn​⋊C2​ with r=−1, and `metacyclic(7, 3, 2)` is the smallest nonabelian group of odd order, of order 21. The library checks that the twisting really is an action by automorphisms, and refuses it otherwise.

```js
import { directProduct, semidirectProduct, metacyclic, cyclic, kleinFour, isIsomorphic } from "@ratmath/structures";

const P = directProduct(cyclic(2), cyclic(3));
String(P);                            // "C2 × C3"
P.isCyclic;                           // true: C2 × C3 is C6

const F21 = metacyclic(7, 3, 2);      // C7 ⋊ C3
F21.order;                            // 21
F21.isAbelian;                        // false

// C4 ⋊ C2 with the generator inverting C4 is the dihedral group of the square
const D = semidirectProduct(cyclic(4), cyclic(2), (h) => (x) => (h ? (4 - x) % 4 : x));
D.order;                              // 8
```

### Groups from a table, or from any multiplication

A finite group is completely described by its Cayley table, the grid of all products. Every row and every column of the table lists each element exactly once (a Latin square), because ax=b has exactly one solution x=a−1b. The converse fails: a Latin square with an identity need not be associative, so `Group.fromTable` checks associativity too.

```js
import { Group, cyclic, kleinFour, isIsomorphic } from "@ratmath/structures";

String(cyclic(4).cayleyTable());
// ·  │ e  a  a² a³
// ───┼────────────
// e  │ e  a  a² a³
// a  │ a  a² a³ e
// a² │ a² a³ e  a
// a³ │ a³ e  a  a²

const V = Group.fromTable([[0, 1, 2, 3], [1, 0, 3, 2], [2, 3, 0, 1], [3, 2, 1, 0]], { labels: ["e", "a", "b", "c"] });
V.isCyclic;                           // false: every element has order 1 or 2
isIsomorphic(V, kleinFour());         // true

// the nonzero numbers mod 11 under multiplication, generated by 2
const U = Group.generate({ generators: [2n], identity: 1n, mul: (a, b) => (a * b) % 11n });
U.order;                              // 10
U.isCyclic;                           // true: 2 is a primitive root mod 11
```

The [explorer](https://ratmath.com/structures/explore.html) takes any of these names, and products of them such as `S3 × C2`; [the table of small groups](https://ratmath.com/structures/homomorphisms.html) names every group of order at most 20.

### Try it

```js
// the symmetries of a square, and its Cayley table
const D = dihedral(4);
PRINT(D.describe());
PRINT(String(D.cayleyTable()));

// every element of D4 with its order
PRINT(D.elements.map((x) => `${D.format(x)}: ${D.elementOrder(x)}`).join(", "));

// GL(2, 3): 48 matrices; its element orders
const G = GL(2, 3);
PRINT(G.describe());
PRINT("element orders:", [...G.orderStatistics()].map(([o, c]) => `${c} of order ${o}`).join(", "));

// even and odd: the sign of each element of S4 against membership in A4
const S4 = symmetric(4), A4 = alternating(4);
PRINT("sign agrees with A4 for every element:", S4.elements.every((p) => isEven(p) === A4.has(p)));
PRINT("(1 2 3 4) has sign", sign("(1 2 3 4)", 4));

// the smallest nonabelian group of odd order
const F = metacyclic(7, 3, 2);
F.describe()
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/classes.html

Groups

## Conjugacy classes and commutators

Two elements are conjugate when one is the other seen from a different point of view. Sorting a group into conjugacy classes, and measuring how far it is from commutative, are the first two ways to see its shape.

### Conjugacy

Elements x and y of G are conjugate when y=gxg−1 for some g∈G. This splits the group into conjugacy classes. In Sn​ two permutations are conjugate exactly when they have the same cycle type, so the classes of Sn​ correspond to the partitions of n: S5​ has 7 of them. In a matrix group, conjugate matrices are similar matrices.

The centraliser C(x)={g:gx=xg} is a subgroup, and the elements gxg−1 are in one-to-one correspondence with the cosets of C(x). So

∣class of x∣=[G:C(x)]=∣C(x)∣∣G∣​,
and every class size divides ∣G∣. The centre Z(G), the elements commuting with everything, is made of the classes of size 1. Adding up the classes gives the class equation

∣G∣=∣Z(G)∣+i∑​[G:C(xi​)],
one term for each class of size more than 1.

```js
import { alternating, dihedral, symmetric, cycleString } from "@ratmath/structures";

const A = alternating(4);
A.conjugacyClasses().map((c) => `${cycleString(c.representative)}: ${c.size}`);
// ["(): 1", "(1 3)(2 4): 3", "(1 2 3): 4", "(1 2 4): 4"]
String(A.classEquation());          // "12 = 1 + 3 + 4 + 4"

const D = dihedral(4);
String(D.classEquation());          // "8 = 2 + 2 + 2 + 2"
D.centre().elements.map((x) => D.format(x));      // ["e", "r²"]
D.centraliser("r").order;           // 4

symmetric(5).conjugacyClasses().length;   // 7, the partitions of 5
```

The class equation has quick consequences. If ∣G∣=pk for a prime p, every term on the right but ∣Z(G)∣ is a multiple of p, so p divides ∣Z(G)∣: a group of prime-power order has a nontrivial centre. It also shows that A4​ has no subgroup of order 6: such a subgroup would have index 2, so it would be normal, so it would be a union of classes including {e}. The class sizes are 1, 3, 4 and 4, and no choice of them containing the 1 adds up to 6 (see [subgroups](https://ratmath.com/structures/subgroups.html)).

### Commutators

The commutator of a and b is [a,b]=a−1b−1ab. It is e exactly when a and b commute. The commutator subgroup (or derived subgroup) G′=[G,G] is the subgroup generated by all commutators. It is normal, and it is the smallest normal subgroup whose quotient G/G′ is abelian. The library computes it as the smallest normal subgroup containing the commutators of the generators, which is the same subgroup.

```js
import { dihedral, symmetric, alternating, GL, SL } from "@ratmath/structures";

const D = dihedral(4);
D.format(D.commutator("r", "s"));   // "r²"
D.derivedSubgroup().order;          // 2

symmetric(4).derivedSubgroup().equals(alternating(4));   // true
GL(2, 3).derivedSubgroup().equals(SL(2, 3));             // true
alternating(5).isPerfect;          // true: A5 is its own commutator subgroup
```

### Solvable and nilpotent groups

Repeating the commutator subgroup gives the derived series G⊇G′⊇G′′⊇⋯. The group is solvable when this reaches the trivial group. The name comes from Galois theory: a polynomial can be solved by radicals exactly when its Galois group is solvable, and S5​ is not, which is why there is no formula for the quintic.

Two other series measure how close a group is to abelian. The lower central series γ1​=G, γi+1​=[γi​,G], and the upper central series Z0​=1, Zi+1​/Zi​=Z(G/Zi​). The group is nilpotent when the lower series reaches 1 (equivalently, the upper series reaches G), and the number of steps is its nilpotency class. Abelian groups have class 1; every group of prime-power order is nilpotent; every nilpotent group is solvable.

```js
import { symmetric, heisenberg, dihedral } from "@ratmath/structures";

symmetric(4).derivedSeries().map((H) => H.order);     // [24, 12, 4, 1]: solvable
symmetric(5).isSolvable;                              // false
symmetric(4).isNilpotent;                             // false
heisenberg(3).lowerCentralSeries().map((H) => H.order);   // [27, 3, 1]
heisenberg(3).nilpotencyClass;                        // 2
dihedral(8).nilpotencyClass;                          // 3
```

### Try it

```js
// the class equation of several groups
for (const G of [symmetric(4), alternating(5), quaternion(), GL(2, 3), SL(2, 5)]) PRINT(`${G}: ${G.classEquation()}`);

// classes of S5 by cycle type: size and the order of their elements
const S = symmetric(5);
for (const c of S.conjugacyClasses()) PRINT(cycleString(c.representative).padEnd(12), "size", c.size, " order", c.order);

// which groups are solvable, nilpotent, simple?
[symmetric(3), symmetric(4), symmetric(5), alternating(5), heisenberg(3), dihedral(8), PSL(2, 7)]
  .map((G) => `${G}: solvable ${G.isSolvable}, nilpotent ${G.isNilpotent}, simple ${G.isSimple}`)
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/subgroups.html

Groups

## Subgroups and quotients

A subgroup is a group living inside a bigger one. Its size always divides the size of the whole, and when it is normal the group can be folded up along it into a smaller group, the quotient.

### Subgroups and Lagrange's theorem

A subgroup H≤G is a subset that is a group with the same product: it contains e and is closed under products and inverses. In a finite group, closure under products is enough. `G.subgroup(list)` gives the subgroup generated by some elements, the smallest one containing them.

The left cosets gH={gh:h∈H} all have ∣H∣ elements and split G into disjoint pieces. So

∣G∣=[G:H]∣H∣,
where the index [G:H] is the number of cosets. This is Lagrange's theorem: the order of a subgroup divides the order of the group. Since ⟨a⟩ has as many elements as the order of a, the order of every element divides ∣G∣ too. The converse fails: A4​ has order 12 but no subgroup of order 6.

```js
import { symmetric, alternating, dihedral } from "@ratmath/structures";

const S = symmetric(4);
const H = S.subgroup(["(1 2 3 4)"]);
H.order;                                 // 4
S.index(H);                              // 6
S.cosets(H).length;                      // 6

S.subgroups().length;                    // 30
S.subgroupClasses().length;              // 11 up to conjugacy
alternating(4).subgroups().map((K) => K.order);   // [1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 4, 12]: no 6
dihedral(6).subgroups().length;          // 16 = τ(6) + σ(6)
```

Listing every subgroup is done by joining cyclic subgroups layer by layer. It is fine for groups of a few hundred elements; `subgroups()` refuses groups larger than 1000 unless told otherwise. The dihedral group Dn​ has τ(n)+σ(n) subgroups (the number and the sum of the divisors of n), which the tests check for n up to 12.

### Normal subgroups and quotients

A subgroup N is normal, written N⊴G, when gNg−1=N for every g; equivalently its left and right cosets agree. A normal subgroup is a union of conjugacy classes, which is how `normalSubgroups()` finds them all without listing every subgroup.

For a normal N the cosets multiply: (aN)(bN)=abN is well defined, and the cosets form the quotient group G/N of order [G:N]. For a subgroup that is not normal this product depends on the representatives chosen, and `quotient` refuses.

```js
import { symmetric, dihedral, quaternion, isIsomorphic, kleinFour, cyclic } from "@ratmath/structures";

const S = symmetric(4);
S.normalSubgroups().map((N) => N.order);      // [1, 4, 12, 24]
const V = S.subgroup(["(1 2)(3 4)", "(1 3)(2 4)"]);
isIsomorphic(S.quotient(V), symmetric(3));    // true: S4/V4 ≅ S3

const D = dihedral(4);
const Q = D.quotient(D.centre());
Q.order;                                      // 4
isIsomorphic(Q, kleinFour());                 // true
String(Q.cosetOf("r"));                       // "rZ"

S.quotient(S.subgroup(["(1 2)"]));            // throws: not a normal subgroup
```

### Composition series

A group is simple when its only normal subgroups are 1 and itself. Cutting a group down by maximal normal subgroups, G=G0​⊵G1​⊵⋯⊵1, gives simple quotients Gi​/Gi+1​, the composition factors. By the Jordan–Hölder theorem they are the same for every such series, up to order: they are the group's building blocks, the way primes are for whole numbers. A finite group is solvable exactly when all its composition factors are cyclic of prime order.

```js
import { symmetric, alternating, PSL } from "@ratmath/structures";

symmetric(4).compositionSeries().factors;   // [2, 3, 2, 2]
String(symmetric(4).compositionSeries());   // "24 ⊳ 12 ⊳ 4 ⊳ 2 ⊳ 1"
symmetric(5).compositionSeries().factors;   // [2, 60]: A5 is a factor
alternating(5).isSimple;                     // true
PSL(2, 7).isSimple;                          // true, order 168
```

### Try it

```js
// all subgroups of S4, up to conjugacy
const S = symmetric(4);
for (const c of S.subgroupClasses()) {
  const id = c.order <= 20 ? identify(c.group).name : String(c.group);
  PRINT(`order ${c.order}, index ${c.index}: ${c.conjugates} conjugate(s), ${c.normal ? "normal" : "not normal"}, ≅ ${id}`);
}

// a quotient: D6 modulo its rotations by a third of a turn
const D = dihedral(6);
const N = D.subgroup(["r^2"]);
const Q = D.quotient(N);
PRINT("|D6/⟨r²⟩| =", Q.order, " isomorphic to", identify(Q).name);
String(Q.cayleyTable())
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/sylow.html

Groups

## Sylow subgroups

Lagrange's theorem says what sizes a subgroup cannot have. Sylow's theorems go the other way: for the largest power of each prime dividing the order, a subgroup of that size always exists, and the number of them is tightly constrained.

### The theorems

Write ∣G∣=pam with p a prime not dividing m. A subgroup of order pa is a Sylow p-subgroup. Sylow's theorems say:

- Sylow p-subgroups exist.

- Any two of them are conjugate, and every subgroup of p-power order lies inside one.

- Their number np​ divides m and satisfies np​≡1(modp).

Since they are all conjugate, np​=[G:N(P)] for any one of them P, where N(P)={g:gPg−1=P} is its normaliser. In particular a Sylow subgroup is normal exactly when np​=1.

### How one is found

`sylowSubgroup(p)` grows a p-subgroup one step at a time. Start with P=1. While ∣P∣, the quotient N(P)/P has order divisible by p (this is the heart of the proof of the first theorem), so by Cauchy's theorem it has an element of order p. Any x∈N(P) whose image in N(P)/P has p-power order makes ⟨P,x⟩=P⟨x⟩ a bigger p-group. When ∣P∣=pa it is a Sylow subgroup, and its conjugates are all the others. The tests compare np​ found this way with a count of all subgroups of order pa, for every prime and every test group up to order 168.

```js
import { alternating, symmetric, GL, PSL, identify } from "@ratmath/structures";

const A = alternating(5);                  // |A5| = 60 = 2²·3·5
[2, 3, 5].map((p) => A.sylowCount(p));    // [5, 10, 6]
identify(A.sylowSubgroup(2)).name;         // "C2 × C2"

const S = symmetric(4);
identify(S.sylowSubgroup(2)).name;         // "D4"
S.sylowSubgroups(3).length;                // 4

const G = GL(2, 3);
identify(G.sylowSubgroup(2)).name;         // "SD16", the semidihedral group
[2, 3, 7].map((p) => PSL(2, 7).sylowCount(p));   // [21, 28, 8]
```

### Using the theorems

The counting condition alone often pins a group down. If ∣G∣=15 then n3​ divides 5 and is 1 mod 3, so n3​=1; likewise n5​ divides 3 and is 1 mod 5, so n5​=1. Both Sylow subgroups are normal, they meet only in e, and G≅C3​×C5​≅C15​: every group of order 15 is cyclic. The same argument works for pq with primes p and p∤q−1.

For order 12, n3​ is 1 or 4. In A4​ it is 4, so there are 4×2=8 elements of order 3, leaving room for just one subgroup of order 4: n2​=1. A simple group of order 60 must have n5​=6, which forces 24 elements of order 5; A5​ is one, and it is the only one.

### Try it

```js
// Sylow counts, with the conditions n_p | m and n_p ≡ 1 (mod p) checked
for (const G of [symmetric(4), alternating(5), GL(2, 3), PSL(2, 7), dihedral(12), metacyclic(7, 3, 2)]) {
  const n = G.order;
  const row = [];
  for (const p of [2, 3, 5, 7]) {
    if (n % p) continue;
    let pa = 1;
    while (n % (pa * p) === 0) pa *= p;
    const np = G.sylowCount(p);
    row.push(`n${p} = ${np} (divides ${n / pa}: ${(n / pa) % np === 0}, ≡ 1 mod ${p}: ${np % p === 1})`);
  }
  PRINT(`${G} (order ${n}):`, row.join("; "));
}
// a Sylow 2-subgroup of S4 and its conjugates
symmetric(4).sylowSubgroups(2).map(String)
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/homomorphisms.html

Groups

## Homomorphisms and isomorphism

A homomorphism is a map between groups that respects products. It is how one group is seen inside, or projected onto, another, and an isomorphism, one that can be reversed, says two groups are the same group in different clothes.

### Homomorphisms

A map f:G→H is a homomorphism when f(ab)=f(a)f(b) for all a,b. Its kernel kerf={x:f(x)=e} is a normal subgroup of G and its image is a subgroup of H. The sign of a permutation is a homomorphism Sn​→C2​ with kernel An​; the determinant is a homomorphism from GL(n,p) to the nonzero numbers mod p with kernel SL(n,p).

A homomorphism is fixed by where it sends a set of generators, but not every choice of images works: the images must satisfy every relation the generators do. `homomorphism(G, H, images)` walks through G from the identity, setting f(xs)=f(x)f(s) for each generator s, and refuses if this ever gives an element two different images. When no clash appears the map is a homomorphism, because every element is a product of generators.

```js
import { homomorphism, tryHomomorphism, cyclic, symmetric, cycleType } from "@ratmath/structures";

// C6 → C3 sending a to a: well defined, since a⁶ = e and a⁶ ↦ a⁶ = e in C3
const f = homomorphism(cyclic(6), cyclic(3), [1]);
f.kernel().order;                 // 2
tryHomomorphism(cyclic(4), cyclic(3), [1]);   // null: a⁴ = e but a⁴ = a in C3

// the sign of a permutation, from a function
const sign = homomorphism(symmetric(4), cyclic(2), (p) => cycleType(p).reduce((s, c) => s + c - 1, 0) % 2);
String(sign);                     // "S4 → C2, (1 2) ↦ a, (1 2 3 4) ↦ a"
sign.kernel().order;              // 12: the kernel is A4
```

### The isomorphism theorems

The three isomorphism theorems say which quotients are which. The library builds the isomorphism each one promises and checks it.

- First: for f:G→H, G/kerf≅imf by xkerf↦f(x). firstIsomorphism(f).

- Second: for H≤G and N⊴G, HN is a subgroup and H/(H∩N)≅HN/N. secondIsomorphism(G, H, N).

- Third: for normal N⊆K, (G/N)/(K/N)≅G/K. thirdIsomorphism(G, N, K).

```js
import { firstIsomorphism, secondIsomorphism, symmetric, alternating, homomorphism, cyclic, cycleType } from "@ratmath/structures";

const S = symmetric(4);
const sign = homomorphism(S, cyclic(2), (p) => cycleType(p).reduce((s, c) => s + c - 1, 0) % 2);
const { quotient, image, iso } = firstIsomorphism(sign);
[quotient.order, image.order, iso.isIsomorphism];   // [2, 2, true]

const V = S.subgroup(["(1 2)(3 4)", "(1 3)(2 4)"]);
const H = S.subgroup(["(1 2 3)", "(1 2)"]);         // a copy of S3
const second = secondIsomorphism(S, H, V);
[second.HN.order, second.HcapN.order];              // [24, 1]: S3 ≅ S4/V4
```

### Is it the same group?

`isomorphism(G, H)` returns an isomorphism or `null`. It first compares invariants (orders, element orders and class sizes, the centre, the commutator subgroup), then searches: it picks a few generators of G, tries for each generator the elements of H with the same order and class size, and abandons a partial choice as soon as it fails to be a one-to-one homomorphism on the subgroup generated so far. Every isomorphism it returns has been checked from scratch.

```js
import { isomorphism, isIsomorphic, PSL, alternating, GL, dihedral, quaternion, symmetric, SL } from "@ratmath/structures";

isIsomorphic(PSL(2, 5), alternating(5));     // true
isIsomorphic(PSL(2, 7), GL(3, 2));           // true: the simple group of order 168, twice
isIsomorphic(dihedral(4), quaternion());     // false, though both have order 8 and 5 classes
isIsomorphic(SL(2, 3), symmetric(4));        // false
String(isomorphism(symmetric(3), dihedral(3)));
// "S3 → D3, (1 2) ↦ s, (1 2 3) ↦ r"
```

### Automorphisms

An isomorphism from a group to itself is an automorphism; together they form the group Aut(G). Conjugation by any g is one, an inner automorphism, and these form a normal subgroup Inn(G)≅G/Z(G).

```js
import { automorphisms, automorphismGroup, cyclic, quaternion, directProduct, GL, symmetric, isIsomorphic } from "@ratmath/structures";

automorphisms(cyclic(12)).length;              // 4 = φ(12): a ↦ a, a⁵, a⁷, a¹¹
automorphisms(quaternion()).length;            // 24
const A = automorphismGroup(directProduct(cyclic(2), cyclic(2), cyclic(2)));
isIsomorphic(A, GL(3, 2));                     // true: Aut(C2³) is GL(3, 2), order 168
automorphismGroup(symmetric(4)).inner.order;   // 24: every automorphism of S4 is inner
```

### The groups of order at most 20

Up to isomorphism there are only a few groups of each small order: 1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 5, 2, 2, 1, 5, 1, 2, 1, 14, 1, 5, 1, 5 for orders 1 to 20. `smallGroups(n)` gives one of each, built from the constructions on the [first page](https://ratmath.com/structures/groups.html), and `identify(G)` says which one a group is. The tests check that the groups listed for each order are pairwise non-isomorphic, and that every subgroup of order at most 20 of S5​, GL(2,3), PSL(2,7) and two groups of order 32 is isomorphic to one of them. In the explorer, `SmallGroup(n, i)` is the i-th group of order n in this list (the order is this library's, not GAP's).

```js
import { smallGroups, identify, directProduct, cyclic, GL, metacyclic } from "@ratmath/structures";

smallGroups(8).map(String);        // ["C8", "C4 × C2", "C2 × C2 × C2", "D4", "Q8"]
smallGroups(16).length;            // 14
identify(GL(2, 3).sylowSubgroup(2)).name;    // "SD16"
identify(metacyclic(5, 4, 2)).name;          // "C5 ⋊ C4", the Frobenius group of order 20
```

### Try it

```js
// the groups of order at most 20, with a few invariants that tell them apart
for (let n = 1; n <= 20; n += 1) {
  const gs = smallGroups(n);
  if (gs.length === 1) continue;
  PRINT(`order ${n}: ` + gs.map((G) => `${G} [${G.isAbelian ? "abelian" : "nonabelian"}, centre ${G.centre().order}, ${G.conjugacyClasses().length} classes]`).join("; "));
}
// D4 and Q8 have the same order and class sizes; their element orders differ
[dihedral(4), quaternion()].map((G) => `${G}: ${[...G.orderStatistics()].map(([o, c]) => `${c}×order ${o}`).join(", ")}`)
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/actions.html

Groups

## Actions and counting

A group acts on a set when each of its elements moves the points around, compatibly with the product. Watching where points can go answers counting questions: how many different necklaces, how many ways to paint a cube.

### Actions, orbits and stabilisers

An action of G on a set X assigns to each g and x a point g⋅x, with e⋅x=x and g⋅(h⋅x)=(gh)⋅x. The orbit of x is everywhere it can be moved, G⋅x; the orbits split X into disjoint pieces. The stabiliser Stab(x)={g:g⋅x=x} is a subgroup, and the points of the orbit match the cosets of the stabiliser, so

∣G⋅x∣⋅∣Stab(x)∣=∣G∣(orbit–stabiliser).
Every named group comes with its natural action as `G.natural`: Dn​ and Cn​ on the vertices 0,…,n−1 of the polygon, Sn​ on 1,…,n, matrix groups on the vectors of Fpn​. `action(G, points, act)` makes any other. Each group element becomes a permutation of the points, built from the generators and checked against `act`, so a rule that is not an action is refused instead of giving wrong counts.

```js
import { dihedral, GL, symmetric, action, conjugationAction, cosetAction, cyclic } from "@ratmath/structures";

const D = dihedral(6);
D.natural.orbit(0);                   // [0, 1, 2, 5, 3, 4]: all six vertices of the hexagon
D.natural.stabiliser(0).order;        // 2: the identity and one reflection; 6 · 2 = 12
D.natural.fixedPoints("s");           // [0, 3]

GL(2, 3).natural.orbits().map((o) => o.length);   // [1, 8]: zero, and all other vectors
conjugationAction(symmetric(4)).orbits().length;  // 5: the conjugacy classes

action(cyclic(4), [0, 1, 2], (g, x) => (x + 1) % 3);  // throws: not an action
```

Two standard actions turn group theory into this language. G acting on itself by left multiplication is free and transitive, and it embeds G in the symmetric group on ∣G∣ points (Cayley's theorem). G acting on the cosets of a subgroup H by g⋅xH=gxH has as kernel the largest normal subgroup inside H. Conjugation acting on elements has the conjugacy classes as orbits, and the class equation is orbit–stabiliser for it.

### The orbit-counting lemma

Counting orbits directly needs the orbits. The lemma usually credited to Burnside (and known to Cauchy and Frobenius) counts them from fixed points:

#orbits=∣G∣1​g∈G∑​∣Fix(g)∣,Fix(g)={x:g⋅x=x}.
To see it, count the pairs (g,x) with g⋅x=x both ways: by g it is the sum on the right; by x it is ∑x​∣Stab(x)∣=∑x​∣G∣/∣G⋅x∣, and each orbit contributes exactly ∣G∣. Since ∣Fix(g)∣ is the same for conjugate elements, the sum can be taken class by class. `countOrbits()` does that, and also counts the orbits directly as a check.

### Necklaces and cubes

A colouring gives each point one of k colours; the group acts on colourings by moving the points, and two colourings are the same up to symmetry when they are in one orbit. `A.onColourings(k)` is that action. For beads on a ring of 6 turned by C6​, the rotation by j steps fixes a colouring exactly when the colouring repeats with period gcd(j,6), which gives 61​(26+21+22+23+22+21)=14 necklaces in two colours; allowing the necklace to be turned over (D6​) gives 13 bracelets.

```js
import { cyclic, dihedral, permutationGroup, burnside } from "@ratmath/structures";

const necklaces = cyclic(6).natural.onColourings(2);
String(necklaces.countOrbits());     // "(1/6)·(64 + 8 + 4 + 4 + 2 + 2) = 14"
dihedral(6).natural.onColourings(2).countOrbits().count;   // 13

// the 24 rotations of a cube, acting on its 6 faces
const cube = permutationGroup([[0, 2, 3, 4, 1, 5], [1, 5, 2, 0, 4, 3]], 6);
cube.order;                                      // 24
String(burnside(cube.natural.onColourings(3)));  // "(1/24)·(729 + 3·81 + 6·27 + 8·9 + 6·27) = 57"
cube.natural.onSubsets(3).orbits().length;       // 2: three faces round a corner, or a band
```

Listing colourings stops being practical around a million of them. For larger counts, and for the full pattern inventory (how many orbits use each colour how often), use Pólya's cycle index in [@ratmath/discrete](https://ratmath.com/discrete/): `countColourings(A.toPermGroup(), k)` and `patternInventory(A.toPermGroup(), colours)` take the image of any action from here.

### Try it

```js
// necklaces with n beads in k colours, by the orbit-counting lemma, against the formula (1/n) Σ φ(d) k^(n/d)
const phi = (n) => [...Array(n).keys()].filter((i) => { let a = i, b = n; while (b) [a, b] = [b, a % b]; return a === 1; }).length;
for (const n of [4, 5, 6, 8]) {
  const k = 3;
  const lemma = cyclic(n).natural.onColourings(k).countOrbits().count;
  let formula = 0;
  for (let d = 1; d <= n; d += 1) if (n % d === 0) formula += phi(d) * k ** (n / d);
  PRINT(`${n} beads, ${k} colours: ${lemma} necklaces (formula ${formula / n})`);
}

// orbit–stabiliser for GL(2, 3) acting on the lines through 0 in F3² (4 of them)
const G = GL(2, 3);
const lines = [[1, 0], [0, 1], [1, 1], [1, 2]];
const norm = ([x, y]) => (x ? [1, (y * x) % 3] : [0, 1]);   // scale so the first nonzero entry is 1
const L = action(G, lines, (A, v) => norm(G.natural.apply(A, v)));
PRINT("orbits:", L.orbits().length, " stabiliser of a line has order", L.stabiliser([1, 0]).order, " kernel (scalars) has order", L.kernel().order);
PRINT("the image of GL(2,3) in S4 has order", fromPermGroup(L.toPermGroup()).order, ": PGL(2,3) ≅ S4");
String(L.countOrbits())
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/presentations.html

Groups

## Presentations and coset enumeration

The shortest description of a group is often a few generators and the rules they obey: a turn of order 4, a flip of order 2, and a flip then a turn is a flip. Coset enumeration turns such a description back into the group itself.

### Generators and relations

A presentation ⟨a,b∣r1​,r2​,…⟩ lists generators and relators, words that are declared equal to the identity. The group it presents is the largest one generated by a,b in which those words are trivial: every other equation in it follows from the relators. A relation u=v is the relator uv−1.

- ⟨a∣an⟩ is the cyclic group Cn​.

- ⟨a,b∣an,b2,(ab)2⟩ is the dihedral group Dn​ of order 2n.

- ⟨a,b∣a2,b3,(ab)k⟩ has order 6, 12, 24, 60 for k=2,3,4,5: S3​,A4​,S4​,A5​, the rotation groups of the regular solids. For k≥6 it is infinite.

- ⟨a,b∣ab=ba⟩ is Z2, and ⟨a,b∣ ⟩ is the free group.

Words are written as on paper: `a^2 b^-1` or `a²b⁻¹`, `(ab)^3`, the commutator `[a, b]` =a−1b−1ab, and a capital letter for an inverse, `A` =a−1.

```js
import { presentation } from "@ratmath/structures";

const P = presentation("a, b | a^2, b^3, (ab)^5");
P.order();                         // 60
P.index(["b"]);                    // 20: the cosets of the subgroup ⟨b⟩ of order 3
String(P.abelianInvariants());     // "1": the group is perfect

const D = presentation("a, b | a^4, b^2, (ab)^2").toGroup();
D.elements.map((x) => D.format(x));   // ["e", "a", "b", "a²", "ab", "a⁻¹b", "a⁻¹", "a²b"]
D.format(D.mul("b", "a"));            // "a⁻¹b"
```

### Todd–Coxeter coset enumeration

Whether a presentation describes a finite group cannot be decided in general (the word problem is unsolvable), but when the group, or the index of a subgroup, is finite, coset enumeration finds it. Given a subgroup H generated by some words, it builds a table of the right cosets Hg and how each generator moves them:

- Start with one coset, H itself, numbered 0.

- For every coset c and every relator r, trace r from c both forwards and backwards through the table. The relator is trivial, so the trace must come back to c. Where the table has a gap, either the two ends meet and the gap is filled (a deduction), or a new coset is defined to continue.

- If a trace ends at a coset d=c, then c and d are the same coset (a coincidence); merge them, and merge whatever that forces.

- When every coset has every generator defined and every relator closes up, the table is complete: the number of cosets is [G:H].

This library uses the Hasselgrove–Leech–Trotter order of work, which defines cosets freely and cleans up with coincidences. If more than `maxCosets` cosets (500,000 by default) are alive at once it stops and says so, which is what an infinite group does. With H=1 the cosets are the elements, and `toGroup()` gives the group with each element printed as a shortest word.

```js
import { presentation } from "@ratmath/structures";

const T = presentation("a, b | a^4, b^2, (ab)^2").enumerate(["b"]);
T.index;                 // 4: ⟨b⟩ has index 4 in D4
T.table;                 // [[1, 0], [3, 2], [0, 1], [2, 3]]: coset c·a and c·b for each c
T.representatives;       // [[], [1], [-1], [1, 1]]: H, Ha, Ha⁻¹, Ha²

// the Fibonacci group F(2, 5): five generators, each the product of the two before
presentation("a, b, c, d, e | ab = c, bc = d, cd = e, de = a, ea = b").order();   // 11

presentation("a, b | a^3, b^3, (ab)^3").order({ maxCosets: 2000 });   // throws: this group is infinite
```

### A presentation of any finite group

Every finite group has a presentation: take its generators, and for each step x→xs in its Cayley graph that is not in a chosen spanning tree, the relator that walks the tree to x, takes the step, and walks back. `presentationOf(G)` does this (it is Schreier's method). The presentations are long but correct, and coset enumeration on them gives back a group isomorphic to G; the tests check this for every group of order up to 20.

```js
import { presentationOf, quaternion, symmetric } from "@ratmath/structures";

String(presentationOf(quaternion()));
// "⟨a, b | b²a⁻², abab⁻¹, ba²b⁻¹a⁻², baba⁻¹, a⁴, a³ba⁻¹b⁻¹, a²b²⟩"
presentationOf(symmetric(4)).order();   // 24
```

### Try it

```js
// the triangle groups ⟨a, b | a², b³, (ab)^k⟩: finite for k ≤ 5
for (let k = 2; k <= 5; k += 1) {
  const P = presentation(`a, b | a^2, b^3, (ab)^${k}`);
  const G = P.toGroup();
  PRINT(`k = ${k}: order ${G.order},`, G.order <= 20 ? `≅ ${identify(G).name}` : G.order === 24 ? `≅ S4: ${isIsomorphic(G, symmetric(4))}` : `≅ A5: ${isIsomorphic(G, alternating(5))}`);
}
// k = 6 is the symmetry group of the hexagonal tiling, infinite: enumeration gives up
try { presentation("a, b | a^2, b^3, (ab)^6").order({ maxCosets: 3000 }); } catch (e) { PRINT("k = 6:", e.message); }

// a subgroup of finite index in it all the same: the kernel of the map to C6 sending a ↦ a³, b ↦ a²
presentation("a, b | a^2, b^3, (ab)^6").index(["a b a^-1 b^-1", "b a b^-1 a^-1", "(ab)^6", "b^-1 a b a", "a b^-1 a b"], { maxCosets: 3000 })
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/characters.html

Groups

## Character tables

A representation turns the elements of a group into matrices. Its character keeps only the traces, and astonishingly that is enough: a small square table of numbers, one row per irreducible representation and one column per conjugacy class, determines how every representation of the group breaks up. Here the table is computed exactly for any group the library can list.

### Representations and characters

A representation of G of degree d is a homomorphism ρ:G→GLd​(C). Its character is χ(g)=trρ(g). Since conjugate matrices have equal traces, χ is constant on conjugacy classes, and χ(1)=d. A representation is irreducible if no proper subspace is preserved by every ρ(g); every representation is a direct sum of irreducible ones (Maschke), so every character is a sum of irreducible characters. The basic facts:

- there are exactly as many irreducible characters as conjugacy classes;

- their degrees divide ∣G∣ and satisfy ∑χ​χ(1)2=∣G∣;

- a representation is determined up to isomorphism by its character.

Because g has finite order n, the matrix ρ(g) is diagonalisable with n-th roots of unity as eigenvalues. So χ(g) is a sum of χ(1) roots of unity: an algebraic integer in the cyclotomic field Q(ζn​). That is why the entries of a table are things like −1, i, 21+5​​ or ζ73​, and why they can be held exactly.

```js
import { characterTable, symmetric, alternating } from "@ratmath/structures";

const T = characterTable(alternating(5));
console.log(String(T));
//       1a  2a  3a          5a          5b
// size   1  15  20          12          12
// χ₁     1   1   1           1           1
// χ₂     3  −1   0  (1 + √5)/2  (1 − √5)/2
// χ₃     3  −1   0  (1 − √5)/2  (1 + √5)/2
// χ₄     4   0   1          −1          −1
// χ₅     5   1  −1           0           0

T.degrees;                        // [1, 3, 3, 4, 5]:  1 + 9 + 9 + 16 + 25 = 60
T.classes[3];                     // { name: "5a", size: 12, order: 5, centralizerOrder: 5, representative, … }
T.irreducibles[1].values[3];      // a Cyclotomic: (1 + √5)/2, exactly
```
