Classes are named by the order of their elements and a letter. Characters are listed by degree with the trivial character first.

### Orthogonality

Class functions have an inner product

⟨χ,ψ⟩=∣G∣1​g∈G∑​χ(g)ψ(g)​,
and the irreducible characters are an orthonormal basis for it: ⟨χi​,χj​⟩=δij​. The columns are orthogonal too: for elements g,h,

χ∑​χ(g)χ(h)​={∣CG​(g)∣0​if g,h are conjugate,otherwise.​
`verify()` checks both relations and the degree sum on the exact values. Every table is verified this way before it is returned, so a wrong table cannot come out quietly.

### How the table is found

Nobody constructs the matrices. The method is Burnside's, made practical by Dixon and Schneider. Let C1​,…,Cr​ be the classes and write Ci​​ for the sum of the elements of Ci​ in the group algebra. These sums multiply among themselves,

Ci​​Cj​​=k∑​aijk​Ck​​,aijk​=#{(x,y)∈Ci​×Cj​:xy=gk​},
and the whole numbers aijk​ can be counted from the multiplication. In an irreducible representation each class sum acts as a scalar ωχ​(Ci​)=∣Ci​∣χ(gi​)/χ(1) (Schur's lemma), so the vector (ωχ​(Ck​))k​ is a common eigenvector of the matrices Mj​=(aijk​)i,k​. There are r such vectors and they are the only common eigenvectors: find them and the table follows.

Dixon's idea was to do the linear algebra in a finite field. Let e be the exponent of G and choose a prime p≡1(mode) with p>2∣G∣​. Then GF(p) contains the e-th roots of unity, the eigenvectors can be found there with no rounding, and the degree χ(1) is recovered from ⟨χ,χ⟩=1. To get back from GF(p) to genuine cyclotomic numbers: χ(g) is ∑k​mk​ζnk​ where mk​ counts how often ζnk​ is an eigenvalue of ρ(g), and a discrete Fourier transform over the powers of g gives

mk​=n1​l=0∑n−1​χ(gl)ζn−kl​.
This is a whole number between 0 and χ(1), so knowing it mod p is knowing it. `describe()` reports the field and the prime used.

```js
const S = characterTable(symmetric(5));
S.describe();     // "S5 of order 120: 7 classes, degrees 1, 1, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6; values in Q(ζ₆₀), found mod 61"
S.verify();       // { rows: true, columns: true, degrees: true, ok: true }
```

### Reading the group from its table

The kernel of a character is {g:χ(g)=χ(1)}, a normal subgroup, and every normal subgroup is an intersection of kernels of irreducible characters. So the table shows all normal subgroups and their orders, and in particular whether the group is simple. The number of characters of degree 1 is the index of the commutator subgroup, and the classes of size 1 make up the centre.

```js
const T4 = characterTable(symmetric(4));
T4.normalSubgroups().map((N) => N.order);   // [1, 4, 12, 24]
T4.irreducibles[2].kernel().order;           // 4: the Klein four-group is the kernel of the degree 2 character
T4.abelianizationOrder;                      // 2
characterTable(alternating(5)).isSimple;     // true
```

The table does not determine the group: the dihedral group D4​ and the quaternion group Q8​ have the same one. They are told apart by the [Frobenius–Schur indicator](https://ratmath.com/structures/class-functions.html), which needs to know which class the squares fall in.

### Cyclotomic numbers

Entries are `Cyclotomic` values: exact elements of Q(ζn​) with arithmetic, complex and Galois conjugates, and a float approximation. They print as whole numbers when they are, as ca+bd​​ when they lie in a quadratic field, and otherwise in powers of ζm​ for the smallest m that works.

```js
import { Cyclotomic } from "@ratmath/structures";
const z = Cyclotomic.root(5);                // ζ₅
String(z.add(z.conj()));                     // "(−1 + √5)/2", which is 2cos(72°)
String(Cyclotomic.root(8).add(Cyclotomic.root(8, 3)));   // "i√2"
z.add(z.conj()).conductor;                   // 5
```

Tables are computed for groups with up to 400 classes. The cost grows with the number of classes and with the exponent of the group: S7​ takes a tenth of a second, M11​ about a second.

### Try it

```js
// The table of S4, verified, and what it says about the group
const T = characterTable(symmetric(4));
PRINT(T.describe());
PRINT(String(T));
PRINT("orthogonality:", T.verify());
PRINT("normal subgroups have orders", T.normalSubgroups().map((N) => N.order), " centre:", T.centreOrder, " |G/G′|:", T.abelianizationOrder);

// A5: irrational entries, and simplicity read off the table
const A = characterTable(alternating(5));
PRINT(String(A));
const g = A.irreducibles[1].values[3];
PRINT("χ₂(5a) =", g, "≈", g.approx().re, "  its conjugate:", g.conjugates()[1], "  simple:", A.isSimple);

// Column orthogonality by hand for the two classes of 5-cycles
let s = Cyclotomic.int(0), t = Cyclotomic.int(0);
for (const chi of A.irreducibles) { s = s.add(chi.values[3].mul(chi.values[3].conj())); t = t.add(chi.values[3].mul(chi.values[4].conj())); }
PRINT("Σ|χ(5a)|² =", s, "= |C(g)|;   Σ χ(5a)χ(5b)* =", t);

// Same table, different groups
const entries = (G) => characterTable(G).irreducibles.map((c) => c.values.join(" ")).join(" | ");
PRINT("D4 and Q8 have the same entries:", entries(dihedral(4)) === entries(quaternion()));
characterTable(PSL(2, 7)).describe()
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/class-functions.html

Groups

## Working with characters

Once the irreducible characters are known, questions about representations become arithmetic on rows of numbers. How does a tensor product break up? What does a permutation action contain? What happens when a representation is restricted to a subgroup, or built up from one? Each is an inner product away.

### Decomposing a character

If ψ is the character of any representation, the irreducible χi​ occurs in it exactly ⟨ψ,χi​⟩ times, by orthonormality. So ψ=∑i​⟨ψ,χi​⟩χi​, and ⟨ψ,ψ⟩=∑mi2​ tells at a glance how complicated ψ is: it is irreducible exactly when this is 1.

```js
import { characterTable, symmetric } from "@ratmath/structures";

const T = characterTable(symmetric(4));
const [triv, sign, two, std, other] = T.irreducibles;     // degrees 1, 1, 2, 3, 3

T.regular.multiplicities();          // [1, 1, 2, 3, 3]: each irreducible occurs as often as its degree
const psi = T.classFunction([4, 0, 2, 1, 0]);             // values on the classes 1a, 2a, 2b, 3a, 4a
psi.norm;                            // 2
psi.decomposition();                 // "χ₁ + χ₄"
```

### Products and squares

The tensor product of two representations has character χψ, the product of values. The square χ2 splits further into a symmetric and an alternating part with characters

S2χ(g)=21​(χ(g)2+χ(g2)),Λ2χ(g)=21​(χ(g)2−χ(g2)).
These need the power map, which says in which class the squares of each class lie; `T.powerMap(k)` gives it for any power, and `chi.adams(k)` is the class function g↦χ(gk).

```js
std.mul(sign).equals(other);         // true: twisting by the sign swaps the two characters of degree 3
std.mul(std).decomposition();        // "χ₁ + χ₃ + χ₄ + χ₅"
std.symmetricSquare().decomposition();   // "χ₁ + χ₃ + χ₄"
std.alternatingSquare().decomposition(); // "χ₅"
```

### Real, complex and quaternionic

The Frobenius–Schur indicator of an irreducible character is

ι(χ)=∣G∣1​g∈G∑​χ(g2)∈{1,0,−1}.
It is 1 when the representation can be written with real matrices, 0 when the character is not real-valued, and −1 when the character is real but the representation is not (it is then quaternionic). The quaternion group's character of degree 2 has indicator −1; the dihedral group's has +1, though the two tables agree entry for entry. Also ∑χ​ι(χ)χ(1) counts the solutions of x2=1.

```js
characterTable(quaternion()).irreducibles[4].indicator();   // −1
characterTable(dihedral(4)).irreducibles[4].indicator();    //  1
characterTable(quaternion()).irreducibles[4].type;          // "quaternionic"
```

### Restriction and induction

A character of G restricts to a character of any subgroup H. In the other direction, a character φ of H induces a character of G of degree [G:H]φ(1):

IndHG​φ(g)=∣H∣1​x∈G,xgx−1∈H∑​φ(xgx−1).
Frobenius reciprocity ties the two together: ⟨Indφ,χ⟩G​=⟨φ,Resχ⟩H​.

```js
const G = symmetric(4);
const H = G.sylowSubgroup(2);                // a dihedral group of order 8
const TH = characterTable(H);

std.restrict(H).decomposition();             // in H's own characters
TH.irreducibles[4].induce(T).decomposition();   // "χ₄ + χ₅": degree 2·3 = 6
TH.irreducibles[4].induce(T).inner(std) === std.restrict(TH).inner(TH.irreducibles[4]);   // true
```

### Permutation characters

When G acts on a finite set, the permutation matrices give a representation whose character counts fixed points. By the [orbit-counting lemma](https://ratmath.com/structures/actions.html), ⟨π,χ1​⟩ is the number of orbits. And ⟨π,π⟩ is the number of orbits on pairs, so a transitive action is doubly transitive exactly when π=χ1​+χ with χ irreducible. The action on the cosets of H has character IndHG​1.

```js
import { action } from "@ratmath/structures";
const X = action(G, [0, 1, 2, 3], (g, x) => g[x]);
const pi = T.permutationCharacter(X);
pi.values.map(String);               // ["4", "0", "2", "1", "0"]
pi.decomposition();                  // "χ₁ + χ₄": doubly transitive
T.permutationCharacter(H).decomposition();   // "χ₁ + χ₃": the action on the three cosets of H
```

### Try it

```js
const G = symmetric(5);
const T = characterTable(G);
PRINT(String(T));
const irr = T.irreducibles;

// every product of two irreducible characters, decomposed
for (let i = 2; i < irr.length; i++) PRINT(`${irr[i].name}² =`, irr[i].mul(irr[i]).decomposition(), "  S² =", irr[i].symmetricSquare().decomposition(), "  Λ² =", irr[i].alternatingSquare().decomposition());

// permutation characters: points, and unordered pairs of points
const points = action(G, [0, 1, 2, 3, 4], (g, x) => g[x]);
const pairs = action(G, [[0,1],[0,2],[0,3],[0,4],[1,2],[1,3],[1,4],[2,3],[2,4],[3,4]], (g, [a, b]) => [g[a], g[b]].sort());
for (const [name, X] of [["points", points], ["pairs", pairs]]) {
  const pi = T.permutationCharacter(X);
  PRINT(`on ${name}:`, pi.values.join(", "), " =", pi.decomposition(), "  ⟨π,π⟩ =", pi.norm);
}

// Frobenius reciprocity for A5 inside S5
const H = G.derivedSubgroup();
const TH = characterTable(H);
for (const phi of TH.irreducibles) PRINT(`Ind ${phi.name} (degree ${phi.degree}) =`, phi.induce(T).decomposition());
for (const chi of irr) PRINT(`Res ${chi.name} =`, chi.restrict(TH).decomposition());

// indicators: every character of a symmetric group is real
irr.map((c) => c.indicator())
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/large-groups.html

Groups

## Large permutation groups

The Rubik's cube group has 43,252,003,274,489,856,000 elements, far too many to list. Yet six permutations of 48 stickers generate it, and from those six alone one can find its exact order, decide whether a scrambled position can be solved, and write the solution as a word in the face turns. The tool is a base and strong generating set, found by the Schreier–Sims algorithm.

### A chain of stabilisers

Let G act on the points 1,…,n. Pick points b1​,b2​,…,bk​ (a base) so that only the identity fixes all of them, and let G(i) be the subgroup fixing b1​,…,bi−1​:

G=G(1)≥G(2)≥⋯≥G(k+1)=1.
By the orbit–stabiliser theorem the index of each step is the size of an orbit, [G(i):G(i+1)]=∣biG(i)​∣, so

∣G∣=i=1∏k​​biG(i)​​.
For the cube the eighteen orbit sizes multiply to the famous number. Each orbit is stored with, for every point in it, one permutation in G(i) carrying bi​ there (a transversal). The whole group of 4.3×1019 elements is described by a few hundred permutations.

### Sifting

To test whether a permutation g is in G: look at where g sends b1​. If that point is not in the first orbit, g∈/G. Otherwise multiply by the inverse of the stored permutation u1​ that does the same; now gu1−1​ fixes b1​, and the question repeats one level down. If g falls through every level and what remains is the identity, then g=uk​⋯u2​u1​ is in G, and that product is the only way to write it with one transversal element from each level. Membership costs at most k multiplications, whatever the order of the group.

### Finding the chain

Schreier's lemma says the stabiliser of a point is generated by the elements ux​suxs−1​, with x running over the orbit and s over the generators. Sims's observation was that almost all of these are redundant: sift each one through the chain built so far and keep it only if something is left over, as a new generator at the level where it stuck. The version here is the deterministic one, so the chain is proved complete, not just probably complete. Each kept generator also remembers how it was made, which is what lets `word` return an expression in the original generators.

```js
import { schreierSims, largeGroups } from "@ratmath/structures";

const G = largeGroups.rubik();          // generators U, D, L, R, F, B on 48 stickers
G.order;                                // 43252003274489856000n
G.base.length;                          // 18
G.orbitLengths;                         // [24, 21, 18, 15, 24, 12, 9, 22, 20, 18, 16, 6, 14, 12, 10, 8, 6, 2]

const g = G.random({ seed: 3 });        // a scrambled cube
G.contains(g);                          // true
const w = G.word(g);                    // { text: "U L³ U D⁻¹ …", length, word, check: true }

// one corner twisted in place: fixes every point not on that corner
G.orbits().map((o) => o.length);        // [24, 24]: corner stickers and edge stickers never mix
```

Permutations are arrays of images counting from 0, as elsewhere in the library, while bases, orbits and blocks are reported counting from 1. Words from sifting are correct but long, tens of thousands of turns for the cube; finding short ones is a different and much harder problem.

### What else the chain gives

With a membership test, a good deal of group theory becomes computable for groups of any size. The normal closure of a set is found by conjugating by generators until nothing new appears; the commutator subgroup is the normal closure of the commutators of the generators, and iterating gives the derived series and a test for solvability. A transitive group is primitive if it preserves no partition of the points into blocks other than the two trivial ones; the smallest block containing two given points is found by Atkinson's method of merging classes.

```js
const M = largeGroups.mathieu(24);
M.order;                                // 244823040n
M.isPrimitive;                          // true
M.isPerfect;                            // true: M24 is simple
M.stabilizer(1).order;                  // 10200960n, the order of M23

const D = schreierSims([[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 0], [5, 4, 3, 2, 1, 0]]);   // symmetries of a hexagon
D.blockSystems();                       // [[[1,3,5],[2,4,6]], [[1,4],[2,5],[3,6]]]: two triangles, three diagonals
D.derivedSeries().map((H) => H.order);  // [12n, 3n, 1n], so it is solvable

G.derivedSubgroup().order;              // 21626001637244928000n: index 2 in the cube group
```

A group small enough to list can be handed to the rest of the library with `toGroup()`, which gives the same kind of object as `symmetric(4)` with classes, subgroups and Sylow theory.

### Try it

```js
// The cube group from its six face turns
const G = largeGroups.rubik();
PRINT("order:", G.order);
PRINT("orbit sizes down the chain:", G.orbitLengths.join(" · "));
PRINT("orbits on stickers:", G.orbits().map((o) => o.length));

// A scramble is in the group, and sifting writes it in face turns
const g = G.random({ seed: 2026 });
const w = G.word(g);
PRINT("scramble is in the group:", G.contains(g), "  word length:", w.length, "  word checks:", w.check);

// Swapping two edge stickers alone is not a legal position
const flip = g.slice();
const edge = G.orbits().find((o) => o.includes(2));
[flip[edge[0] - 1], flip[edge[1] - 1]] = [flip[edge[1] - 1], flip[edge[0] - 1]];
PRINT("after swapping two edge stickers:", G.contains(flip));

// The commutator subgroup has index 2: positions reached by an even number of quarter turns
PRINT("index of the commutator subgroup:", G.order / G.derivedSubgroup().order);

// Mathieu groups: orders, primitivity, point stabilisers
for (const n of [11, 12, 22, 23, 24]) {
  const M = largeGroups.mathieu(n);
  PRINT(`M${n}: order ${M.order}, primitive ${M.isPrimitive}, perfect ${M.isPerfect}, stabiliser of a point has order ${M.stabilizer(1).order}`);
}
largeGroups.symmetric(30).describe()
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/abelian.html

Modules

## Abelian groups

Every finitely generated abelian group is a product of cyclic groups, in exactly one standard way. Finding that product from generators and relations is integer linear algebra: the Smith normal form.

### The structure theorem

A finitely generated abelian group is isomorphic to

Z/d1​×Z/d2​×⋯×Z/dk​×Zr,d1​∣d2​∣⋯∣dk​, di​>1,
and the invariant factors di​ and the rank r are determined by the group. Splitting each di​ into prime powers gives the other standard form, by elementary divisors: Z/12≅Z/4×Z/3 by the Chinese remainder theorem. So the abelian groups of order n=∏piai​​ correspond to choosing a partition of each ai​, and there are ∏p(ai​) of them: six of order 72=2332.

```js
import { abelianGroup, cyclicProduct, abelianGroups } from "@ratmath/structures";

String(cyclicProduct([4, 6]));                       // "Z/2 × Z/12"
cyclicProduct([4, 6]).toString({ primary: true });   // "Z/2 × Z/4 × Z/3"
cyclicProduct([3, 5]).isCyclic;                      // true: Z/3 × Z/5 ≅ Z/15
abelianGroups(72).map(String);
// ["Z/72", "Z/3 × Z/24", "Z/2 × Z/36", "Z/6 × Z/12", "Z/2 × Z/2 × Z/18", "Z/2 × Z/6 × Z/6"]
abelianGroup([2, 4]).order;                          // 8n
```

### From generators and relations

Write the group additively, with generators x1​,…,xn​ and relations ∑j​rij​xj​=0. It is Zn/L, where L is spanned by the rows of the relation matrix R. Row operations on R (with integer multipliers, and swaps) change the relations but not L; column operations change the generators. The Smith normal form uses both to reach

URV=diag(d1​,d2​,…),d1​∣d2​∣⋯,
with U, V integer matrices of determinant ±1. The new generators y=V−1x then satisfy just di​yi​=0: the structure theorem, computed. The algorithm brings the smallest entry to the corner, divides it into its row and column, and if it fails to divide some other entry, adds that row in and goes again; the corner entry gets smaller each time, so it stops.

```js
import { fromRelations, smithForm } from "@ratmath/structures";

// three generators, three relations
const R = [[2, 4, 4], [-6, 6, 12], [10, -4, -16]];
smithForm(R).diagonal;              // [2n, 6n, 12n]
const G = fromRelations(R);
String(G);                          // "Z/2 × Z/6 × Z/12"
G.order;                            // 144n
G.generators.map((g) => `${g.order}: ${g.vector}`);   // ["2: 1,2,2", "6: 0,3,4", "12: 0,1,1"]

String(fromRelations([[2, 0, 0]], 3));   // "Z/2 × Z^2": no relation on two of the generators
```

The last line reads: the element x1​+2x2​+2x3​ has order 2, 3x2​+4x3​ has order 6, x2​+x3​ has order 12, and together they generate the group as a direct product. The tests check the Smith forms against @ratmath/linalg's own, and that each listed generator has exactly the stated order.

### Abelianising a group

For any group, G/G′ is abelian, the largest abelian quotient. Given a presentation, it is the abelian group with the same generators and the relators read additively (count how many times each generator appears, with signs). So `abelianInvariants` works for infinite groups too, and for a finite group (through a presentation of it) it agrees with [G.quotient(G.derivedSubgroup())](https://ratmath.com/structures/classes.html).

```js
import { abelianInvariants, presentation, GL, symmetric } from "@ratmath/structures";

String(abelianInvariants(GL(2, 3)));                            // "Z/2"
String(abelianInvariants(presentation("a, b | a^2, b^3, (ab)^3")));   // "Z/3"
String(abelianInvariants(presentation("a, b | [a, b]")));       // "Z^2"
```

### Try it

```js
// how many abelian groups of each order up to 32, and the biggest families
const counts = [];
for (let n = 1; n <= 32; n += 1) counts.push(abelianGroups(n).length);
PRINT("abelian groups of order 1 … 32:", counts.join(" "));
PRINT("order 32:", abelianGroups(32).map(String).join(", "));

// a random relation matrix and the group it presents
const R = [[3, 6, 9, 0], [2, 4, 8, 6], [0, 6, 0, 12]];
const S = smithForm(R);
PRINT("Smith form diagonal:", S.diagonal);
PRINT("group:", fromRelations(R), " in prime powers:", fromRelations(R).toString({ primary: true }));
abelianInvariants(directProduct(symmetric(3), cyclic(4)))
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/modules.html

Modules

## Modules over Q[x]

A matrix is a way for the variable x to act on vectors. Seen like that, the classification of matrices up to similarity is the same theorem as the classification of abelian groups, with polynomials in place of whole numbers.

### A matrix as a module

A module over a ring is like a vector space whose scalars come from the ring. Abelian groups are the modules over Z. A square matrix A over Q makes Qn a module over the polynomial ring Q[x]: a polynomial f acts on a vector v as f(A)v.

Q[x] has division with remainder, just like Z, so the same Smith normal form works over it, and the same structure theorem holds. The relations of this module are the columns of xI−A (they say that x acting on ej​ is the j-th column of A), so

Qn≅Q[x]/(f1​)⊕⋯⊕Q[x]/(fk​),f1​∣f2​∣⋯∣fk​,
where the fi​ are the monic non-constant diagonal entries of the Smith form of xI−A: the invariant factors of A. Their product is the characteristic polynomial and the last one is the minimal polynomial.

```js
import { matrixModule } from "@ratmath/structures";

const M = matrixModule([[2, 1, 0, 0], [0, 2, 0, 0], [0, 0, 2, 0], [0, 0, 0, 3]]);
String(M);                          // "Q[x]/(x − 2) ⊕ Q[x]/(x³ − 7x² + 16x − 12)"
String(M.minimalPolynomial);        // "x³ − 7x² + 16x − 12"
String(M.characteristicPolynomial); // "x⁴ − 9x³ + 30x² − 44x + 24"
M.elementaryDivisors.map((e) => String(e.divisor));   // ["x − 2", "x − 3", "x² − 4x + 4"]
M.isCyclic;                         // false: two summands
```

### The rational canonical form

On Q[x]/(f) with f=xd+cd−1​xd−1+⋯+c0​, the basis 1,x,…,xd−1 is moved by x as 1↦x↦x2↦⋯↦xd=−c0​−c1​x−⋯. That is the companion matrix of f: ones below the diagonal and −c0​,…,−cd−1​ down the last column. Putting the companion blocks of the invariant factors together gives the rational canonical form of A: two matrices are similar over Q exactly when they have the same one. It needs no eigenvalues, so it works when the characteristic polynomial does not factor. The elementary divisors (the prime-power parts of the invariant factors) give the finer primary decomposition; when they are all powers of linear factors they are the Jordan blocks.

```js
import { matrixModule } from "@ratmath/structures";

const M = matrixModule([[0, -1, 0], [1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 2]]);   // a quarter turn, and a stretch
String(M);                       // "Q[x]/(x³ − 2x² + x − 2)": cyclic
M.elementaryDivisors.map((e) => String(e.divisor));   // ["x − 2", "x² + 1"]
M.rationalCanonical.map((r) => r.map(String).join(" "));   // ["0 0 2", "1 0 -1", "0 1 2"]

matrixModule([[2, 0], [0, 2]]).isCyclic;   // false: Q[x]/(x − 2) ⊕ Q[x]/(x − 2)
matrixModule([[1, 1], [0, 1]]).isCyclic;   // true: Q[x]/((x − 1)²)
```

This is the same computation as @ratmath/linalg's `similarity(A)`, done a second way: the tests compare the invariant factors, minimal polynomials and rational canonical forms of the two on many matrices. The Smith form itself is available over any Euclidean domain as `smithForm(A, domain)`, with `ZZ` and `polynomialDomain("x")` built in.

```js
import { smithForm, polynomialDomain } from "@ratmath/structures";

const Qx = polynomialDomain("x");
smithForm([["x^2 - 1", "x - 1"], ["x + 1", "x^2 + x"]], Qx).diagonal.map(String);
// ["1", "x⁴ + x³ − 2x² − x + 1"]
```

### Try it

```js
// matrices that share a characteristic polynomial but are not similar
const cases = {
  "2I": [[2, 0, 0], [0, 2, 0], [0, 0, 2]],
  "one Jordan block": [[2, 1, 0], [0, 2, 1], [0, 0, 2]],
  "a block and a 1×1": [[2, 1, 0], [0, 2, 0], [0, 0, 2]],
};
for (const [name, A] of Object.entries(cases)) {
  const M = matrixModule(A);
  PRINT(`${name}: ${M}   minimal polynomial ${M.minimalPolynomial}`);
}

// the rational canonical form of a matrix whose characteristic polynomial does not factor over Q
const M = matrixModule([[1, 2, 0], [0, 1, 3], [1, 0, 1]]);
PRINT("invariant factors:", M.invariantFactors.map(String));
M.rationalCanonical.map((r) => r.map(String).join("  "))
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/homology.html

Modules

## Chain complexes and homology

Homology turns a space built from cells into a list of abelian groups. Once the cells and their boundaries are written down, everything is integer linear algebra: the Smith normal form of each boundary matrix gives the free part and the torsion.

### Chain complexes

A cell complex has nk​ cells in dimension k. The chain group Ck​=Znk​ has one generator per k-cell, and the boundary map ∂k​:Ck​→Ck−1​ sends a cell to the signed sum of the cells on its boundary. The boundary of a boundary is empty, so ∂k−1​∂k​=0, and the cycles ker∂k​ contain the boundaries im∂k+1​. The homology is the quotient

Hk​=ker∂k​/im∂k+1​.
`chainComplex` takes the list [∂1​,∂2​,…]. Each ∂k​ has one column per k-cell holding its boundary, and one row per (k−1)-cell. It checks ∂∂=0 and refuses a list that is not a chain complex.

```js
import { chainComplex } from "@ratmath/structures";

// The torus: one vertex v, edges a, b, one face glued along a b a⁻¹ b⁻¹.
// ∂a = v − v = 0, ∂b = 0, ∂(face) = a + b − a − b = 0.
const T = chainComplex([[[0, 0]], [[0], [0]]]);
String(T);                 // "H0 = Z, H1 = Z^2, H2 = Z"
T.eulerCharacteristic;     // 0 = 1 − 2 + 1

// The projective plane: face glued along a a, so ∂(face) = 2a.
const P = chainComplex([[[0]], [[2]]]);
String(P);                 // "H0 = Z, H1 = Z/2, H2 = 0"
```

### Homology from the Smith normal form

Invertible integer row and column operations bring ∂k​ to the diagonal form diag(d1​,…,drk​​,0,…) with d1​∣d2​∣⋯ (see [abelian groups](https://ratmath.com/structures/abelian.html)). Then ker∂k​ is free of rank nk​−rk​, and inside it im∂k+1​ is spanned by di​ei​ for the invariant factors of ∂k+1​. So

Hk​≅Znk​−rk​−rk+1​⊕di​>1⨁​Z/di​,
where the di​ are those of ∂k+1​. For the Klein bottle, glued along aba−1b, ∂2​=2b and H1​=Z⊕Z/2.

```js
const K = chainComplex([[[0, 0]], [[0], [2]]]);
String(K.homology(1));          // "Z/2 × Z"
chainComplex([[[0, 0]], [[2, 6], [4, 8]]]).homology(1).toString();   // "Z/2 × Z/4": Smith form diag(2, 4)
```

### Betti numbers, χ and other coefficients

The Betti number bk​ is the rank of Hk​, the number of copies of Z. Over a field the same recipe gives a vector space: over Q its dimension is bk​, and over Z/p the ranks are counted mod p, so torsion divisible by p shows up twice (the universal coefficient theorem: dimHk​(Z/p)=bk​+tk​+tk−1​, with tk​ the number of invariant factors of Hk​ divisible by p). In every case the alternating sum of Betti numbers is the Euler characteristic χ=∑(−1)knk​, which needs no homology at all.

```js
P.betti();                              // [1, 0, 0]
P.betti({ coefficients: "Z/2" });       // [1, 1, 1]: the Z/2 in H1 is counted in H1 and in H2
String(P.homology(2, { coefficients: "Z/2" }));   // "Z/2"
P.eulerCharacteristic;                  // 1
```

Glued polygons, simplicial complexes and their homology are in [@ratmath/geo](https://ratmath.com/geo/), which builds these boundary matrices for you.

### Try it

```js
// Real projective spaces RPⁿ: one cell per dimension, ∂k = 0 for k odd, 2 for k even
for (let n = 1; n <= 5; n += 1) {
  const mats = Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => [[(i + 1) % 2 === 0 ? 2 : 0]]);
  const C = chainComplex(mats);
  PRINT(`RP${n}:`, String(C), "  mod 2:", C.betti({ coefficients: "Z/2" }).join(" "), "  χ =", C.eulerCharacteristic);
}
// The boundary of a tetrahedron is a sphere: build ∂1 and ∂2 by hand
const edges = [[1, 2], [1, 3], [1, 4], [2, 3], [2, 4], [3, 4]];
const faces = [[1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 4], [1, 3, 4], [2, 3, 4]];
const d1 = [1, 2, 3, 4].map((v) => edges.map(([a, b]) => (v === b ? 1 : v === a ? -1 : 0)));
const d2 = edges.map((e) => faces.map((f) => {
  const i = f.findIndex((_, t) => f.filter((_, s) => s !== t).join() === e.join());
  return i < 0 ? 0 : i % 2 ? -1 : 1;
}));
chainComplex([d1, d2]).toString()
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/polynomials.html

Polynomials

## Polynomials in several variables

Choose the variables, and every polynomial in them lives in one ring. Arithmetic is exact, and a polynomial prints the way you would write it.

### The ring K[x₁, …, xₙ]

Fix a field K of coefficients and variables x1​,…,xn​. A monomial is a product of powers xa=x1a1​​⋯xnan​​ with whole-number exponents, and a polynomial is a finite sum

f=a∑​ca​xa,ca​∈K.
Two polynomials are equal exactly when they have the same coefficients. Sums and products follow the usual rules, with xa⋅xb=xa+b, and the result is a ring K[x1​,…,xn​]. The total degree of a monomial is a1​+⋯+an​, and the degree of f is the largest total degree among its terms.

The library stores only the nonzero terms (a sparse representation), so x100y−1 takes two entries, and multiplication costs the product of the numbers of terms.

### Making polynomials

```js
import { ring } from "@ratmath/structures";

const R = ring("x, y, z");            // Q[x, y, z], terms ordered by grevlex
const [x, y, z] = R.gens;             // the variables as polynomials
const f = R.poly("x^2 y - 3/2 x z + 1");
const g = x.pow(2).mul(y).sub(x.mul(z).mul("3/2")).add(1);
f.equals(g);                          // true
String(f);                            // "x²y − (3/2)xz + 1"
f.toText();                           // "x^2*y - 3/2*x*z + 1"   (R.poly reads this back)
f.toTeX();                            // "x^{2}y - \\frac{3}{2}xz + 1"
```

Text allows juxtaposition for products (`3xy`), `^` or `**` for powers, parentheses, and exact numbers in any form Core reads: `3/4`, `1.25`, `0.#3` (one third). Dividing is allowed when it comes out exactly, as in `(x^2 - 1)/(x - 1)`. Every method that takes a polynomial also takes text or a number.

### Looking inside

```js
f.degree();              // 3      total degree
f.degree("x");           // 2      degree in x
f.degrees();             // { x: 2, y: 1, z: 1 }
f.variables();           // ["x", "y", "z"]
f.coefficient({ x: 1, z: 1 });    // Rational −3/2
f.coefficients("x");     // [1, −(3/2)z, y]   as a polynomial in x, constant first
f.leadingTerm();         // x²y  (largest in the ring's monomial order)
f.terms();               // [{ coefficient, exponents, monomial }, …]
f.isHomogeneous();       // false
```

### Calculus and substitution

Partial derivatives are taken term by term: ∂x​(cxayb)=acxa−1yb. Substitution replaces a variable by a number or another polynomial of the ring; evaluating at a point gives an exact number.

```js
f.diff("x");                      // 2xy − (3/2)z
f.gradient();                     // [∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y, ∂f/∂z]
f.subs({ z: "x + y" });           // still in Q[x, y, z]
f.at({ x: 2, y: "1/3", z: 1 });   // Rational −2/3
f.compose({ x: "s + t", y: "s - t", z: 1 }, ring("s, t"));   // a change of variables
f.homogenize("h");                // every term brought up to degree 3 with a new variable h
```

### Other coefficient fields

A ring takes any field object RatMath uses, such as those of [@ratmath/algebraic](https://ratmath.com/algebraic/finite-fields.html). Over the integers modulo 5 the "freshman's dream" (x+y)5=x5+y5 is true, because every middle binomial coefficient is divisible by 5.

```js
import { ring, primeField, NumberField } from "@ratmath/structures";

const S = ring("x, y", { field: primeField(5) });
String(S.poly("(x + y)^5"));          // "x⁵ + y⁵"

const K = NumberField.quadratic(2);   // Q(√2)
const T = ring("x", { field: K });
const r = T.constant(K.gen);          // √2 as a constant polynomial
String(T.gens[0].add(r).pow(2));      // "x² + 2√2·x + 2"
```

### Try it

```js
const R = ring("x, y, z");
const f = R.poly("x^2 y - 3/2 x z + 1");
PRINT("f =", f, "  degree", f.degree(), "  degrees", JSON.stringify(f.degrees()));
PRINT("∂f/∂x =", f.diff("x"));
PRINT("f at (2, 1/3, 1) =", f.at({ x: 2, y: "1/3", z: 1 }));
PRINT("after x = s + t, y = s − t, z = 1:", f.compose({ x: "s + t", y: "s - t", z: 1 }, ring("s, t")));

// (x + y)^p = x^p + y^p in characteristic p
for (const p of [2, 3, 5, 7]) PRINT(`mod ${p}: (x + y)^${p} =`, ring("x, y", { field: primeField(p) }).poly(`(x + y)^${p}`));

// the binomial theorem in three variables: the coefficients of (x + y + z)^4
R.poly("(x + y + z)^4").terms().map((t) => `${t.coefficient}·${t.monomial}`)
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/orders.html

Polynomials

## Monomial orders and division

With one variable the terms of a polynomial line up by degree. With several there is a choice to make, and the choice decides what "the leading term" is and what a remainder looks like.

One polynomial, three orders

### What an order must do

A monomial order is a way of comparing monomials that is

- total: any two different monomials are comparable,

- compatible with multiplication: if xa>xb then xaxc>xbxc,

- a well-order: 1 is the smallest monomial, so no sequence of monomials decreases for ever.

The last property is what makes division stop. The three standard orders, with variables ranked x>y>z:

- lex (lexicographic): compare the exponent of x; if equal, of y; and so on. So x>y100. It is the order that eliminates variables.

- grlex (graded lexicographic): larger total degree wins, ties are broken by lex.

- grevlex (graded reverse lexicographic): larger total degree wins; among equals, the monomial with the smaller power of the last variable is larger. So xz in grevlex, although xz>y2 in grlex. It is the default here because computations in it tend to stay smallest.

```js
import { ring } from "@ratmath/structures";

const f = "x y^2 z + x^2 + y^3 + x z^2";
String(ring("x, y, z", { order: "lex" }).poly(f));      // "x² + xy²z + xz² + y³"
String(ring("x, y, z", { order: "grlex" }).poly(f));    // "xy²z + xz² + y³ + x²"
String(ring("x, y, z", { order: "grevlex" }).poly(f));  // "xy²z + y³ + xz² + x²"

// your own: any comparison of exponent lists, here lex with z ranked first
const zFirst = (a, b) => a[2] - b[2] || a[0] - b[0] || a[1] - b[1];
String(ring("x, y, z", { order: zFirst }).poly(f));     // "xz² + xy²z + x² + y³"
```

### The division algorithm

Given f and divisors g1​,…,gk​, the algorithm writes

f=q1​g1​+⋯+qk​gk​+r,
where no term of the remainder r is divisible by any leading term LT(gi​). It works like long division: look at the leading term of what is left; if some LT(gi​) divides it, subtract the right multiple of gi​ and record it in qi​ (taking the first gi​ that works); otherwise move that term to the remainder. Each step lowers the leading monomial, so the well-order guarantees an end.

With one divisor the remainder is zero exactly when it divides f. With several divisors something new happens: the remainder can depend on the order in which the divisors are listed. In the last two examples xy2−x=x(y2−1) is plainly a combination of the divisors, yet one listing leaves the remainder −x−y.

So a nonzero remainder does not show that f lies outside the ideal generated by the divisors. The cure is to replace the divisors by a Gröbner basis of the same ideal, for which the remainder is unique. The page on [Gröbner bases](https://ratmath.com/structures/groebner.html) takes that up.

```js
const R = ring("x, y", { order: "lex" });
const f = R.poly("x^2 y + x y^2 + y^2");
const { quotients, remainder } = f.divmod([R.poly("x y - 1"), R.poly("y^2 - 1")]);
quotients.map(String);     // ["x + y", "1"]
String(remainder);         // "x + y + 1"

f.rem([R.poly("y^2 - 1"), R.poly("x y - 1")]);   // 2x + 1: the other listing
R.poly("x^3 + y^3").div("x + y");                // x² − xy + y²  (exact division, or it throws)
```

### Try it

```js
// The same division in each order, and with the divisors swapped.
const f = "x^2 y + x y^2 + y^2", g1 = "x y - 1", g2 = "y^2 - 1";
for (const order of ["lex", "grlex", "grevlex"]) {
  const R = ring("x, y", { order });
  const a = R.poly(f).divmod([R.poly(g1), R.poly(g2)]);
  const b = R.poly(f).divmod([R.poly(g2), R.poly(g1)]);
  PRINT(order, " remainder:", a.remainder, "  swapped:", b.remainder);
  // check f = q1 g1 + q2 g2 + r
  const back = a.quotients[0].mul(g1).add(a.quotients[1].mul(g2)).add(a.remainder);
  PRINT("   adds back up:", back.equals(R.poly(f)));
}
// the three orders disagree about these pairs
const pairs = [["x z", "y^2"], ["x", "y^3"], ["x y^2", "x^2 z"]];
pairs.map(([a, b]) => ["lex", "grlex", "grevlex"].map((order) => {
  const R = ring("x, y, z", { order });
  return `${order}: ${R.poly(a)} ${R.cmp(R.poly(a).leadingExponents(), R.poly(b).leadingExponents()) > 0 ? ">" : "<"} ${R.poly(b)}`;
}).join("   "))
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/gcd.html

Polynomials

## Greatest common divisors

Polynomials in several variables factor uniquely, so any two of them have a greatest common divisor. Finding it without factoring is what keeps fractions of polynomials in lowest terms.

### Why a gcd exists

K[x1​,…,xn​] is a unique factorisation domain: every polynomial is a product of irreducible ones, uniquely up to order and constant factors. The gcd of f and g is the product of the irreducible factors they share, and it is determined up to a constant; the library returns the one whose leading coefficient is 1.

With one variable Euclid's algorithm finds it by repeated division with remainder. With several variables that fails as it stands: dividing x2+y by yx+1 as polynomials in x would need the coefficient 1/y.

### Contents and Gauss's lemma

Pick a main variable, say x, and view f as a polynomial in x whose coefficients are polynomials in the other variables. Its content is the gcd of those coefficients and its primitive part is f divided by the content:

(y2−1)x2+(y+1)x=content(y+1)​​⋅primitive part((y−1)x2+x)​​.
Gauss's lemma says the product of primitive polynomials is primitive. It follows that

gcd(f,g)=gcd(contf,contg)⋅gcd(ppf,ppg),
where the first gcd involves one variable fewer (so the method recurses) and the second can be found by a version of Euclid's algorithm.

### Pseudo-remainders

To divide a by b in x without fractions, first multiply a by a power of the leading coefficient of b. The pseudo-remainder r satisfies

lc(b)dega−degb+1a=qb+r,degx​r<degx​b.
Replacing (a,b) by (b,ppr) until the remainder is zero gives the gcd of the primitive parts. Taking the primitive part at every step (the primitive remainder sequence) stops the coefficients from growing out of hand.

```js
import { ring, gcd, lcm, content, primitivePart } from "@ratmath/structures";

const R = ring("x, y");
const f = R.poly("(y^2 - 1) x^2 + (y + 1) x");
String(content(f, "x"));                    // "y + 1"
String(primitivePart(f, "x"));              // "x²y − x² + x"
String(gcd(R.poly("x^3 - y^3"), R.poly("x^2 - y^2")));   // "x − y"
String(lcm(R.poly("x^2 - y^2"), R.poly("(x + y)^2")));   // "x³ + x²y − xy² − y³"
gcd([f, "x y + x", "x^2"]);                 // any number of polynomials: x
```

The same code runs over any exact field: modulo a prime, in GF(pᵏ), or over a number field.

### Square-free decomposition

A polynomial is square-free when no irreducible factor is repeated. In characteristic 0 a repeated factor of f is also a factor of its derivative: if f=pkh then f′=pk−1(kp′h+ph′). So gcd(f,∂f/∂x) collects the repeated factors, and Yun's algorithm uses a chain of such gcds to write

f=c⋅f1​⋅f22​⋅f33​⋯
with every fk​ square-free and no two sharing a factor. No factoring is needed, and it is the first step of factoring.

```js
import { squareFree, squareFreePart } from "@ratmath/structures";

const g = R.poly("3 (x + y)^3 (x - y)^2 (x y + 1)");
squareFree(g);            // { unit: 3, factors: [{ factor: xy + 1, multiplicity: 1 },
                          //                      { factor: x − y,  multiplicity: 2 },
                          //                      { factor: x + y,  multiplicity: 3 }] }
String(squareFreePart(g));   // the product of the distinct factors
```

### Try it

```js
const R = ring("x, y");
// two polynomials built with a hidden common factor
const hidden = R.poly("x^2 + x y - 2y + 1");
const a = hidden.mul("x^3 - y^2 + 3");
const b = hidden.mul("2 x y^2 + x - 5");
PRINT("a has", a.length, "terms, b has", b.length);
PRINT("gcd(a, b) =", gcd(a, b));
PRINT("lcm degree:", lcm(a, b).degree(), " = ", a.degree(), "+", b.degree(), "−", gcd(a, b).degree());

// repeated factors show up in gcd(f, f')
const f = R.poly("(x + y)^3 (x - y)^2 (x y + 1)");
PRINT("gcd(f, ∂f/∂x) =", gcd(f, f.diff("x")));
for (const { factor: p, multiplicity } of squareFree(f).factors) PRINT("  ", p, "with multiplicity", multiplicity);

// the same over the integers modulo 7
const S = ring("x, y", { field: primeField(7) });
gcd(S.poly("x^7 - x"), S.poly("(x - 3)(x - 5)(x^2 + 1)"))
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/factoring.html

Polynomials

## Factoring

x³ + y³ + z³ − 3xyz = (x + y + z)(x² + y² + z² − xy − xz − yz). Factoring finds the irreducible pieces of any polynomial with rational coefficients, in any number of variables.

### What the answer means

A polynomial is irreducible over Q when it is not a product of two polynomials of lower degree with rational coefficients. Every nonzero polynomial is a product

f=c⋅p1m1​​⋯pkmk​​
of irreducible ones, uniquely up to order and sign. The library returns each pi​ with whole-number coefficients having no common factor, and puts the leftover rational number in `unit`.

The field matters. x2+y2 is irreducible over Q but equals (x+iy)(x−iy) once i is allowed; x2−2y2 is irreducible over Q but splits over Q(√2). Curiously x2+y2−1, the circle, stays irreducible over every field of characteristic other than 2.

### How it is done: Kronecker's substitution

Factoring in one variable is a solved problem (the [Zassenhaus method](https://ratmath.com/algebraic/factoring.html) in @ratmath/algebraic). Kronecker's idea reduces several variables to one.

- Remove repeated factors with the square-free decomposition, and make the coefficients whole numbers.

- Substitute. Choose d larger than the degree of f in every variable and replace x1​→t,x2​→td,x3​→td2, … A monomial x1a1​​x2a2​​x3a3​​ becomes ta1​+a2​d+a3​d2: its exponents are the digits of one number in base d. Distinct monomials with all exponents below d therefore stay distinct, and the substitution can be undone.

- Factor the image f(t,td,td2,…) in the single variable t.

- Recombine. Any true factor g of f has exponents below d as well, so its image is a product of some of the one-variable factors. Try each product of 1, 2, … of them: read its exponents back in base d and test whether the result divides f. Whatever divides is a factor; if nothing does, f is irreducible.

For f=x2−y2 take d=3: the image is t2−t6=−t2(t−1)(t+1)(t2+1). The product t(t2+1)=t3+t reads back as y+x, which divides f.

The method is simple and always right, but the image has degree about dn, so it suits the polynomials of a course or a calculator rather than very large ones. The library refuses (with a clear error) when the image would pass degree 60,000.

```js
import { ring, factor, isIrreducible } from "@ratmath/structures";

const R = ring("x, y");
const { unit, factors } = factor(R.poly("2/3 x^4 y - 2/3 y^5"));
String(unit);                                   // "2/3"
factors.map((t) => [String(t.factor), t.multiplicity]);
        // [["y", 1], ["x + y", 1], ["x − y", 1], ["x² + y²", 1]]
isIrreducible(R.poly("x^2 + y^2 - 1"));         // true
```

### Try it

```js
const R = ring("x, y, z");
const show = (text) => {
  const { unit, factors } = factor(R.poly(text));
  const parts = factors.map(({ factor: p, multiplicity: m }) => `(${p})${m > 1 ? "^" + m : ""}`);
  PRINT(text, " = ", String(unit) === "1" ? "" : `${unit} · `, parts.join(" "));
};
show("x^3 + y^3 + z^3 - 3xyz");
show("x^4 + 4y^4");                 // Sophie Germain's identity
show("(x + y)^4 - z^4");
show("x^2 y^2 - 2 x y z + z^2");
show("x^6 - y^6");

// Which of x^n + y^n are irreducible over Q?  (Exactly the powers of 2.)
const S = ring("x, y");
Array.from({ length: 8 }, (_, i) => i + 1).filter((n) => isIrreducible(S.poly(`x^${n} + y^${n}`)))
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/resultants.html

Elimination

## Resultants and discriminants

Two equations in x and y can be turned into one equation in x alone. The resultant does it with a determinant, and tells you exactly where two curves meet.

Where two curves meet

= 0

= 0

### The resultant

Take two polynomials in x, with coefficients that may involve other variables:

f=am​xm+⋯+a0​,g=bn​xn+⋯+b0​.
They share a root (or a common factor) exactly when there are nonzero u,v with degu, degv and uf+vg=0. Written out coefficient by coefficient, that is a square system of m+n linear equations whose matrix is the Sylvester matrix: n shifted rows of the coefficients of f above m shifted rows of those of g. Its determinant is the resultant:

Resx​(f,g)=detSyl(f,g)=amn​bnm​i,j∏​(αi​−βj​),
where the αi​ and βj​ are the roots of f and g. So the resultant vanishes exactly when f and g have a common root in x.

When f and g also involve y, the resultant with respect to y is a polynomial in x alone. Its roots are the x-coordinates of the common points of the two curves (together with any x where both leading coefficients vanish). The variable y has been eliminated.

```js
import { ring, resultant, sylvester, discriminant } from "@ratmath/structures";

const R = ring("x, y");
const circle = R.poly("x^2 + y^2 - 1");
const parabola = R.poly("y - x^2");
String(resultant(circle, parabola, "y"));    // "x⁴ + x² − 1"
sylvester(circle, parabola, "y");            // [[1, 0, x² − 1], [1, −x², 0], [0, 1, −x²]]
```

### The discriminant

A polynomial has a repeated root exactly when it shares a root with its derivative. The discriminant is the resultant of f and f′, normalised:

Disc(f)=an​(−1)n(n−1)/2​Resx​(f,f′)=an2n−2​i<j∏​(αi​−αj​)2.
For a quadratic it is the familiar b2−4ac, and for x3+px+q it is −4p3−27q2. For a curve f(x,y)=0, the discriminant with respect to y vanishes at the x where the curve has a vertical tangent or a singular point.

### Determinants without fractions

Gaussian elimination on a matrix of polynomials would fill it with fractions. Bareiss elimination avoids them: the update

mij​←previous pivotmij​mkk​−mik​mkj​​
always divides exactly, because every entry it produces is itself a minor of the original matrix (Sylvester's identity). The entries stay polynomials and stay as small as possible, and the last pivot is the determinant.

```js
import { det, jacobian, hessian } from "@ratmath/structures";

const S = ring("x, y, z");
const [x, y, z] = S.gens;
String(det([[1, x, x.pow(2)], [1, y, y.pow(2)], [1, z, z.pow(2)]]));
        // the Vandermonde determinant (y − x)(z − x)(z − y), expanded

const T = ring("u, v");
const J = jacobian([T.poly("u^2 - v^2"), T.poly("2 u v")]);   // rows are gradients
String(det(J));                                              // "4u² + 4v²"
hessian(T.poly("u^3 - 3 u v^2"));                            // second partial derivatives
```

### Try it

```js
const R = ring("x, y");
const f = R.poly("x^2 + y^2 - 5");
const g = R.poly("x y - 2");
const rx = resultant(f, g, "y");
PRINT("eliminating y:", rx, "=", factor(rx).factors.map((t) => `(${t.factor})`).join(""));
const ry = resultant(f, g, "x");
PRINT("eliminating x:", ry);
// the four intersection points are (±1, ±2) and (±2, ±1); check them
for (const [px, py] of [[1, 2], [2, 1], [-1, -2], [-2, -1]]) PRINT(`  (${px}, ${py}):`, f.at([px, py]), g.at([px, py]));

// the discriminant of the general cubic
const C = ring("a, b, c, d, x");
PRINT("cubic discriminant:", discriminant(C.poly("a x^3 + b x^2 + c x + d"), "x"));

// a 5 × 5 determinant in one parameter: the characteristic polynomial of a path graph
const T = ring("t");
const M = Array.from({ length: 5 }, (_, i) => Array.from({ length: 5 }, (_, j) => (i === j ? T.gens[0] : Math.abs(i - j) === 1 ? -1 : 0)));
factor(det(M, T)).factors.map((t) => String(t.factor))
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/rational-functions.html

Elimination

## Rational functions

Fractions of polynomials form a field, just as fractions of whole numbers do. Because it is a field, everything linear algebra does with numbers it can do with formulas.

### The field of fractions

A rational function is a fraction p/q of polynomials with q=0, where p/q and r/s are the same when ps=qr. With

qp​+sr​=qsps+qr​,qp​⋅sr​=qspr​,(qp​)−1=pq​
they form a field, written K(x1​,…,xn​): the smallest field containing the polynomial ring, in the same way Q is built from the integers.

A fraction has many names, so the library keeps each one in a single standard form. The numerator and denominator are divided by their [gcd](https://ratmath.com/structures/gcd.html) (lowest terms); over Q both then get whole-number coefficients with no common factor and the denominator's leading coefficient is made positive. Two rational functions are equal exactly when their standard forms match, which is what makes "is this expression zero?" a question with a definite answer.

```js
import { ring, fractions } from "@ratmath/structures";

const R = ring("x, y");
const F = fractions(R);                      // the field Q(x, y)
const a = F.parse("1/(x + y)");
const b = F.parse("1/(x - y)");
String(a.add(b));                            // "2x/(x² − y²)"
String(a.div(b));                            // "(x − y)/(x + y)"
String(F.parse("(x^2 - y^2)/(x - y)"));      // "x + y"
a.add(b).num; a.add(b).den;                  // the two polynomials
a.diff("x");                                 // −1/(x² + 2xy + y²)   (the quotient rule)
a.subs({ y: 1 });                            // 1/(x + 1)
a.at({ x: 2, y: 1 });                        // Rational 1/3
```

### A field object

`fractions(R)` is also a field object: it carries `zero`, `one`, `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `div`, `neg` and `sign`, the shape every RatMath library uses to say "do arithmetic here". Anything written against that shape works with formulas. In particular the elimination, determinant and inverse of [@ratmath/linalg](https://ratmath.com/linalg/)'s `field` module accept it, which gives exact linear algebra with symbolic parameters:

```js
import { field } from "@ratmath/linalg";
import { ring, fractions } from "@ratmath/structures";

const F = fractions(ring("a, b, c, d"));
const [a, b, c, d] = F.gens;
field.det([[a, b], [c, d]], F);              // −bc + ad
field.inverse([[a, b], [c, d]], F);          // [[−d/(bc − ad), b/(bc − ad)], [c/(bc − ad), −a/(bc − ad)]]

const G = fractions(ring("t"));
field.rref([[1, G.parse("t"), 1], [G.parse("t"), 1, 1]], G);
        // x = 1/(t + 1), y = 1/(t + 1): the solution of the system as a formula in t
```

One caution comes with formulas: a result such as 1/(t+1) is correct as a rational function, and says nothing about the special value t=−1, where the original system has no solution. Elimination over the field treats any nonzero polynomial as a legitimate pivot.

### Why the gcd matters

Without reduction to lowest terms, fractions grow without bound: adding n fractions multiplies n denominators together. Each operation here ends with one gcd, and sums are formed over the least common denominator, so the answer is as small as it can be.

### Try it

```js
const F = fractions(ring("x, y"));
const a = F.parse("1/(x + y)"), b = F.parse("1/(x - y)");
PRINT("a + b =", a.add(b), "   a/b =", a.div(b));

// a telescoping sum: 1/(k(k+1)) = 1/k − 1/(k+1), with x in place of the starting point
const G = fractions(ring("x"));
let sum = G.zero;
for (let k = 0; k < 6; k += 1) sum = sum.add(G.parse(`1/((x + ${k})(x + ${k + 1}))`));
PRINT("six terms add up to", sum);

// Gauss–Jordan elimination written against the field interface: works for any field object
function inverse(K, m) {
  const n = m.length;
  const w = m.map((row, i) => [...row, ...m.map((_, j) => (i === j ? K.one : K.zero))]);
  for (let c = 0; c < n; c += 1) {
    const p = w.findIndex((row, i) => i >= c && K.sign(row[c]) !== 0);
    if (p < 0) throw new Error("singular");
    [w[c], w[p]] = [w[p], w[c]];
    const lead = w[c][c];
    w[c] = w[c].map((v) => K.div(v, lead));
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i += 1) if (i !== c) { const k = w[i][c]; w[i] = w[i].map((v, j) => K.sub(v, K.mul(k, w[c][j]))); }
  }
  return w.map((row) => row.slice(n));
}
const H = fractions(ring("t"));
const t = H.gens[0];
const M = [[t, 1, 0], [1, t, 1], [0, 1, t]];
for (const row of inverse(H, M)) PRINT(row.map(String).join("    "));
PRINT("the denominators vanish where det = ", det(M.map((row) => row.map((v) => H.from(v).num))), "= 0");
inverse(H, M)[0][0].at({ t: 2 })
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/groebner.html

Ideals and Gröbner bases

## Gröbner bases

A Gröbner basis is a set of generators for which division with remainder works. With one in hand, questions about a system of polynomial equations become mechanical: is this polynomial a consequence of those, are there solutions, how many.

### The trouble with division

With one variable, dividing f by g answers the question "is f a multiple of g?": yes exactly when the remainder is zero. With several variables and several divisors, the question becomes "is f a combination q1​g1​+⋯+qs​gs​?", that is, does f lie in the [ideal](https://ratmath.com/structures/ideals.html) the gi​ generate. [Division by a list](https://ratmath.com/structures/orders.html) still produces a remainder, but the remainder depends on the order in which the divisors are tried, and it can be nonzero for a polynomial that is in the ideal.

```js
import { ring, groebner } from "@ratmath/structures";

const R = ring("x, y");
const g1 = R.poly("x y - 1");
const g2 = R.poly("y^2 - 1");
const f = R.poly("x^2 y + x y^2 + y^2");
String(f.rem([g1, g2]));           // "x + y + 1"
String(f.rem([g2, g1]));           // "2x + 1": a different remainder
String(R.poly("x - y").rem([g1, g2]));   // "x − y", yet x − y = y·g1 − x·g2 is in the ideal
```

The cure is to replace the generators by a better set that generates the same ideal.

### What a Gröbner basis is

Fix a [monomial order](https://ratmath.com/structures/orders.html), and write LM(f) for the leading monomial of f. A finite set G inside an ideal I is a Gröbner basis of I when

for every nonzero f∈I,LM(f) is divisible by LM(g) for some g∈G.
Division by such a set behaves the way division should. The remainder no longer depends on the order of the divisors; it is the unique representative of f modulo I built from monomials that no leading monomial of G divides (the normal form of f). In particular

f∈I⟺the remainder of f on division by G is 0.
Every ideal has one (this is Hilbert's basis theorem at work), and once the basis is reduced, meaning each element has leading coefficient 1 and no term divisible by another element's leading monomial, it is unique. So two ideals are equal exactly when their reduced Gröbner bases are the same list.

```js
const G = groebner([g1, g2]);
G.basis.map(String);              // ["x − y", "y² − 1"]
String(G.reduce(f));              // "2y + 1", whatever the order of division
G.contains(R.poly("x - y"));      // true
```

### Buchberger's algorithm

Division gets stuck because leading terms can cancel. The simplest cancellation between two polynomials is their S-polynomial: multiply each by the smallest monomial that makes the leading terms equal, and subtract.

S(f,g)=LT(f)L​f−LT(g)L​g,L=lcm(LM(f),LM(g)).
Buchberger's criterion. G is a Gröbner basis of the ideal it generates exactly when every S(gi​,gj​) leaves remainder zero on division by G.

That is a finite test, and it is also an algorithm: whenever an S-polynomial leaves a nonzero remainder, add the remainder to the set and continue. The ideal of leading monomials grows each time, and such a chain cannot grow for ever, so the process stops.

Most pairs never need to be reduced. If two leading monomials share no variable, the S-polynomial always reduces to zero. And a pair can be skipped when a third element's leading monomial divides their lcm and both pairs with it are dealt with. This library applies both tests (in the form due to Gebauer and Möller), takes the pair with the smallest lcm first, and over the rationals works with whole-number coefficients so that no fractions are carried. `G.stats` says how much work was done.

```js
import { sPolynomial } from "@ratmath/structures";

String(sPolynomial(g1, g2));      // "x − y": y·g1 − x·g2
G.stats;                          // { pairs: 2, zero: 1, skipped: 1, added: 3 }
```

### Certificates

An answer of this kind should be checkable without trusting the algorithm. Two checks are built in.

- G.express(f) writes a member of the ideal as a combination of the original generators, f=∑qi​fi​, and multiplies it out to confirm. That is a proof of membership anyone can verify by expanding.

- G.verify() re-runs Buchberger's criterion from scratch on the finished basis, and checks that the basis and the generators define the same ideal.

```js
const ex = G.express(R.poly("x - y"));
ex.cofactors.map(String);         // ["y", "−x"]:  x − y = y·(xy − 1) − x·(y² − 1)
ex.check;                         // true
G.verify();   // { generatorsReduce: true, sPairsReduce: true, basisInIdeal: true, sPairsChecked: 2, ok: true }
```

### The order matters

The basis depends on the monomial order, and different orders are good for different things.

- lex eliminates: the basis contains polynomials in the last variable alone, then in the last two, and so on, like a triangular linear system. It is also the slowest and its polynomials are the largest.

- grevlex (the default) usually gives the smallest basis in the least time. Use it for membership, dimension, and counting solutions.

- eliminationOrder(n, [i, j]) is the middle way: it ranks the listed variables above the rest and is grevlex within each block. This is what elimination uses.

```js
const L = ring("x, y, z", { order: "lex" });
const twisted = ["y - x^2", "z - x^3"];           // the twisted cubic (t, t², t³)
groebner(twisted.map((t) => L.poly(t))).basis.map(String);
      // ["y³ − z²", "xz − y²", "xy − z", "x² − y"]: the first involves y and z only
const V = ring("x, y, z");                        // grevlex
groebner(twisted.map((t) => V.poly(t))).basis.map(String);
      // ["y² − xz", "xy − z", "x² − y"]: the three quadrics that cut out the curve
```

### What the basis tells you at once

The leading monomials alone carry a good deal of information.

- The basis is {1} exactly when the equations have no common solution, even over the complex numbers (G.isTrivial).

- The monomials that no leading monomial divides are the standard monomials. They form a basis of the quotient ring as a vector space.

- There are finitely many standard monomials exactly when the system has finitely many solutions, and then their number is the number of solutions counted with multiplicity (G.quotientDimension).

- G.dimension is the dimension of the solution set: 0 for points, 1 for curves, 2 for surfaces.

```js
const C = groebner([R.poly("x^2 + y^2 - 1"), R.poly("x y - 1/2")]);
C.dimension;                             // 0
C.standardMonomials().map(String);       // ["1", "y", "x", "y²"]
C.quotientDimension;                     // 4: a circle and a hyperbola meet in 4 points, with multiplicity
```

### How far it goes

The worst case for Gröbner bases is very bad (degrees can grow doubly exponentially in the number of variables), but the systems that come up in practice are usually far from it. As a guide, on standard benchmarks this implementation takes about 20 ms for cyclic-5 (5 variables, 70 solutions), 50 ms for katsura-5 (6 variables, 32 solutions) and a few seconds for cyclic-6 (156 solutions). The options `maxPairs` and `timeLimit` (milliseconds) stop a run that is going nowhere. Coefficients may come from any exact field: the rationals, a prime field, a finite field or a number field.

### Try it

```js
// Three symmetric equations: power sums 6, 14, 36
const L = ring("x, y, z", { order: "lex" });
const sys = ["x + y + z - 6", "x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 14", "x^3 + y^3 + z^3 - 36"].map((t) => L.poly(t));
const G = groebner(sys);
PRINT("lex basis:");
for (const g of G.basis) PRINT("  ", g);
PRINT("last one factors:", factor(G.basis[0]).factors.map((t) => `(${t.factor})`).join(""));
PRINT("solutions with multiplicity:", G.quotientDimension, " verified:", G.verify().ok);

// A certificate: e₃ − 6 is in the ideal, so xyz = 6 follows from the three equations
const f = L.poly("x y z - 6");
const ex = G.express(f);
PRINT("xyz − 6 =", ex.cofactors.map((q, i) => `(${q})·f${i + 1}`).join(" + "));
PRINT("multiplied out and compared:", ex.check);

// The same ideal in grevlex, and the work each order took
const V = ring("x, y, z");
const H = groebner(sys.map((p) => p.into(V)));
PRINT("grevlex basis:", H.basis.map(String).join(",  "));
[G.stats, H.stats]
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/ideals.html

Ideals and Gröbner bases

## Ideals

An ideal is everything that follows from a set of polynomial equations by adding and multiplying. This page is the dictionary between ideals and the shapes their equations cut out, and how each entry is computed.

### Ideals

Let R=K[x1​,…,xn​]. An ideal of R is a set of polynomials closed under addition and under multiplication by any polynomial. The ideal generated by f1​,…,fs​ is the set of all combinations

⟨f1​,…,fs​⟩={q1​f1​+⋯+qs​fs​:qi​∈R}.
These are exactly the equations that follow from f1​=0,…,fs​=0 by adding and multiplying. Hilbert's basis theorem says every ideal of R is generated by finitely many polynomials, so every ideal can be held as a list.

The same ideal has many generating lists. To compare ideals, or to test whether a polynomial is in one, the library computes a [Gröbner basis](https://ratmath.com/structures/groebner.html), the first time it is needed.

```js
import { ring, ideal } from "@ratmath/structures";

const R = ring("x, y, z");
const I = ideal(R, ["x z - y^2", "x^3 - z^2"]);
String(I);                         // "(−y² + xz, x³ − z²)"
I.contains("x^3 z - y^2 z^2");     // false
I.contains("x^4 z - x z^3");       // true: x z · (x³ − z²)
String(I.reduce("y^4"));           // "x²z²": the normal form of y⁴ modulo I
I.dimension;                       // 1: the solution set is a curve
I.equals(ideal(R, ["y^2 - x z", "z^2 - x^3", "x^4 z - x z^3"]));   // true
```

### Algebra and geometry

An ideal I has a solution set V(I), the points where every polynomial of I vanishes. Operations on ideals correspond to operations on solution sets:

| Ideals | Solution sets | Method |

| I+J (generators of both) | V(I)∩V(J) | I.add(J) |

| I⋅J (products of generators) | V(I)∪V(J) | I.mul(J) |

| I∩J | V(I)∪V(J) | I.intersect(J) |

| I:J={f:fJ⊆I} | contains V(I)∖V(J) | I.quotient(J) |

| I:f∞ (saturation) | the closure of V(I)∖V(f) | I.saturate(f) |

| I∩K[some variables] | the closure of the projection | I.eliminate(vars) |

| I​ | the same set V(I) | I.radical() |

The product and the intersection have the same solutions, and IJ⊆I∩J always, but they can differ as ideals: ⟨x⟩⋅⟨x⟩=⟨x2⟩ while ⟨x⟩∩⟨x⟩=⟨x⟩.

```js
const A = ideal(R, ["x", "y"]);        // the z-axis
const B = ideal(R, ["z"]);             // the plane z = 0
String(A.add(B));                      // "(x, y, z)": the origin
A.intersect(B).basis.map(String);      // ["yz", "xz"]: the axis together with the plane
A.mul(B).equals(A.intersect(B));       // true here

const S = ring("x, y");
const J = ideal(S, ["x^2", "x y"]);    // the y-axis, with something extra at the origin
J.quotient("x").basis.map(String);     // ["y", "x"]
J.radical().basis.map(String);         // ["x"]
J.saturate("y").basis.map(String);     // ["x"]: away from y = 0 the ideal is just (x)
```

Intersections are computed with a classical trick: introduce a new variable t, form tI+(1−t)J, and eliminate t. The quotient by one polynomial is (I∩⟨g⟩)/g, and saturation adds 1−tf and eliminates t.

### Elimination

The elimination theorem: if G is a Gröbner basis of I for an order in which every monomial containing x1​,…,xk​ ranks above every monomial without them, then the elements of G that do not involve x1​,…,xk​ are a Gröbner basis of I∩K[xk+1​,…,xn​]. So eliminating variables is a matter of choosing the order and reading off part of the basis.

A typical use is finding the equation of a curve or surface given by parameters. The curve x=t2−1, y=t3−t is the solution set of x−t2+1=0, y−t3+t=0 in (t,x,y)-space, projected to the (x,y)-plane:

```js
const T = ring("t, x, y");
ideal(T, ["x - t^2 + 1", "y - t^3 + t"]).eliminate("t").basis.map(String);
      // ["x³ + x² − y²"]: the nodal cubic y² = x²(x + 1)

const U = ring("s, t, x, y, z");
ideal(U, ["x - s t", "y - s", "z - t^2"]).eliminate(["s", "t"]).basis.map(String);
      // ["y²z − x²"]: the Whitney umbrella
```

Compare [resultants](https://ratmath.com/structures/resultants.html), which eliminate one variable from two polynomials. Elimination ideals handle any number of each and add no extra factors.

### Radicals and the Nullstellensatz

Different ideals can have the same solutions: ⟨x⟩ and ⟨x2⟩ both describe x=0. The radical I​ is the set of polynomials some power of which lies in I. Hilbert's Nullstellensatz says that over an algebraically closed field such as the complex numbers,

f vanishes at every point of V(I)⟺f∈I​,
and in particular V(I) is empty exactly when 1∈I. So "does f=0 follow from the equations?" has a definite algebraic answer, and it can be tested without finding the radical: f∈I​ exactly when 1∈I+⟨1−tf⟩ for a new variable t (Rabinowitsch's trick).

```js
const Q = ideal(S, ["x^2", "y^3"]);
Q.contains("x + y");                   // false
Q.radicalContains("x + y");            // true
Q.exponentOf("x + y");                 // 4: (x + y)⁴ is in Q and (x + y)³ is not

const cert = Q.radicalContains("x + y", { certificate: true });
cert.power;                            // 4
cert.cofactors.map(String);            // ["x² + 4xy + 6y²", "4x + y"]
      // (x + y)⁴ = (x² + 4xy + 6y²)·x² + (4x + y)·y³, and cert.check confirms it
```

The certificate is a proof: an explicit identity fk=∑ci​fi​ that can be checked by multiplying out. This is how a theorem of geometry is proved by algebra: write the hypotheses as polynomial equations, and show the conclusion lies in the radical of the ideal they generate.

`I.radical()` itself is computed for ideals with finitely many solutions (by adding the square-free part of each variable's minimal polynomial, a method due to Seidenberg), for ideals with one generator, and for ideals generated by monomials. It throws for the rest; `radicalContains` works for every ideal.

### Prime and maximal ideals

An ideal P=R is prime when fg∈P forces f∈P or g∈P; its solution set cannot be split into two smaller ones. It is maximal when no proper ideal is larger; over the complex numbers the maximal ideals are the single points ⟨x1​−a1​,…,xn​−an​⟩. Over the rationals a maximal ideal is a point together with all its conjugates.

```js
ideal(S, ["x^2 + y^2 - 1"]).isPrime();        // true: the circle is one piece
ideal(S, ["x y"]).isPrime();                  // false: two lines
ideal(S, ["x - 1", "y - 2"]).isMaximal();     // true: the point (1, 2)
ideal(S, ["x^2 - 2", "y - x"]).isMaximal();   // true: the pair (±√2, ±√2), one point over Q
ideal(S, ["x^2 - 1", "y"]).isMaximal();       // false: two rational points
```

`isMaximal` is decided over Q for every ideal. `isPrime` is decided for ideals with finitely many solutions, for one generator, and for linear generators, and returns `null` otherwise: a general test needs primary decomposition, which this library does not have.

### Try it

```js
// Where do a sphere and a cylinder meet, seen from above?
const R = ring("x, y, z");
const sphere = "x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 4";
const cylinder = "(x - 1)^2 + y^2 - 1";
const curve = ideal(R, [sphere, cylinder]);          // Viviani's curve
PRINT("dimension:", curve.dimension);
PRINT("shadow on the xz-plane:", curve.eliminate("y").basis.map(String).join(", "));
PRINT("shadow on the yz-plane:", curve.eliminate("x").basis.map(String).join(", "));

// A theorem by algebra: on that curve, z² = 4 − 2x. With a certificate.
const cert = curve.radicalContains("z^2 + 2x - 4", { certificate: true });
PRINT("z² + 2x − 4 vanishes on the curve:", cert.holds, " power:", cert.power);
PRINT("  =", cert.cofactors.map((c, i) => `(${c})·(${curve.generators[i]})`).join(" + "), " check:", cert.check);

// Two ideals with the same solutions
const S = ring("x, y");
const fat = ideal(S, ["x^2", "x y", "y^2"]);
const thin = ideal(S, ["x", "y"]);
PRINT("fat ⊂ thin:", fat.isSubsetOf(thin), " equal:", fat.equals(thin), " radical of fat:", fat.radical().basis.map(String).join(", "));
PRINT("degree (points with multiplicity):", fat.degree, "against", thin.degree);
fat.equals(thin.pow(2))
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/systems.html

Ideals and Gröbner bases

## Solving polynomial systems

A system of polynomial equations with finitely many solutions can be solved exactly: every solution found, counted with its multiplicity, and each coordinate given as an algebraic number, not a rounded decimal.

### How many solutions?

Let I be the [ideal](https://ratmath.com/structures/ideals.html) generated by the equations, and G a [Gröbner basis](https://ratmath.com/structures/groebner.html) of it. Three things can happen, and the basis says which.

- No solutions, even over the complex numbers: exactly when G={1}. (This is the Nullstellensatz.)

- Finitely many: exactly when, for every variable xi​, some power xik​ is the leading monomial of an element of G. Then the quotient ring K[x1​,…,xn​]/I is a finite-dimensional vector space, and its dimension is the number of complex solutions counted with multiplicity.

- Infinitely many otherwise: a curve, a surface or more, whose dimension is I.dimension.

```js
import { ring, ideal, solve } from "@ratmath/structures";

const R = ring("x, y");
const I = ideal(R, ["x^2 + y^2 - 1", "y - x^2"]);     // a circle and a parabola
I.dimension;        // 0
I.degree;           // 4 complex solutions, with multiplicity
```

### Triangular form

With the lex order, a Gröbner basis of a system with finitely many solutions contains a polynomial in the last variable alone. Solve it, substitute each root into the rest, and continue upwards, just as with back-substitution in linear algebra.

```js
import { groebner } from "@ratmath/structures";

const L = ring("x, y", { order: "lex" });
groebner([L.poly("x^2 + y^2 - 1"), L.poly("y - x^2")]).basis.map(String);
      // ["y² + y − 1", "x² − y"]:  y = (−1 ± √5)/2, then x = ±√y
```

That is fine by hand, but it means computing with roots of roots. The library uses a different route that needs only one polynomial in one variable.

### One polynomial for all the solutions

Choose a linear form u=c1​x1​+⋯+cn​xn​ that takes a different value at each solution (a separating form; almost every choice works). Multiplication by u is a linear map on the finite-dimensional quotient ring, and its minimal polynomial m(u) has exactly the values of u at the solutions as its roots. Each coordinate is then a polynomial in u:

m(u)=0,x1​=p1​(u),…,xn​=pn​(u).
This is a rational univariate representation of the solution set. Every solution corresponds to one root of m, so the solutions are counted and located by [isolating the roots](https://ratmath.com/algebraic/) of a single polynomial with exact arithmetic.

```js
const s = solve(R, ["x^2 + y^2 - 1", "y - x^2"]);
s.count;                                   // 4 distinct complex solutions
s.real.length;                             // 2 of them real
s.parametrization.form;                    // { x: 1, y: 0 }: u = x separates them
s.parametrization.minimalPolynomial.map(String);   // ["-1", "0", "1", "0", "1"]: u⁴ + u² − 1
s.parametrization.coordinates.y.map(String);       // ["0", "0", "1", "0"]: y = u²
```

The polynomial m is then factored over the rationals. Each irreducible factor is one component: a set of solutions that are conjugate to each other, with coordinates in the number field Q(θ) that the factor defines. The solutions are algebraic numbers held exactly, so they can be compared, added, and printed to any number of digits.

```js
const p = s.real[1];
String(p);                 // "(x = 0.786151377757…, y = 0.618033988749…)"
p.approx;                  // { x: 0.7861513777574233, y: 0.6180339887498948 }
p.values.y;                // the exact algebraic number (√5 − 1)/2
p.coordinates.y;           // θ², an element of Q(θ) with θ⁴ + θ² − 1 = 0
s.components.map((c) => [c.degree, c.realCount]);     // [[4, 2]]

solve(R, ["x^2 + y^2 - 5", "x y - 2"]).real.map(String);
      // ["(x = -2, y = -1)", "(x = -1, y = -2)", "(x = 1, y = 2)", "(x = 2, y = 1)"]
```

### Multiplicity

A tangent line meets a parabola at one point that counts twice. In the algebra, the quotient ring has dimension 2 but only one point, and the ideal is not [radical](https://ratmath.com/structures/ideals.html). The solver reports both numbers, and finds the points from the radical.

```js
const t = solve(R, ["y - x^2", "y"]);     // the parabola and its tangent at the vertex
t.count;            // 1
t.multiplicity;     // 2
t.radical;          // false
```

Bézout's theorem says two plane curves of degrees d and e with no common component meet in de points, counted with multiplicity, in the complex projective plane. The count here is of the points in the affine plane, so it is at most de, and less when some intersections are at infinity.

### Complex solutions, none, or too many

```js
const c = solve(R, ["x^2 - y", "y^2 - x"], { complex: true });
c.real.map(String);       // ["(x = 0, y = 0)", "(x = 1, y = 1)"]
c.complex.map(String);    // ["(x = −1/2 − i√3/2, y = −1/2 + i√3/2)", "(x = −1/2 + i√3/2, y = −1/2 − i√3/2)"]

solve(R, ["x^2 + y^2 - 1", "x - 2"]).real;       // []: two complex solutions, none real
solve(R, ["x y - 1", "x"]).count;                // 0: no solutions at all
solve(R, ["x y - 1", "x^2 y - x"]);              // { finite: false, dimension: 1, … }: the whole hyperbola
```

When there are infinitely many solutions there is no list to give. [Elimination](https://ratmath.com/structures/ideals.html) then describes the solution set through its projections, and adding equations (a plane, a normalisation) cuts it down to points.

The solver works over the rationals. The linear algebra is exact and happens in a space whose dimension is the number of solutions, so systems with up to a few hundred solutions are practical.

### Try it

```js
// Three spheres: where do they meet? (The problem behind GPS.)
const R = ring("x, y, z");
const spheres = ["x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 9", "(x - 4)^2 + y^2 + z^2 - 9", "(x - 2)^2 + (y - 3)^2 + z^2 - 6"];
const s = solve(R, spheres);
PRINT("solutions:", s.count, " real:", s.real.length);
for (const p of s.real) PRINT("  ", p, "  ≈", Object.values(p.approx).map((v) => v.toFixed(6)).join(", "));

// Lagrange multipliers: the extreme values of x y on the ellipse x² + 4y² = 8
const L = ring("x, y, k");
const crit = solve(L, ["y - 2 k x", "x - 8 k y", "x^2 + 4 y^2 - 8"]);
PRINT("critical points:", crit.count);
for (const p of crit.real) PRINT("  ", p, "  x y =", p.approx.x * p.approx.y);

// A system whose solutions need a field of degree 4
const S = ring("x, y");
const q = solve(S, ["x^2 + y^2 - 4", "x y - 1"]);
PRINT("minimal polynomial of the component:", q.components[0].minimalPolynomial.join(", "), "(constant first)");
PRINT("x =", q.components[0].coordinates.x, "  y =", q.components[0].coordinates.y);
q.real.map(String)
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/quotients.html

Ideals and Gröbner bases

## Quotient rings

Setting some polynomials to zero makes a new ring. In it x can be a square root of 2, or a number whose square is 0, or a point on a circle. This page shows how to compute in such a ring and how to tell what kind of ring it is.

### Computing modulo an ideal

Let I be an [ideal](https://ratmath.com/structures/ideals.html) of R=K[x1​,…,xn​]. Two polynomials are congruent modulo I when their difference is in I. The congruence classes can be added and multiplied through any representatives, and they form the quotient ring R/I: the polynomials with the relations f=0 for f∈I imposed. If I is the ideal of a curve or surface, R/I is the ring of polynomial functions on it.

To compute in R/I each class needs one preferred representative, and a [Gröbner basis](https://ratmath.com/structures/groebner.html) provides it: the remainder on division, which uses only standard monomials (those no leading monomial divides). The standard monomials are a basis of R/I as a vector space over K.

```js
import { ring, ideal } from "@ratmath/structures";

const R = ring("x");
const A = ideal(R, ["x^2 - 2"]).quotientRing();
String(A);                       // "Q[x]/(x² − 2)"
const a = A.gens[0];             // the class of x: a square root of 2
String(a.mul(a));                // "2"
String(a.add(1).pow(3));         // "5x + 7":  (1 + √2)³ = 7 + 5√2
String(a.add(1).inverse());      // "x − 1":   1/(1 + √2) = √2 − 1
A.dimension;                     // 2: the basis is 1, x
A.isField();                     // true
```

### Units, zero divisors, nilpotents

In a quotient ring the elements sort themselves into kinds that do not occur among polynomials.

- A unit has an inverse. The class of f is a unit exactly when I+⟨f⟩ is the whole ring, that is, when f has no zero on V(I) over the complex numbers.

- A zero divisor is a nonzero element with a nonzero partner whose product is zero. They appear when the solution set has several pieces: a function that vanishes on one piece times one that vanishes on the other.

- A nilpotent element has a power equal to zero. They appear when the ideal is not radical, and record multiplicity.

```js
const B = ideal(R, ["x^2 - 1"]).quotientRing();     // two points, x = 1 and x = −1
const b = B.gens[0];
String(b.sub(1).mul(b.add(1)));      // "0": two nonzero elements with product zero
b.sub(1).isZeroDivisor();            // true
b.isUnit();                          // true: x·x = 1
B.isField();                         // false

const D = ideal(R, ["x^2"]).quotientRing();         // the dual numbers
const e = D.gens[0];
e.isNilpotent();                     // true: ε² = 0
String(e.add(3).pow(4));             // "108x + 81": (3 + ε)⁴ = 3⁴ + 4·3³ε, value and derivative together
String(e.add(1).inverse());          // "−x + 1"
D.isReduced();                       // false
```

When the quotient is finite-dimensional, all of this is linear algebra. Multiplication by an element is a linear map on the standard monomials (`a.matrix()`); the element is a unit exactly when that matrix is invertible, a zero divisor when it is singular, and nilpotent when the matrix is. Its minimal polynomial is the minimal polynomial of the matrix.

### Fields and domains

R/I is a field⟺I is maximal,R/I is an integral domain⟺I is prime.
