Every finite extension of Q arises as a quotient by a maximal ideal: Q[x]/⟨x2−2⟩=Q(2​), Q[x]/⟨x2+1⟩=Q(i), and with more variables, fields generated by several roots at once. `A.asField()` hands the quotient back as a field that a new polynomial ring can take its coefficients from.

```js
import { gcd } from "@ratmath/structures";

const W = ideal(ring("w"), ["w^2 + w + 1"]).quotientRing();   // Q(ω), ω a cube root of 1
const w = W.gens[0];
String(w.pow(3));                    // "1"
String(w.inverse());                 // "−w − 1": ω² = −ω − 1

const C = ideal(ring("x, y"), ["x^2 + y^2 - 1"]).quotientRing();   // functions on the circle
const [x, y] = C.gens;
String(x.pow(2).add(y.pow(2)));      // "1"
C.isFinite;                          // false: infinitely many standard monomials
C.isIntegralDomain();                // true: the circle is irreducible
```

The [algebraic](https://ratmath.com/algebraic/) package has number fields with more machinery (embeddings, Galois groups). Quotient rings here are more general, since the ideal need not be maximal and may have any number of variables.

### The Chinese remainder theorem

Two ideals are comaximal when I+J=R: their solution sets do not meet. Then

R/(I∩J)≅R/I×R/J,I∩J=IJ.
In words: a function on two separate pieces is a function on each, chosen independently. The proof is constructive. Write 1=a+b with a∈I and b∈J; then fb+ga is congruent to f modulo I and to g modulo J. For whole numbers this is the classical theorem about [congruences](https://ratmath.com/structures/modular.html); for points on a line it is Lagrange interpolation.

```js
import { chineseRemainder } from "@ratmath/structures";

const P = ideal(R, ["x - 1"]);
const Q = ideal(R, ["x + 1"]);
const c = chineseRemainder(P, Q);
c.comaximal;                     // true
[String(c.a), String(c.b)];      // ["−(1/2)x + 1/2", "(1/2)x + 1/2"]: a ∈ P, b ∈ Q, a + b = 1
String(c.lift("5", "-3"));       // "4x + 1": the line through (1, 5) and (−1, −3)
String(c.intersection);          // "(x² − 1)"
```

### Try it

```js
// The field Q(√2, √3) as a quotient in two variables
const R = ring("a, b");
const K = ideal(R, ["a^2 - 2", "b^2 - 3"]).quotientRing();
const [a, b] = K.gens;
PRINT(String(K), " dimension:", K.dimension, " basis:", K.basis.map(String).join(", "), " field:", K.isField());
const s = a.add(b);                                // √2 + √3
PRINT("1/(√2 + √3) =", s.inverse());
PRINT("minimal polynomial of √2 + √3, constant first:", s.minimalPolynomial().join(", "));
PRINT("multiplication by √2 + √3 as a matrix:");
for (const row of s.matrix()) PRINT("  ", row.join("  "));

// Not a field: Q[x]/(x³ − x) is three copies of Q, by the Chinese remainder theorem
const S = ring("x");
const T = ideal(S, ["x^3 - x"]).quotientRing();
const x = T.gens[0];
PRINT("x is a zero divisor:", x.isZeroDivisor(), "  x² − 1 too:", x.pow(2).sub(1).isZeroDivisor(), "  x + 2 is a unit:", x.add(2).isUnit());
PRINT("1/(x + 2) =", x.add(2).inverse());
// idempotents pick out the three points
const e0 = T.of("1 - x^2"), e1 = T.of("(x^2 + x)/2"), e2 = T.of("(x^2 - x)/2");
[e0, e1, e2].map((e) => e.mul(e).equals(e) && !e.isZero())
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/modular.html

Rings of numbers

## The integers mod n

Clock arithmetic, taken seriously. The ring Z/n is small enough to list and rich enough to show units, zero divisors, ideals and the Chinese remainder theorem in action.

### The ring Z/n

Two whole numbers are congruent modulo n when they differ by a multiple of n. The n congruence classes 0,1,…,n−1 can be added and multiplied, and form the ring Z/n. It is the [quotient](https://ratmath.com/structures/quotients.html) of Z by the ideal of multiples of n, and the first example of nearly every idea in ring theory.

```js
import { Zn } from "@ratmath/structures";

const Z = Zn(12);
Z.add(7, 8);          // 3n
Z.mul(5, 7);          // 11n
Z.pow(7, 100);        // 1n
Z.inverse(5);         // 5n, because 5·5 = 25 = 1
Z.isUnit(4);          // false
```

Elements are BigInts in the range 0 to n − 1, so the modulus can be as large as you like. Numbers and BigInts are both accepted.

### Units and zero divisors

Every nonzero class is one or the other:

a is a unit in Z/n⟺gcd(a,n)=1,otherwise a⋅gcd(a,n)n​=0.
The inverse comes from the extended Euclidean algorithm: if sa+tn=1 then s is the inverse of a. The number of units is Euler's φ(n). So Z/n is a field exactly when n is prime, and for composite n it is not even an integral domain.

Two more kinds of element are worth finding.

- Nilpotents, with some power equal to 0: the multiples of the product of the distinct primes dividing n. There are none except 0 exactly when n is square-free.

- Idempotents, with e2=e: there are 2k of them when n has k distinct prime factors, and they are the key to the next section.

```js
Z.units();            // [1n, 5n, 7n, 11n]
Z.zeroDivisors();     // [2n, 3n, 4n, 6n, 8n, 9n, 10n]
Z.nilpotents();       // [0n, 6n]
Z.idempotents();      // [0n, 1n, 4n, 9n]
Zn(7).isField;        // true
Zn(30).isReduced;     // true: 30 is square-free, so no nilpotents
```

### The Chinese remainder theorem

If m and n have no common factor, a number modulo mn is the same thing as a pair: a number modulo m and a number modulo n.

Z/mn≅Z/m×Z/n(gcd(m,n)=1).
Splitting n into prime powers, Z/n is a product of rings Z/pk, and everything about Z/n can be read off one prime at a time. The idempotents are the elements that are 0 or 1 in each factor.

```js
import { crt } from "@ratmath/structures";

crt([2, 3, 2], [3, 5, 7]);     // { value: 23n, modulus: 105n }: Sunzi's problem
crt([1, 3], [4, 6]);           // { value: 9n, modulus: 12n }: moduli need not be coprime
crt([1, 2], [4, 6]);           // null: odd and even at once

const d = Zn(60).decompose();
d.moduli;                      // [4n, 3n, 5n]
d.to(47);                      // [3n, 2n, 2n]
d.from([3, 2, 2]);             // 47n
d.idempotents;                 // [45n, 40n, 36n]: 45 is 1 mod 4 and 0 mod 3 and 5
```

### Ideals

Every ideal of Z/n is generated by a divisor d of n, and the quotient by it is Z/d. The ideal is prime exactly when it is maximal, exactly when d is prime.

```js
Zn(12).ideals().map((I) => `(${I.generator}) of size ${I.size}, quotient ${I.quotient}${I.isMaximal ? ", maximal" : ""}`);
// ["(1) of size 12, quotient Z/1", "(2) of size 6, quotient Z/2, maximal", "(3) of size 4, quotient Z/3, maximal",
//  "(4) of size 3, quotient Z/4", "(6) of size 2, quotient Z/6", "(0) of size 1, quotient Z/12"]
```

### The group of units

The units form a group under multiplication, of order φ(n). By the Chinese remainder theorem it is the product of the unit groups of the prime-power factors, and those are known: cyclic for an odd prime power, and for 2k with k≥3 the product of a group of order 2 and a cyclic group of order 2k−2. So the unit group is cyclic, with a single generator called a primitive root, exactly when n is 1, 2, 4, pk or 2pk for an odd prime p.

```js
Zn(7).primitiveRoot();       // 3n: the powers of 3 are 3, 2, 6, 4, 5, 1
Zn(7).orderOf(2);            // 3n
Zn(9).unitGroup().text;      // "C6"
Zn(8).unitGroup().text;      // "C2 × C2"
Zn(8).primitiveRoot();       // null
Zn(15).unitGroup().text;     // "C2 × C4"
Zn(24).unitGroup().text;     // "C2 × C2 × C2": every unit squares to 1
```

For a prime modulus, `Zn(p).asField()` gives the field for use as polynomial coefficients. The [number theory](https://ratmath.com/numtheory/) package goes further with congruences: quadratic residues, discrete logarithms, and the like.

### Try it

```js
// Everything about Z/60, one prime power at a time
const Z = Zn(60);
const d = Z.decompose();
PRINT(String(Z), "splits as", d.moduli.map((m) => `Z/${m}`).join(" × "));
PRINT("units:", String(Z.unitCount), " group:", Z.unitGroup().text);
PRINT("idempotents:", Z.idempotents().join(", "));
PRINT("each as (mod 4, mod 3, mod 5):", Z.idempotents().map((e) => `${e} → (${d.to(e).join(",")})`).join("   "));
PRINT("nilpotents:", Z.nilpotents().join(", "));

// Fast arithmetic by remainders: multiply two big numbers modulo small primes, then recombine
const primes = [10007, 10009, 10037, 10039, 10061];
const a = 123456789n, b = 987654321n;
const residues = primes.map((p) => Zn(p).mul(a, b));
const back = crt(residues, primes);
PRINT("a·b from its remainders:", String(back.value), " correct:", back.value === a * b);

// Which moduli up to 30 have a primitive root?
Array.from({ length: 29 }, (_, i) => i + 2).filter((n) => Zn(n).primitiveRoot() !== null).join(" ")
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/quadratic.html

Rings of numbers

## Quadratic integer rings

Adjoin a square root to the whole numbers and arithmetic changes. Sometimes primes still factor uniquely; sometimes 6 factors in two different ways. Ideals repair the damage, and the class group measures it.

### The rings

Let d be a square-free whole number other than 1. The quadratic integers for d are the numbers a+bω with a,b whole numbers, where

ω=d​  if d≡2,3(mod4),ω=21+d​​  if d≡1(mod4).
(The halves are allowed in the second case because ω then satisfies ω2−ω+41−d​=0, with whole-number coefficients.) They form a ring, the ring of integers of the field Q(d​). For d=−1 it is the Gaussian integers Z[i], and for d=−3 the Eisenstein integers.

The conjugate of x+yd​ is x−yd​, and the norm is the product of the two, a whole number:

N(x+yd​)=x2−dy2,N(αβ)=N(α)N(β).

```js
import { quadraticRing, gaussianIntegers } from "@ratmath/structures";

const K = quadraticRing(-5);
String(K);                       // "Z[√−5]"
const a = K.sqrt(1, 1);          // 1 + √−5
String(a.mul(a));                // "−4 + 2√−5"
a.norm();                        // 6n
String(a.conj());                // "1 − √−5"
String(quadraticRing(5).omega);  // "(1 + √5)/2": the golden ratio
```

### Units

An element is a unit exactly when its norm is ±1. For d there are only finitely many: ±1, except the four powers of i when d=−1 and the six sixth roots of unity when d=−3. For d>0 there are infinitely many, all of the form ±εk for one fundamental unit ε>1. Finding it is solving Pell's equation x2−dy2=±1 (or ±4), and the continued fraction of d​ does it. The fundamental unit can be surprisingly large.

```js
String(quadraticRing(2).fundamentalUnit);     // "1 + √2", norm −1
String(quadraticRing(7).fundamentalUnit);     // "8 + 3√7":  8² − 7·3² = 1
String(quadraticRing(61).fundamentalUnit);    // "(39 + 5√61)/2"
String(quadraticRing(94).fundamentalUnit);    // "2143295 + 221064√94"
gaussianIntegers().units.list.map(String);    // ["1", "i", "−1", "−i"]
```

### Division with remainder

In the Gaussian integers one can divide with a remainder of smaller norm: compute the exact quotient in Q(i) and round both coordinates. So Euclid's algorithm works, greatest common divisors exist, and factorisation into primes is unique, exactly as for whole numbers. The same holds in a handful of other rings (for example d=−2,−3,−7,−11,2,3,5,13), called norm-Euclidean.

```js
const G = gaussianIntegers();
const { quotient, remainder } = G.divmod(G.of(27, 23), G.of(8, 1));
[String(quotient), String(remainder)];        // ["4 + 2i", "−3 + 3i"]: norm 18 is less than 65
String(G.gcd(G.of(11, 3), G.of(1, 8)).gcd);   // "2 + i"

const f = G.factor(2210);
f.factors.map(({ prime, exponent }) => `${prime}${exponent > 1 ? "^" + exponent : ""}`);
      // ["1 + i^2", "2 − i", "2 + i", "3 + 2i", "3 − 2i", "4 − i", "4 + i"]: 2210 = 2·5·13·17
```

A whole-number prime p behaves in one of three ways in the ring. It can stay prime (inert), become a product of two different primes (split), or become the square of a prime, up to a unit (ramified). In Z[i]: 2 ramifies, primes p≡1(mod4) split (that is Fermat's theorem that such a prime is a sum of two squares), and primes p≡3(mod4) are inert.

### When unique factorisation fails

An element is irreducible when it is not a product of two non-units. It is prime when it cannot divide a product without dividing a factor. For whole numbers these are the same thing. In Z[−5​] they are not:

6=2⋅3=(1+−5​)(1−−5​).
All four factors are irreducible, since their norms are 4, 9, 6, 6 and no element has norm 2 or 3 (x2+5y2 never equals 2 or 3). But none is prime: 2 divides the product on the right without dividing either factor. So 6 has two genuinely different factorisations.

```js
K.factorizations(6).map((f) => f.factors.map(String));
      // [["2", "3"], ["1 + √−5", "1 − √−5"]]
K.isIrreducible(2);              // true
K.isPrimeElement(2);             // false
K.elementsOfNorm(2);             // []
K.isUFD;                         // false
```

### Ideals put it right

Kummer and Dedekind's repair: factor ideals, not elements. In these rings every nonzero ideal is a product of prime ideals in exactly one way. The two factorisations of 6 are two ways of grouping the same four prime ideals:

⟨2⟩=p2,⟨3⟩=qqˉ​,⟨1+−5​⟩=pq,⟨1−−5​⟩=pqˉ​,
with p=⟨2,1+−5​⟩ and q=⟨3,1+−5​⟩. None of p,q,qˉ​ is generated by a single element, which is why they were invisible among the numbers.

```js
const p = K.ideal(2, a);                 // (2, 1 + √−5)
const q = K.ideal(3, a);
p.norm;                                  // 2n: the quotient by p has 2 elements
p.isPrime();                             // true
p.isPrincipal();                         // false
String(p.mul(p));                        // "(2)"
String(p.mul(q));                        // "(1 + √−5)"
String(p.mul(q).generator());            // "1 + √−5"
K.ideal(6).factor().map(({ prime, exponent }) => `${prime}^${exponent}`);
      // ["(2, 1 + √−5)^2", "(3, 2 + √−5)^1", "(3, 1 + √−5)^1"]
K.splitting(7).kind;                     // "split"
```

### The class group

How badly does unique factorisation fail? Call two ideals equivalent when one is the other multiplied by a number of the field. The classes form a finite abelian group under multiplication, the class group, and its size h is the class number. The principal ideals are the identity class, so

h=1⟺every ideal is principal⟺factorisation of elements is unique.
The class group is computable because every class contains an ideal of norm at most the Minkowski bound (π2​∣D∣​ for an imaginary ring and 21​D​ for a real one, where D is the discriminant). So it is enough to look at the primes above the small whole-number primes and work out which products are principal.

```js
K.classNumber();                              // 2
p.isEquivalentTo(q);                          // true: both are in the one non-principal class
quadraticRing(-23).classGroup().text;         // "C3"
quadraticRing(-65).classGroup().text;         // "C2 × C4"
quadraticRing(10).classNumber();              // 2: 6 = 2·3 = (4 + √10)(4 − √10)
[-1, -2, -3, -7, -11, -19, -43, -67, -163].map((d) => quadraticRing(d).classNumber());
      // all 1, and by the Baker–Heegner–Stark theorem no other negative d has class number 1
quadraticRing(-19).isPID;                     // true, although
quadraticRing(-19).isNormEuclidean;           // false
```

Class groups are found by listing ideals up to the Minkowski bound and testing which are principal, which suits discriminants up to a few thousand. Whether there are infinitely many real quadratic rings of class number 1 is an open problem.

### Try it

```js
// Sums of two squares: a prime p is x² + y² exactly when it splits in Z[i]
const G = gaussianIntegers();
for (const p of [5, 13, 29, 97, 1009]) {
  const { factors } = G.factor(p);
  const z = factors[0].prime;
  PRINT(`${p} = (${z})(${z.conj()}) = ${z.a}² + ${z.b < 0n ? -z.b : z.b}²`);
}
PRINT("7 stays prime:", G.isIrreducible(7), "  2 ramifies:", G.splitting(2).kind);

// Class numbers of Z[√d] and friends for small negative d
const hs = [];
for (let d = -1; d >= -30; d -= 1) {
  let squarefree = true;
  for (let k = 2; k * k <= -d; k += 1) if (d % (k * k) === 0) squarefree = false;
  if (squarefree) hs.push(`${d}: ${quadraticRing(d).classNumber()}`);
}
PRINT("class numbers:", hs.join("   "));

// A number with five factorisations in Z[√−5]
const K = quadraticRing(-5);
const ways = K.factorizations(18);
for (const f of ways) PRINT("18 =", (String(f.unit) === "1" ? "" : `(${f.unit})·`) + f.factors.map((q) => `(${q})`).join("·"));
PRINT("but one factorisation into prime ideals:", K.ideal(18).factor().map(({ prime, exponent }) => `${prime}^${exponent}`).join(" · "));

// Pell's equation x² − 61y² = 1 (Fermat's challenge): square the fundamental unit until the norm is 1 and the halves go
const P = quadraticRing(61);
let u = P.fundamentalUnit;
PRINT("fundamental unit:", u, " norm", String(u.norm()));
u = u.pow(6);
String(u)
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/towers.html

Fields

## Field extensions and towers

Adjoin 2​ to the rationals, then a cube root of that. The result is a field of degree 6 in which every element is an exact combination of six basis elements, and every question about it (inverses, minimal polynomials, which polynomials split) has an exact answer.

### Adjoining a root

If f is irreducible over a field k, the quotient k[x]/(f) is a field containing k in which the class of x is a root of f. It is written k(a) with f(a)=0. As a vector space over k it has basis 1,a,…,an−1 where n=degf; this dimension is the degree [k(a):k]. Repeating the step gives a tower:

Q⊂Q(a)⊂Q(a,b)⊂⋯
`extension` takes the defining polynomials in order. Each may use the generators before it, and each is checked to be irreducible over the field built so far (a step that fails says so and shows the factors).

```js
import { extension } from "@ratmath/structures";

const K = extension({ a: "a^2 - 2", b: "b^3 - a" });
K.degree;                       // 6
K.towerLaw();                   // "[Q(a, b) : Q] = [Q(a, b) : Q(a)]·[Q(a) : Q] = 3·2 = 6"
K.basis.map(String);            // ["1", "b", "b²", "a", "ab", "ab²"]

const x = K.a.add(K.b);         // generators are K.a and K.b; K.of("a b + 1/2") reads text
x.mul(x.inverse()).toString();  // "1"
K.b.pow(3).equals(K.a);         // true
```

### The tower law

If k⊂F⊂K then [K:k]=[K:F][F:k]: products of a basis of F over k with a basis of K over F form a basis of K over k. That is exactly the basis `K.basis` lists. One consequence does a great deal of work on the [ruler and compass](https://ratmath.com/structures/constructions.html) page: the degree of any element of K divides [K:Q], so a field reached by square roots alone, of degree 2m, cannot contain a root of an irreducible cubic.

### Minimal polynomials

Every element x of K satisfies a unique monic irreducible polynomial over Q, its minimal polynomial; its degree is [Q(x):Q]. It is found by linear algebra: write 1,x,x2,… in the basis and stop at the first power that depends on the earlier ones. The same works over any level of the tower. The norm and trace are the determinant and trace of multiplication by x.

```js
x.minimalPolynomialText();      // "x⁶ − 6x⁴ − 18": degree 6, so Q(a + b) is all of K
K.a.degree;                     // 2
K.b.minimalPolynomialText();    // "x⁶ − 2": b is a sixth root of 2
K.b.minimalPolynomialOver(1).map(String);   // ["−a", "0", "0", "1"]: x³ − a over Q(a)
K.b.norm().toString();          // "-2"
x.approx();                     // 2.5366…, under the embedding with the largest real roots
```

### Primitive elements

The primitive element theorem says a finite extension of Q is always generated by one element: Q(a,b)=Q(θ) for a suitable θ, usually a+b or a+2b. `primitiveElement()` finds one, with its minimal polynomial and each generator written in terms of it. Internally the whole tower is carried on such a θ, by the number fields of [@ratmath/algebraic](https://ratmath.com/algebraic/), with exact changes of basis between the two descriptions.

```js
const L = extension({ a: "a^2 - 2", b: "b^2 - 3" });
const p = L.primitiveElement();
String(p.element);              // "a + b"
p.text;                         // "x⁴ − 10x² + 1"
p.expressions;                  // { a: "(1/2)θ³ − (9/2)θ", b: "−(1/2)θ³ + (11/2)θ" }
```

### Roots and factors over the field

A polynomial irreducible over Q may factor over a bigger field. `factor` factors over K (by Trager's method: take a norm down to Q, factor there, and take gcds back up), and `roots` lists the roots that lie in K.

```js
L.roots("x^2 - 6").map((r) => String(r.value));     // ["ab", "−ab"]: √6 = √2·√3
L.factor("x^4 - 10x^2 + 1").map((f) => f.text);     // four linear factors: L is the splitting field
L.factor("x^4 - 2").map((f) => f.text);             // ["x² + a", "x² − a"]
L.subfield(L.a.mul(L.b));                            // { degree: 2, text: "x² − 6", isWhole: false }
```

Automorphisms, fixed fields and the Galois correspondence are on the [next page](https://ratmath.com/structures/galois.html). Towers work comfortably up to degree 8 or so; degree 16 is slow.

### Try it

```js
// Q(√2, ∛√2): a tower of degree 2·3
const K = extension({ a: "a^2 - 2", b: "b^3 - a" });
PRINT(K.describe());
PRINT(K.towerLaw());
PRINT("basis:", K.basis.map(String).join(", "));

// arithmetic and minimal polynomials
const x = K.a.add(K.b);
PRINT("x = a + b,  1/x =", x.inverse());
PRINT("minimal polynomial of x:", x.minimalPolynomialText(), "  degree", x.degree);
PRINT("x ≈", x.approx(), "  norm", x.norm(), "  trace", x.trace());

// every element's degree divides 6
for (const t of ["a", "b", "b^2", "a b", "a + b^2", "b^3 + 1"]) {
  const y = K.of(t);
  PRINT(`  ${y}: degree ${y.degree}, minimal polynomial ${y.minimalPolynomialText()}`);
}

// √2 and √3 together: a primitive element and what splits
const L = extension({ a: "a^2 - 2", b: "b^2 - 3" });
const p = L.primitiveElement();
PRINT("Q(√2, √3) = Q(θ) with θ =", p.element, "a root of", p.text);
PRINT("√6 in the field:", L.roots("x^2 - 6").map((r) => String(r.value)));
PRINT("x⁴ − 2 over it:", L.factor("x^4 - 2").map((f) => f.text));
L.factor("x^4 - 10x^2 + 1").map((f) => f.text)
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/galois.html

Fields

## Automorphisms and the Galois correspondence

The symmetries of a field extension form a group, and when the extension has as many symmetries as its degree allows, the subgroups of that group match the fields in between, one for one and upside down. Here both sides are computed and laid next to each other.

### Automorphisms

An automorphism of K is a bijection σ:K→K respecting sums and products. It must fix every rational number, and it must send a root of a rational polynomial to a root of the same polynomial, because f(σ(x))=σ(f(x))=0. So an automorphism of Q(θ) is determined by where it sends θ, and the choices are exactly the roots of the minimal polynomial of θ that lie in the field. That is how they are found: the tower is rewritten on a primitive element, its minimal polynomial is factored over the field itself, and each linear factor is an automorphism.

```js
import { extension, identify } from "@ratmath/structures";

const L = extension({ a: "a^2 - 2", b: "b^2 - 3" });
L.automorphisms().map(String);
// ["a ↦ a, b ↦ b", "a ↦ −a, b ↦ −b", "a ↦ a, b ↦ −b", "a ↦ −a, b ↦ b"]

const s = L.automorphisms()[2];
String(s.apply(L.of("a + b + a b")));   // "−ab + a − b"
```

### Galois extensions

There are never more automorphisms than the degree. When there are exactly [K:Q] of them the extension is Galois, and the group of automorphisms is its Galois group Gal(K/Q). Equivalently, K is the splitting field of a polynomial: it is generated by all the roots of something. The field Q(32​) is not Galois, since the other two cube roots of 2 are not real and so not in it; adjoining a cube root of unity w repairs that.

```js
extension({ c: "c^3 - 2" }).isGalois;                  // false: only the identity
const S = extension({ c: "c^3 - 2", w: "w^2 + w + 1" });
S.isGalois;                                            // true
identify(S.galoisGroup()).name;                        // "S3"
```

`galoisGroup()` returns an ordinary finite group of the library, whose elements are the automorphisms, so its subgroups, classes and quotients are all available.

### The correspondence

For a subgroup H of the Galois group, the elements of K fixed by everything in H form a field KH. For a field F between Q and K, the automorphisms fixing F pointwise form a subgroup. The fundamental theorem of Galois theory says that for a Galois extension these two maps are inverse to each other, and:

- bigger subgroups fix smaller fields, with [KH:Q]=[G:H];

- KH is itself Galois over Q exactly when H is a normal subgroup, and then its Galois group is G/H.

A fixed field is a null space: σ(x)=x is a set of linear equations on the coordinates of x. `fixedField` solves them, then looks for a single generator, trying sums and products of the conjugates of basis elements first so that the answer is recognisable.

```js
const G = S.galoisGroup();
for (const H of [...G.subgroups()].sort((x, y) => x.order - y.order)) {
  const F = S.fixedField([...H.elements]);
  console.log(H.order, G.isNormal(H), F.degree, String(F.generator), F.text);
}
// 1 true  6 "c + w"   x⁶ + 3x⁵ + 6x⁴ + 3x³ + 9x + 9
// 2 false 3 "cw + c"  x³ + 2
// 2 false 3 "−cw"     x³ + 2
// 2 false 3 "c"       x³ − 2
// 3 true  2 "w"       x² + x + 1
// 6 true  1 "1"       x − 1
```

The three subgroups of order 2 are conjugate and not normal, and they fix the three cubic fields Q(c), Q(cw), Q(cw2), none of which is Galois. The normal subgroup of order 3 fixes Q(w), which is.

### Galois groups of polynomials

The Galois group of a polynomial is the Galois group of its splitting field, acting on the roots. Building the splitting field as a tower is one way to get it, but its degree can be as large as n!. For a polynomial of degree up to 7 the group is found far faster from the roots themselves, by [@ratmath/algebraic](https://ratmath.com/algebraic/); that is what [solving by radicals](https://ratmath.com/structures/radicals.html) starts from.

### Try it

```js
// The splitting field of x³ − 2 and its lattice of subfields
const S = extension({ c: "c^3 - 2", w: "w^2 + w + 1" });
PRINT(S.describe(), " Galois:", S.isGalois);
const G = S.galoisGroup();
PRINT("Galois group:", identify(G).name);
for (const s of S.automorphisms()) PRINT("  ", String(s));

PRINT("subgroup order | normal | fixed field");
for (const H of [...G.subgroups()].sort((x, y) => x.order - y.order)) {
  const F = S.fixedField([...H.elements]);
  PRINT(`  ${H.order} | ${G.isNormal(H)} | degree ${F.degree}, generated by ${F.generator} with ${F.text} = 0`);
}

// the fifth roots of unity: a cyclic group of order 4, and √5 inside
const C = extension({ z: "z^4 + z^3 + z^2 + z + 1" });
const s = C.automorphisms().find((t) => t.apply(C.z).equals(C.z.pow(4)));   // complex conjugation, z ↦ z⁴
PRINT("the field fixed by z ↦ z⁴ is generated by a root of", C.fixedField([s]).text, "and so is Q(√5)");
C.roots("x^2 - 5").map((r) => String(r.value))
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/radicals.html

Fields

## Solving by radicals

The quadratic formula has cousins for cubics and quartics, and none for the general quintic. Galois explained why: a polynomial has a formula in radicals exactly when its Galois group is solvable. This page decides the question for a given polynomial and, when the answer is yes, writes the roots out, then checks each formula against the root it claims to be.

### The theorem

A number is expressible by radicals if it can be reached from the rationals by the four operations and taking n-th roots. A group G is solvable if it has a chain of subgroups

G=G0​⊳G1​⊳⋯⊳Gm​=1
with each Gi+1​ normal in Gi​ and each index [Gi​:Gi+1​] a prime. Galois's theorem: the roots of an irreducible f are expressible by radicals if and only if the Galois group of f is solvable. Every group of order below 60 is solvable, and so are all subgroups of S4​, which is why degrees up to 4 always have formulas. A5​ and S5​ are not, and most quintics have one of those two as their group.

```js
import { solveByRadicals } from "@ratmath/structures";

const r = solveByRadicals("x^5 - x - 1");
r.solvable;               // false
r.factors[0].group;       // "S5"
r.reason;                 // "the Galois group S5 of x⁵ − x − 1, of order 120, is not solvable: …"

const q = solveByRadicals("x^5 - 5x + 12");
q.factors[0].group;       // "D5", of order 10
q.factors[0].chain;       // [2, 5]: a square root, then a fifth root
```

### One step: Lagrange resolvents

The chain turns into a tower of fields by the [Galois correspondence](https://ratmath.com/structures/galois.html), each step of prime degree p with a cyclic group generated by some σ. Let ω be a primitive p-th root of unity. For x in the upper field, the Lagrange resolvents are

rj​=k=0∑p−1​ωjkσk(x),j=0,…,p−1.
Applying σ multiplies rj​ by ω−j, so rjp​ is unchanged by σ: it lies in the lower field (with ω adjoined). Hence each rj​ is a p-th root of something already known, and x is recovered from them:

x=p1​(r0​+r1​+⋯+rp−1​).
For p=2 this is the quadratic formula, and for a cubic it is Cardano's. Climbing the tower one prime at a time expresses the roots of f by nested radicals.

### How the formulas are made exact

The work is carried out on the roots themselves. Every quantity in the tower is held as its full set of conjugates, each a small box in the complex plane known to hold the true value, with the Galois group permuting them. Arithmetic on boxes can never prove that two things are equal; what makes the results exact is algebra: a quantity fixed by the whole group is rational, its denominator is bounded in advance, and a box containing a single fraction with such a denominator identifies it. Zero is recognised the same way, through norms. So the integers appearing under the radicals are proved, not rounded.

Which of the p possible p-th roots is meant matters. A radical nz​ here always means the real root when z is real and one exists (positive for even n), and otherwise the principal root, the one with the smallest angle. Where the resolvent is a different root, the needed root of unity is written in.

```js
const { roots } = solveByRadicals("x^3 + x + 1").factors[0];
const e = roots[0].expression;
e.inline();               // "(−∛(108 + 12·√93) − ∛(108 − 12·√93))/6"
e.toTeX();                // the same for typesetting
e.approx();               // −0.6823278038280193
e.check(50);              // { agrees: true, digits: 50 }: recomputed from the formula alone
e.indices;                // [2, 3]: square and cube roots
```

Long answers are given in steps: `text` uses names r1​,r2​,… and `definitions` says what each is. `check(digits)` evaluates the formula from the inside out with certified complex arithmetic and compares with the root located independently, so a wrong branch anywhere would show.

### Solvable quintics

An irreducible quintic is solvable exactly when its group is C5​, D5​ or the Frobenius group F20​. All three occur:

- x5−2 has group F20​ and roots ζk52​;

- x5−5x+12 has group D5​; its real root needs 5​, a square root of −10−25​ and four fifth roots;

- x5+x4−4x3−3x2+3x+1, whose roots are 2cos(2πk/11), has group C5​.

Irreducible factors up to degree 7 are handled; x7−7x+3 has the simple group of order 168 and no formula.

### Roots of unity

The cyclotomic polynomials have abelian Galois groups, so every root of unity is expressible by radicals: a real surprise for ζ7​ or ζ11​, and Gauss's first great discovery for ζ17​, where square roots suffice. `rootOfUnityByRadicals(n)` gives e2πi/n. The formulas above use ζ3​ and ζ5​ written out, and name larger ones.

```js
import { rootOfUnityByRadicals } from "@ratmath/structures";
rootOfUnityByRadicals(5).inline();    // "(−1 + √5 + √(−10 − 2·√5))/4"
rootOfUnityByRadicals(12).inline();   // "(i + √3)/2"
rootOfUnityByRadicals(7).text;        // "ζ₇", with definitions r₁ = ∛(28 − 84·i·√3), …
```

### Try it

```js
// Decide solvability and print formulas, each checked to 40 digits
for (const f of ["x^3 + x + 1", "x^4 - 4x + 2", "x^5 - 2", "x^5 - x - 1", "x^5 + 20x + 16"]) {
  const r = solveByRadicals(f);
  const g = r.factors[0];
  PRINT(`${r.text}: Galois group ${g.group} of order ${g.order}, ${r.solvable ? "solvable in steps " + g.chain.join(", ") : "NOT solvable"}`);
  if (!r.solvable) continue;
  const e = g.roots[0].expression;
  PRINT("   a root:", e.inline({ maxLength: 200 }) ?? e.text);
  PRINT("   ≈", e.approx(), "  checked:", g.roots.every((x) => x.expression.check(40).agrees));
}

// A dihedral quintic, step by step
const q = solveByRadicals("x^5 - 5x + 12").factors[0];
const e = q.roots[0].expression;
PRINT("x⁵ − 5x + 12, group", q.group, ": real root =", e.text, "where");
for (const d of e.definitions) PRINT("   ", d.text);
PRINT("   value", e.evaluate(30).re, "  check", e.check(60));

// cos(2π/7) needs a cube root of a complex number: the casus irreducibilis
const z = rootOfUnityByRadicals(7);
for (const d of z.definitions) PRINT(d.text);
z.check(50)
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/constructions.html

Fields

## Ruler and compass

For two thousand years nobody could double a cube, trisect an angle or draw a regular heptagon with ruler and compass. Field theory shows why in a few lines: a constructible length lives in a tower of square roots, so its degree is a power of 2. The same theory says exactly which regular polygons can be drawn, and writes the square roots down.

### Constructible numbers

Start with two points a unit apart. A ruler draws the line through two known points, a compass the circle about one known point through another, and new points appear where lines and circles cross. A real number is constructible if a segment of that length can be reached. Sums, differences, products and quotients of constructible numbers are constructible (by similar triangles), and so is the square root of one (by a semicircle). Conversely, intersecting lines and circles only ever solves linear and quadratic equations. So:

x is constructible exactly when it lies in a field Km​ at the top of a tower Q=K0​⊂K1​⊂⋯⊂Km​ with every step of degree 2.

By the [tower law](https://ratmath.com/structures/towers.html) such a number has degree 2k over Q. That necessary condition already settles the classical problems. It is not quite sufficient: a root of x4+x+1 has degree 4, but there is no field of degree 2 below it. The complete criterion, used by `constructible`, is that the splitting field has degree a power of 2, that is, the Galois group is a 2-group.

```js
import { constructible } from "@ratmath/structures";

constructible("x^4 - 2").constructible;       // true: group D4 of order 8
constructible("x^3 - 2").constructible;       // false: degree 3
constructible("x^4 + x + 1").constructible;   // false: degree 4, but the group is S4 of order 24
constructible("x^4 + x + 1").reason;          // says so in words
```

When the answer is yes, each root comes with an expression in square roots alone, from [solving by radicals](https://ratmath.com/structures/radicals.html).

### The three classical problems

- Doubling the cube asks for 32​, a root of the irreducible x3−2: degree 3, impossible.

- Trisecting an angle θ asks for cos(θ/3) given c=cosθ. The triple-angle formula cosθ=4cos3(θ/3)−3cos(θ/3) makes it a root of 4x3−3x−c. For θ=60° that is 8x3−6x−1, irreducible, so the 60° angle cannot be trisected and there is no general method. Some angles can: for θ=90° the cubic factors.

- Squaring the circle asks for π​. Constructible numbers are algebraic and π is not (Lindemann, 1882). This one is quoted, not computed.

```js
import { classicalProblems } from "@ratmath/structures";

classicalProblems.doublingTheCube().possible;     // false
classicalProblems.trisecting("1/2").reason;       // "8x³ − 6x − 1 is irreducible, so cos(θ/3) has degree 3 over Q, …"
classicalProblems.trisecting("0").possible;       // true: a right angle can be trisected
classicalProblems.squaringTheCircle().reason;
```

### Regular polygons

Drawing a regular n-gon means constructing cos(2π/n), which generates a field of degree φ(n)/2 inside the cyclotomic field. That field is Galois with an abelian group, so the degree test is the whole story. Gauss (sufficiency, 1796) and Wantzel (necessity, 1837):

The regular n-gon is constructible exactly when φ(n) is a power of 2, that is, when n is a power of 2 times a product of distinct Fermat primes 3,5,17,257,65537.

So the 7-gon, 9-gon, 11-gon and 13-gon are impossible, and the 17-gon is possible, which Gauss found at nineteen. For a Fermat prime p the Galois group of the p-th roots of unity is cyclic of order p−1=2m. Halving the group m times splits the roots into sums called Gaussian periods; each period satisfies a quadratic whose coefficients are periods from the level before. `regularPolygon` follows that chain and then combines prime factors by the addition formula for cosines and powers of 2 by the half-angle formula.

```js
import { regularPolygon } from "@ratmath/structures";

const p = regularPolygon(17);
p.constructible;          // true
p.cos.inline();           // "(−1 + √17 + √(34 − 2·√17) + 2·√(17 + 3·√17 − √(170 + 38·√17)))/16"
p.cos.usesOnlySquareRoots; // true
p.cos.check(50);          // { agrees: true, digits: 50 }

regularPolygon(7).reason; // "φ(7) = 6 is not a power of 2, so cos(2π/7) has degree 3 over Q …"
regularPolygon(257).cos.size;   // 66: the 257-gon takes 66 square roots
```

The formula for 17 is Gauss's own, up to the order of the terms. The 65537-gon is constructible too, but its formula is left to the patient.

`constructiblePolygon(n)` is another name for `regularPolygon(n)`. The theorem also reaches `constructible`: when a factor has degree 8 or more (beyond the Galois groups computed directly) but is, coefficient for coefficient, the minimal polynomial of cos(2π/n) or of 2cos(2π/n) from algebraic's `cosMinimal`, its splitting field is Q(cos2π/n), abelian of degree φ(n)/2, and the answer is decided. Only the finitely many n with φ(n)=2deg can match. Any other polynomial of such a degree is still left undecided.

```js
import { cosMinimal } from "@ratmath/algebraic";
constructible(cosMinimal(17)).constructible;   // true: it is the minimal polynomial of cos(2π/17)
constructible("x^8 - 2").constructible;        // null: degree 8, not a cosine, left undecided
```

### Try it

```js
// Which regular polygons up to 30 sides can be constructed?
const yes = [], no = [];
for (let n = 3; n <= 30; n++) (regularPolygon(n).constructible ? yes : no).push(n);
PRINT("constructible:", yes.join(", "));
PRINT("not:", no.join(", "));

// Gauss's heptadecagon
const p = regularPolygon(17);
PRINT("cos(2π/17) =", p.cos.inline());
PRINT("  =", p.cos.evaluate(40).re, "  agrees with the cosine to 60 digits:", p.cos.check(60).agrees);

// Smaller cases
for (const n of [5, 8, 12, 15, 16, 20, 24]) PRINT(`cos(2π/${n}) =`, regularPolygon(n).cos.inline());

// The classical problems
for (const q of [classicalProblems.doublingTheCube(), classicalProblems.trisecting("1/2"), classicalProblems.trisecting("0"), classicalProblems.squaringTheCircle()])
  PRINT(q.possible ? "possible:  " : "impossible:", q.problem, "—", q.reason);

// Degree a power of 2 is not enough
const c = constructible("x^4 + x + 1");
PRINT(c.reason);

// Degree 8: decided by Gauss–Wantzel once it is recognised as cos(2π/17)'s minimal polynomial
PRINT(constructible(cosMinimal(17)).reason);
regularPolygon(257).cos.size + " square roots in the formula for the 257-gon"
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/conway.html

Fields

## Conway polynomials

There is one field with pn elements, but many ways to write it down, one for each irreducible polynomial of degree n mod p. Conway polynomials are an agreed choice, made so that the fields for different n fit inside one another in a fixed way. Computer algebra systems share tables of them; here they are computed from the definition.

### The problem they solve

GF(pn) is built as GF(p)[x]/(f) for an irreducible f of degree n. Two people choosing different f get isomorphic fields, but an element such as x2+1 means different things to each, and there are n isomorphisms to choose from. Worse, GF(pm) sits inside GF(pn) whenever m divides n, and working with several fields at once needs those inclusions to agree with each other.

### The definition

The Conway polynomial Cp,n​ is the monic polynomial of degree n over GF(p) that is

- primitive: its root a generates the multiplicative group, so every non-zero element is a power of a;

- compatible: for every m dividing n, the power a(pn−1)/(pm−1) is a root of Cp,m​;

- first among all such, in a particular order: write f=xn−cn−1​xn−1+cn−2​xn−2−… with alternating signs and compare the words cn−1​cn−2​…c0​, digits 0, as in a dictionary.

Condition 2 is what makes the embeddings fit: the standard generator of the small field is a fixed power of the standard generator of the big one. The alternating signs make Cp,1​=x−g with g the smallest primitive root mod p. The definition is recursive, and nothing shortcuts it: the search walks through candidates in order, testing primitivity (by the prime factors of pn−1) and compatibility. That is quick for the fields one meets in practice and hopeless for large ones, which is why the published tables stop where they do.

```js
import { conwayPolynomial, conwayField } from "@ratmath/structures";

conwayPolynomial(2, 8);          // [1n, 0n, 1n, 1n, 1n, 0n, 0n, 0n, 1n], constant first: x⁸ + x⁴ + x³ + x² + 1
conwayPolynomial(3, 4);          // x⁴ + 2x³ + 2
conwayPolynomial(5, 1);          // x + 3, that is x − 2: 2 is the smallest primitive root mod 5
```

The polynomial for GF(28) is not the one in the AES cipher (x8+x4+x3+x+1, which is irreducible but not primitive). The search reproduces the published values for every case tried in the tests, 23 of them.

### The standard fields

`conwayField(p, n)` is the field built on that polynomial: the same kind of object as `galoisField` gives, plus its standard generator and the embeddings of the subfields.

```js
const F = conwayField(2, 4);     // GF(16) = GF(2)[a]/(a⁴ + a + 1)
F.text;                          // "x⁴ + x + 1"
F.order(F.gen);                  // 15n: a generates the whole multiplicative group

const e = F.embed(2);            // GF(4) inside GF(16)
e.exponent;                      // 5: the generator of GF(4) is a⁵
F.format(e.image);               // "a² + a", a root of x² + x + 1 = C(2,2)
```

Because every non-zero element is a power of a, multiplication can be done by adding exponents, and `F.log` gives the exponent: the discrete logarithm, by table for fields this small.

### Try it

```js
// A small table of Conway polynomials, found by search
const show = (c, p) => c.map((v, i) => [v, i]).filter(([v]) => v).reverse()
  .map(([v, i]) => (i === 0 ? `${v}` : `${v === 1n ? "" : v}x${i > 1 ? "^" + i : ""}`)).join(" + ");
for (const p of [2, 3, 5, 7]) {
  for (let n = 1; n <= (p === 2 ? 8 : 4); n++) PRINT(`C(${p},${n}) =`, show(conwayPolynomial(p, n), p));
}

// GF(64) and its subfields GF(2), GF(4), GF(8): generators are fixed powers of a
const F = conwayField(2, 6);
PRINT("GF(64) on", F.text, " order of a:", F.order(F.gen));
for (const m of [1, 2, 3]) {
  const e = F.embed(m);
  PRINT(`  GF(2^${m}): generator a^${e.exponent} = ${F.format(e.image)}, of order ${F.order(e.image)}`);
}
// compatibility: the image of GF(4)'s generator inside GF(64) is a root of C(2,2) = x² + x + 1
const b = F.embed(2).image;
F.format(F.add(F.add(F.mul(b, b), b), F.one))
```

---

Page: https://ratmath.com/structures/symmetric.html

Symmetry

## Symmetric polynomials

A polynomial that does not change when its variables are shuffled can always be rewritten using just a few building blocks. That is why you can know the sum of the squares of the roots of an equation without solving it.

### The building blocks

A polynomial in x1​,…,xn​ is symmetric when every permutation of the variables leaves it unchanged. The elementary symmetric polynomials are

e1​=i∑​xi​,e2​=i<j∑​xi​xj​,…,en​=x1​x2​⋯xn​,
so ek​ is the sum of all products of k different variables. They are exactly the coefficients that appear when a product of linear factors is multiplied out (Vieta's formulas):

(t−x1​)(t−x2​)⋯(t−xn​)=tn−e1​tn−1+e2​tn−2−⋯+(−1)nen​.
Two other families are the power sums pk​=x1k​+⋯+xnk​ and the complete homogeneous polynomials hk​, the sum of all monomials of degree k.

### The fundamental theorem

Every symmetric polynomial is a polynomial in e1​,…,en​, in exactly one way. The proof is an algorithm, and it is the one the library runs.

Order the monomials [lexicographically](https://ratmath.com/structures/orders.html). Because f is symmetric, its leading monomial x1a1​​⋯xnan​​ has a1​≥a2​≥⋯≥an​ (otherwise a permutation of it would be larger). The product

e1a1​−a2​​e2a2​−a3​​⋯enan​​
has the same leading monomial. Subtract the right multiple of it from f: what is left is symmetric with a smaller leading monomial. Repeat until nothing is left.

For f=x2+y2: the leading monomial is x2, matched by e12​=x2+2xy+y2. The difference is −2xy=−2e2​. So x2+y2=e12​−2e2​.

```js
import { ring, elementary, powerSum, completeHomogeneous, isSymmetric, toElementary } from "@ratmath/structures";

const R = ring("x, y, z");
String(elementary(R, 2));                    // "xy + xz + yz"
String(powerSum(R, 3));                      // "x³ + y³ + z³"
isSymmetric(R.poly("x^2 y + y^2 z + z^2 x")); // false: only cyclic shifts fix it

const { polynomial, ring: E } = toElementary(powerSum(R, 3));
String(polynomial);                          // "e1³ − 3e1·e2 + 3e3"
E.vars;                                      // ["e1", "e2", "e3"]
// substituting the elementary polynomials back recovers the original
polynomial.compose([elementary(R, 1), elementary(R, 2), elementary(R, 3)]).equals(powerSum(R, 3));   // true
```

### Roots without solving

If x1​,…,xn​ are the roots of tn+cn−1​tn−1+⋯+c0​, Vieta's formulas give ek​=(−1)kcn−k​. Any symmetric expression in the roots is then a polynomial in the coefficients. The roots of t3−2t2−5t+6 have e1​=2, e2​=−5, e3​=−6, so the sum of their cubes is e13​−3e1​e2​+3e3​=8+30−18=20. (The roots are 1, −2 and 3, and indeed 1−8+27=20.)

The formulas for power sums are Newton's identities, and the [discriminant](https://ratmath.com/structures/resultants.html) is the symmetric polynomial ∏i​(xi​−xj​)2 written in the coefficients. The same theorem is the starting point of Galois theory: the symmetric functions of the roots are the ones that lie in the base field.

### Try it

```js
const R = ring("x, y, z");
// Newton's identities: power sums in terms of e1, e2, e3
for (let k = 1; k <= 5; k += 1) PRINT(`p${k} =`, toElementary(powerSum(R, k)).polynomial);

// the discriminant of a cubic, from the roots
const disc = toElementary(R.poly("(x - y)^2 (x - z)^2 (y - z)^2")).polynomial;
PRINT("∏(xi − xj)² =", disc);

// sum of the fifth powers of the roots of t³ − 2t² − 5t + 6, without finding them
const p5 = toElementary(powerSum(R, 5)).polynomial;
PRINT("sum of fifth powers of the roots:", p5.at({ e1: 2, e2: -5, e3: -6 }), " (check: 1 − 32 + 243 = 212)");

// complete homogeneous polynomials obey h2 = e1² − e2, h3 = e1³ − 2e1e2 + e3
[2, 3, 4].map((k) => `h${k} = ${toElementary(completeHomogeneous(R, k)).polynomial}`)
```
